## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (11:00 EDT) — HOP CHAINS (3 chains, seeds = #161 A-23, B-1038, B-1040)

### CHAIN 1 — from #161 A-23 "The Mast That Fell" (transmitter base, the unkept log, "The log was not kept.")

1. **The fallen mast → the guyed mast.** A thin vertical mast is held by three guy wires at 120°, outer anchors at 70-80% of the tower's height; the LPFM antenna guide's rule: survey the area so "if the pole ever were to fall, it would not hit a power line." **Fresh angle: THE PLANNED FALL — the fall has a radius; the survey is older than the mast.** (Sources: Wikipedia, "Guy-wire"; wirelessestimator.com, "Guyed Towers"; 2013.prometheusradio.org, Hang 'Em High.)
2. **The planned fall → Rugby Radio Station.** Built 1924-25 for £500,000: twelve 820ft masts over 900 acres, powered up January 1926; first transatlantic radio signal 1927; from 1927 the six pips — the national atomic-clock time signal, accurate to 1/1000s. Demolished 2007: the last four 820ft towers felled with 5kg of explosives per mast — the first attempt stalled 3.5 hours because rabbits had nibbled through the plastic fuse tubing. **Fresh angle: THE RABBIT DELAY — eighty years of masts fell on schedule except for the rabbits.** (Sources: thefreelibrary.com, Coventry Telegraph pieces; swling.com, Signal Issue 50 review.)
3. **Rugby's pips → the time on the wire.** The pips are the station's heartbeat — six beeps the whole nation sets its clocks by. **Fresh angle: THE PIPS — the most-watched seconds in radio are six of them.** (Pairs with B-39's missing beep.)
4. **The guarded silence → dead air vs dark.** Dead air = silence with the carrier still up — "one of the worst things that can occur"; stations install silence sensors / off-air alarms that alert staff after a few seconds; the FCC holds a 30-day limit for going silent without approval. A dark station = no carrier at all. **Fresh angle: THE CARRIER — the mast can be empty and still be on the air; dead air is not off the air.** (Sources: Wikipedia, "Dead air"; tvtechnology.com, "Dead Air Remembered.")
5. **The carrier with nothing on it → the official log.** Every United Kingdom ship must keep an official logbook in a Secretary-of-State-approved form; intentionally destroying or mutilating an entry is an offence; entries in order of date, NO BLANKS left; every important accident or damage to ship or cargo must be entered; entries are admissible in evidence. **Fresh angle: THE UNKEPT LOG — the law requires the book; a blank is the offense, and the book is evidence.** (Sources: legislation.gov.uk, Merchant Shipping Act 1995 s.77; captsschaudhari.com on the 1958 Act; iomshipregistry.com.)
6. **The unkept log → the mast again.** The mast fell and the book has no entry — the verdict needs the paperwork. **Fresh angle: THE FALL WITH NO ENTRY — the mast fell in the book's only blank.**

Canon-steer note: #161 A-23 already staged "The log was not kept." — Chain 1 steers deliberately around it: the guy field, the silence sensor, the carrier, the rabbit delay are adjacent rooms, not the same room.

### CHAIN 2 — from B-1038 "The Bailed Dinghy" (boathouse, the boat is dry, "The boat is dry.")

1. **The bailed boat → the hand bailer.** The seed's whole action is bailing; the tool itself is ancient and named. An Iron Age wooden hand bailer is among the Nydam Mose bog finds (Denmark); the Norwegian "auskjer" is still a traditional hand bailer; modern race regulations still require a hand bailer aboard some classes. **Fresh angle: THE HAND BAILER — the tool is older than the boat's job; every scoop is a filing.** (Sources: Wikipedia, "Bailing (boats)".)
2. **The hand bailer → the self-bailing deck.** What the seed does by hand was engineered away — a hull that bails itself by gravity. The RNLI Life-boat Journal records "self-emptying or self-baling" introduced into life-boats only once the 19th century was "well advanced"; plans for a 1911 self-bailing lifeboat put the deck *higher than the waterline* so it drains on its own. **Fresh angle: THE SELF-BAILING — the deck higher than the waterline; the verdict built into the architecture.** (Sources: RNLI Life-boat Journal archive; Wikipedia, "Bailing (boats)".)
3. **The self-bailing deck → the dry dock.** Even a self-bailing boat must be hauled out; bailing stops and the institution removes the water. Norfolk Navy Yard Dry Dock 1, Portsmouth, Virginia — first dry dock in the western hemisphere; opened June 17, 1833 (the Bunker Hill anniversary); first vessel the 74-gun USS Delaware; built 1827–1834 of Massachusetts granite for $974,365.65; National Historic Landmark 1971, still in daily use. **Fresh angle: THE DRY DOCK — the state's bathtub; an entire warship drained for inspection.** (Sources: navsea.navy.mil; usnhistory.navylive.dodlive.mil.)
4. **The dry dock → the Plimsoll load line.** On the drained hull you can read her depth as a legal line — the seed's private verdict "The boat is dry" meets the state's verdict of how wet she may legally be. Samuel Plimsoll (1824–1898), MP for Derby, campaigned against "coffin ships"; the 1876 Merchant Shipping Act forced a maximum-loading line on every British merchant hull — but owners could paint it anywhere (some put it on the funnel); position compulsory only in 1890; the mark is a circle with a horizontal bar; the 1930 International Load Line Convention was adopted by 54 nations. **Fresh angle: THE LOAD LINE — the state paints a circle-and-bar on the hull; the line the water must not cross.** (Sources: usni.org Naval History; victorianweb.org.)
5. **The load line → draft marks and the boot-top stripe.** Beside the legal line sit the working numerals — the ruler for her depth. Metric draft marks are numerals 10 cm high at bow, stern, and midships on both sides; the top of a numeral is the whole-decimeter value (water at the top of the "6" reads 6.10 m); imperial marks are 6 inches apart; the boot-top is the painted band at the waterline between anti-fouling and topside paint. **Fresh angle: THE DRAFT MARKS — the hull carries its own depth as a ruler; the boat announces its sinking in numerals.** (Sources: merchantnavyinfo.com; modelboatmayhem.co.uk.)
6. **The draft marks → the hauled-out verdict.** With the water gone and every mark readable, the dry dock issues the seed's exact verdict at institutional scale. Dry-dock practice names the formal "critical period" — the interval from when the stern first takes the keel blocks until the whole ship's weight is borne by them; afterwards she is "completely borne." Keel blocks are concrete/dense-wood cuboids (Biles, 1908: minimum 4 ft / 1.2 m keel height for working access), and docking plans alternate block positions between dockings so no patch of hull hides twice. **Fresh angle: THE BORNE — the institution declares the boat "borne"; the critical period is the verdict.** (Sources: marineinsight.com; Wikipedia, "Keel block".)

### CHAIN 3 — from B-1040 "The Split Log" (lumber yard, "The wood is ready.")

1. **The split log → the cord is a law.** The bumper splits one log; firewood is sold by the stack, and the stack has a legal size. A cord is 4×4×8 ft = 128 cubic feet **by law** (NIST Handbook 130); "truckload," "face cord," "rack," and "rick" are legally meaningless terms — sellers using them are a weights-and-measures offense. **Fresh angle: THE CORD — a cord is 128 cubic feet by law; "face cord" is not a measurement.** (Sources: NIST ncwm-firewood-factspdf; evansvillegov.org weights & measures; news.maryland.gov.)
2. **The cord → the Holzhausen.** A cord must be stacked, and the roundest stack is the cylindrical "wood house." Traditional dimensions per a Canadian chimney sweep's field account: a **10-foot-diameter circle around a 10-foot center pole**, bark-shingle roof; the chimney shape draws air up the middle and dries wet splits in a single summer — the wind whistles one note through the chimney. **Fresh angle: THE WOOD HOUSE — the chimney stack dries wet splits in a summer; the beehive is a machine.** (Sources: thechimneysweep.ca; outdoorguide.com; sandpointreader.com.)
3. **The wood house → the 20% rule.** The Holzhausen is a drying machine; dryness has a number, and the number has an institution. EPA Burn Wise: seasoned firewood must read **20% moisture or less**; Vermont runs a statewide loan program putting free moisture meters in **63 public libraries** so residents can test before burning. **Fresh angle: THE 20% RULE — twenty or less; the borrowed meter is the institution.** (Sources: EPA via dvids; Morning Ag Clips on the Vermont DEC program.)
4. **The 20% rule → the froe.** Seasoning "begins in earnest when this seal is broken by splitting the wood" — so the splitting tool is the qualification. Museum catalog record: the **froe** (shingle-maker's blade) must be driven with a **wooden** mallet — an iron maul would damage it; Colonial-era American plantations nicknamed it the "Middleboard Tool." **Fresh angle: THE FROE — the wooden mallet protects the blade; the tool that protects the tool.** (Sources: Tangle Web museum catalog; forgottenskillz.com; histoiresdecheznous.ca.)
5. **The froe → the hammer that brands.** From the hammer that splits to the hammer that marks: river-drive loggers branded each log's butt to sort them at the mills. Minnesota's **1858 law** required logging marks to be registered with the state — **over 20,000 marks** were registered; Voyageurs National Park's archives hold **27 cast-iron stamp hammers** (4–5 lb) whose raised letters compressed the brand inches into the wood. **Fresh angle: THE STAMP HAMMER — the hammer that marks: 20,000 registered brands; the butt end is the address.** (Sources: National Parks Traveler; 36 CFR 223.195 via GovInfo.)
6. **The stamp hammer → the king's mark.** The oldest brand on American wood was the state's: the King's broad arrow. Weare, New Hampshire, **April 13–14, 1772**: the King's surveyor had slashed the **broad arrow** (three axe cuts reserving every white pine over 12 inches diameter for the Royal Navy) onto mill owners' timber; sawmill owner **Ebenezer Mudgett** and townsmen beat Sheriff Benjamin Whiting in his sleep at the Pine Tree Tavern and drove him out — offenders had been named in the *New Hampshire Gazette* on Feb 7, 1772, more than a year before the Boston Tea Party. **Fresh angle: THE KING'S MARK — the broad arrow: the state's mark on the king's trees; the riot was the reply.** (Sources: Wikipedia, "Pine Tree Riot"; Weare Junior Historical Society pamphlet 1972; amac.us.)

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (12:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### CHAIN 1 — from N-71 "The Quarter's Auction" (NEWS, #158) — the auction, steering around owned territory

1. **N-71's auction → the sale under the spear.** Roman auctions of war spoils and state property were held *sub hasta* — "under the spear": soldiers planted their spears in the ground to mark their space, and the sale was done beneath them (Cicero, De lege agraria II.25). The word "auction" itself comes from Latin *auctio* — a sale by increase of bids, from *augeo*, to increase. **Fresh angle: THE SPEAR IN THE GROUND — the auction began as war plunder sold under a planted spear; the state's oldest sales grammar.** (Sources: e-periodica.ch, "Collectors at auction"; Britannica-adjacent numismatic survey citing Cicero.)
2. **The spear → the inch of candle.** England, 17th-18th c.: sales "by an inch of candle" — known in England by 1641 (House of Lords records); John Milton, 1652: "selling by inch of candle" as "the most probable means to procure the true value of the goods." Pepys's diary records the Admiralty selling surplus ships "by an inch of candle" (Nov 1660, Sept 1662) — and the winning-bid trick: the wick flares up slightly just before expiring; see the flare, shout the final bid. The anti-snipe auction, three centuries early. **Fresh angle (lineage — OWNED: shipped B-648 "The Inch of Candle"; carried as lineage only): the candle was the clock, and the clock confessed before it died.**
3. **The candle's flare → the auction cry.** The auctioneer's chant — "bid calling," "the auction cry," "the cattle rattle": a rhythmic repetition of the have and the want with filler words ("dollar bid," "now," "will ya give me?") that give bidders time to think. Before closing, the three calls: "Going once, going twice, sold!" or "Going, going, gone!" — then the gavel bangs the lectern and the bidding is over. **Fresh angle: THE THREE CALLS — the close is a rhythm of three; the count is the contract.** (Sources: Wikipedia "Auction chant"; NAA-affiliated auction school pattern.)
4. **The three calls → the gavel.** The auctioneer stands at a lectern with a gavel; the blow ends the bidding before the winning bid is announced. **Fresh angle (carried inside "The Going Once" — the hammer is the verdict's sound): the blow is the sale.** (Source: Wikipedia "Auction chant.")
5. **The gavel → the descending clock.** The Dutch auction: the auctioneer starts high and the price FALLS — the clock descends, and the first bidder wins. The inverse auction: no rising, only falling; the bid stops the fall. **Fresh angle: THE FALLING PRICE — the auction played backwards; the descent is the bidding.** (Source: FasterCapital auction history survey.)
6. **The descending clock → the reserve.** The secret floor: the price below which nothing sells — the minimum placed on all lots. If the high bid misses the reserve, the lot is not sold. **Fresh angle (lineage, carried as lore only — THE RESERVE: the blank surface of the auction; the floor nobody sees): the sale has a bottom that is never announced.**

Canon-steer note: Chain 1 deliberately routes AROUND owned candle territory — B-648 "The Inch of Candle" (shipped) is carried as lineage only. The new facts mined: the sub hasta, the three-call chant, the gavel, the Dutch clock, the reserve.

### CHAIN 2 — from B-39's missing beep / the pips lore (steering around owned pips territory)

1. **B-39's missing beep → the six pips.** The Greenwich Time Signal: first broadcast by the BBC on Tuesday, February 5, 1924, at 9:30pm — the brainchild of Astronomer Royal Sir Frank Dyson and Sir John Reith. Six pips at one-second intervals; the first five 0.1s each, the final pip 0.5s, and the hour changes at the very START of the long pip. The pacing was taken from a long-case pendulum clock whose movement generated electrical impulses sent to the BBC studios at Savoy Hill. **Fresh angle (lineage — owned: B-333 "The Seventh Pip", N-43 "The Seventh Pip", [DRAFTED] "The Pips", [READY] "The Speaking Clock", [DRAFTED] "The Hour Mark" venture; carried as lineage only): the six are the institution.**
2. **The six pips → the seventh.** When a leap second occurs, the pips get a seventh: short pips through 23:59:60, the long pip at 00:00:00. Before leap seconds were conceived in 1972, all six pips were equal length — the long one exists so the hour is never ambiguous. **Fresh angle (lineage — owned: shipped B-333/N-43; carried as lineage only): the extra pip is the Earth's correction.** (Source: Wikipedia "Greenwich Time Signal".)
3. **The seventh → the rule of three.** BBC Radio 4's standing rule (Katy Hubbard, head of presentation): "we will allow three out of context, but not the long final pip." The long pip belongs to the hour alone; "crashing the pips" — talking over them — was discouraged for a century. **Fresh angle: THE RULE OF THREE — the network's broadcast grammar becomes law: three out of context, never the long one.** (Source: countrylife.co.uk, Radio 4 presentation.)
4. **The rule → the woman who carried the time.** Ruth Belville: from 1892 to 1940 she carried her family's 18th-century pocket watch ("Arnold") door to door across London, selling the correct time to subscribers — through the whole radio age, while the pips were being broadcast. The pocket watch outlived the telegraph it competed with; Ethel Cain, the speaking clock's voice, lived round the corner from her in Croydon. **Fresh angle: THE TIME LADY — she walked the time door to door; the telegraph lied, the walk did not.** (Source: Science Museum blog, "Ruth Belville: the Greenwich time lady".)
5. **The time lady → the regulator.** The Dent regulator clocks at Greenwich: their pendula were fitted with electrical contacts that sent a signal to the BBC every second — the pendulum was the wire's metronome. The seconds rode the wire from the observatory to the studio. **Fresh angle: THE REGULATOR — the pendulum sent the seconds down the wire; the clock was a transmitter.** (Sources: historysnacks.io; YouTube "5th February 1924" documentary notes.)
6. **The regulator → the first voice.** Ethel 'Jane' Cain, a London telephone exchange worker chosen from 15,000 operators, recorded the speaking clock in "jerks" — "At the Third Stroke," the hours, the seconds, "precisely" — optically onto glass disks, July 24, 1936, dial TIM (846). **Fresh angle (lineage — owned: [READY] "The Speaking Clock" NETWORK episode; carried as lineage only): the voice was the number.**

Canon-steer note: Chain 2's six-pip, seventh-pip, speaking-clock, and time-ball nodes are ALL owned (B-333, N-43, B-226, [DRAFTED] "The Pips"/"The Third Stroke"/"The Hour Mark", [READY] "The Speaking Clock"). This run banks only what the mining left: THE RULE OF THREE (meme/lore), THE TIME LADY, THE REGULATOR, and THE LONG PIP as a guarded rule.

### CHAIN 3 — from PA-27 "The Receiving Cage" (#159) — the lost property office

1. **PA-27's receiving cage → the Service des Objets Trouvés.** Paris's centralized lost-and-found: the Préfecture de Police's office at 36 rue des Morillons. A thousand objects a day lost in the Paris suburbs and airports; 186,000 objects delivered in 2011 alone. Top three: identity documents, keys, glasses. Unclaimed items are stored, then auctioned, donated, or disposed. **Fresh angle: THE WAREHOUSE OF THE FORGOTTEN — the city keeps what the city loses; the shelf is the archive of inattention.** (Sources: Wikipedia "Musée du Service des Objets Trouvés"; Selectra expat guide.)
2. **The warehouse → the museum of the unclaimed.** The Service maintains the Musée du Service des Objets Trouvés — a museum of what nobody claimed: a lobster found at Paris-Orly, a funerary urn lost in the metro near Père Lachaise, a fireman's helmet, skulls, a wooden leg, wedding dresses, a 100kg roll of copper. Not open to the public. **Fresh angle (production-note material): the unclaimed has its own museum — the weirdest shelf in the network's world.** (Source: Wikipedia.)
3. **The museum → the unclaimed auction.** Unclaimed luggage and freight are sold at auction: the U.S. "Unclaimed Baggage" operation has run 55+ years, publishing an annual Found Report (samurai swords, a fully assembled robot, diamond grills, a suitcase of rat poison). **Fresh angle: THE UNCLAIMED LOT — what no one claims, the state sells; the auction is the shelf's last resort.** (Sources: Parade; Unclaimed Baggage Found Report.)
4. **The unclaimed lot → the chant (Chain 1 convergence).** The unclaimed auction is sold with the auctioneer's three calls — Chain 1's "Going once, going twice, sold!" closes Chain 3's lots. The chains converge: the sub hasta's descendant sells the lost property office's orphans. **Fresh angle (carried as the convergence note): the spear's grandchildren sell the umbrella nobody claimed.**
5. **The lot → the claim check.** The numbered half-ticket: the stub torn at the counter, one half kept by the claimant, one half on the item. The claim is the verdict — the halves must match. **Fresh angle: THE TORN HALF — the tear is the verdict; the match is the release.** (Sources: moneysavingexpert lost-luggage process; airline property-irregularity procedure.)
6. **The claim check → the cage (chain closes).** The claim check returns to PA-27's receiving cage — the torn half meets the item on the shelf. The chain closes where it started: the cage is the office's stage door.

Canon-steer note: Chain 3 is fresh ground — PA-27's cage had never been chained outward. No owned territory touched (the unclaimed-auction node flagged vs Chain 1's "The Sub Hasta"/"The Going Once" as lineage, not collision).

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (13:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### CHAIN 1 — from B-1004 "The Unit Check" (padlock tug, lock holds) — the lock that reports

1. **B-1004's tug (padlock holds) → the Chubb detector lock.** 1818: Jeremiah Chubb patents the "detector lock" in Portsmouth — a four-lever lock where a picked or wrong-key lever trips the *regulator*, jamming the bolt. The lock does not merely resist the attempt — it REMEMBERS it: afterwards even the TRUE key will not open it until the reset key is used, giving "the possessor of the true key evidence that an attempt has been made to violate the lock." Fresh angle: THE DETECTOR — the lock that reports the tug; the violation leaves evidence on the lock, not on the door. (Sources: Wikipedia "Chubb detector lock"; historywebsite.co.uk "The House of Chubb" — specification quote: "the lock is what I call detected.")
2. **The remembering lock → the convict who couldn't pick it.** Portsmouth Dockyard offered a prison-hulk locksmith his FREE PARDON plus £100 if he could pick the detector lock; he had picked every lock presented to him. After two to three months of trying he admitted defeat. Fresh angle: THE FAILED PICK — the expert stays locked out; the attempt's failure is the advertisement. (Source: Wikipedia "Chubb detector lock.")
3. **The failed pick → the security becomes the tool.** 1851 Great Exhibition: Alfred Hobbs finally picked the Chubb lock — by turning the detector mechanism into a DECODING instrument, reading the levers off the defense itself. The feature that reported attempts became the instrument of the attempt. Fresh angle: THE SECURITY BECOMES THE TOOL — the defense reads back as instructions. (Source: thefreelibrary.com "Under lock and key" — Hobbs "converted its detector mechanism into a decoding instrument.")
4. **The defense read back → the delay instead of the denial.** James Sargent's time-delay locks (bank safes): the lock does not say no — it says LATER. The vault keeps you waiting; the wait is the lock. Fresh angle: THE DELAY — time is the lock; the denial is just the fastest form of it. (Source: vocal.media locksmithing survey — Sargent "time-delay locks and combination locks... used in high-security environments like banks.")
5. **The delay → the numbered lead.** Railway and customs plombs: a numbered lead seal on a wagon door — it does not stop anyone; it DIES loudly. A broken seal with the number recorded is the report. Fresh angle: THE NUMBERED LEAD — the seal's whole job is to die as evidence. (Source: production-adjacent — seal practice; carried as lore.)
6. **The lead seal → the GPO locks.** 1823: Chubb awarded a special licence by King George IV and became the SOLE supplier of locks to the General Post Office. Chain closes: the mail's doors and the unit's doors share a supplier — B-1004's padlock is in the post. Fresh angle: THE GPO LOCKS — the mail was always locked with the network's locks. (Source: Wikipedia "Chubb Locks.")

### CHAIN 2 — from B-1005 "The Lit Panel" (control room, one switch, one lamp lit) — the building's veins

1. **B-1005's lamp (one on) → the annunciator.** Hotel and office call boards: numbered flags or shutters DROP when a room rings — the board shows the REQUEST, not the requester. A whole building's wants as falling numbers. Fresh angle: THE DROPPED FLAG — the request is a falling number; the board never shows who. (Source: period hotel-equipment practice; carried as production research.)
2. **The falling number → the night bell.** One bell for the whole sleeping building; the night porter rings it once and the building settles. Fresh angle: THE NIGHT BELL — one sound owns the whole dark. (Source: hotel service ritual; carried as production research.)
3. **The night bell → the cash ball.** 1880: William S. Lamson, a Lowell notion store — he SAWED CROQUET BALLS IN HALF, hollowed them out, and rolled them down inclined wooden troughs from the sales counter to the cashier's desk; the money went up, the change came back the same way. The till never held money. Fresh angle: THE CASH BALL — the money travels; the drawer is always empty. (Sources: brassregisters.com Lamson collection — "he sawed croquet balls in two, hollowed them out, and rolled them in inclined wooden troughs"; Wikipedia "Lamson Engineering Company Ltd.")
4. **The trough → the flying fox.** The wire system: the clerk put cash and the sales slip into a metal capsule, TWISTED it onto the overhead wire, and pulled a handle — the capsule was FLUNG along the wire to the cash office. Lamson Paragon's Rapid Wire. Fresh angle: THE FLUNG CAPSULE — the receipt flies; the clerk stays put. (Source: vintage-radio.net "Vintage money-transfer systems" — "a little carriage... flung along an overhead wire by a pull of a handle.")
5. **The wire → the whoosh.** Pneumatic post: cash and receipts shot "up the tube" to a central cashier, change and the receipt rubber-stamped PAID came back the same way. Wanamaker's first department-store tube went in in 1880. The tube is still in use (Tesco checkouts whoosh to the back office). Fresh angle: THE TUBE — the building inhales the money; the receipt is stamped PAID and exhaled back. (Source: vintage-radio.net — "the payment and receipt got sent 'up the tube' to a central cashier, change and the receipt [rubber-stamped 'paid'] came back the same way.")
6. **The tube → the building as a body.** Money, mail, waste, water — every tube, wire, trough, and duct is a vein. The cash office is the heart; the building is the body and it has circulation. Fresh angle: THE VEINS — the building has veins; the money travels them. (Source: synthesis of Chain 2; motif candidate.)

### CHAIN 3 — from B-1006 "The File Drawer" (open at 4s, shut at 9.5s, "Kept.") — the morgue

1. **B-1006's drawer → the newspaper morgue.** The New York Times Archival Library is called "the morgue" — clippings and photo archives in the basement of the old New York Herald Tribune building, West 41st Street; created 1907 by Carr Van Anda; clippings collection stopped June 1990; now run by ONE man (Jeff Roth). Fresh angle: THE MORGUE — the newspaper calls its own memory the morgue; the file's nickname is already a death joke. (Source: Wikipedia "The New York Times Archival Library.")
2. **The morgue → the advance drawer.** Two filing cabinets of "Advanced Obits," alphabetically arranged, pre-written with proposed layouts — including one typed in 1931 about a teenage woman pilot at the dawn of commercial aviation, for whom editors "just assumed they'd soon need a death notice." When she died in her 90s, the Times was ready. Fresh angle (lineage — OWNED: shipped N-64 "The Advance Obituary," the advance-drawer beat; carried as lineage only): THE DRAWER IS AHEAD — the filing happens before the living does; the drawer waits, not the world. (Source: NPR/Obit transcript — Roth: the 1931 obit "typed up... about a teenager, a woman pilot"; untappedcities.com — "two filing cabinets of 'Advanced Obits' alphabetically arranged.")
3. **The advance drawer → the card.** "This is the card catalogue" (Jeff Roth, Obit): geographical clippings, thousands of drawers — knowledge the size of an index card. Fresh angle: THE CARD — the archive's atom; knowledge in 3x5 inches. (Source: NPR/Obit transcript.)
4. **The card → the serendipity.** A.M. Rosenthal on the morgue: "The joy of [the morgue] was that you would find what you did not know you were looking for." Fresh angle: THE UNORDERED — the search finds the wrong thing and it is right. (Source: untappedcities.com — Rosenthal quote.)
5. **The serendipity → the dispersed morgue.** Sections of the collection were shipped to the New York Public Library and the University of Texas; the archive stopped collecting in 1990. The memory LEFT the building — the building forgot how to remember. Fresh angle: THE DISPERSED MORGUE — the building's memory was lent out; it remembers elsewhere. (Source: Wikipedia "The New York Times Archival Library" — "sections of the collection have been sent to other repositories.")
6. **The dispersal → the kept filing.** B-1006's verdict: drawer shut at 9.5s, "Kept." The real morgues stopped filing in 1990 — OUR basement archive files on. Fresh angle: THE KEPT — the real drawers stopped; ours did not. (Source: chain closes where it started — B-1006.)

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (13:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F91 — THE ATTEMPT WANTS EVIDENCE.** From the detector lock (the true key refusing to turn is a whole story in one state): the attempt is most legible when its EVIDENCE survives it — not the pick breaking, but the lock reporting the pick. Production rule: in pass/fail beats, stage the evidence of the attempt, never the attempt — the 9.5s endpoint carries the history; the audience reads the before from the after.
- **10S-F92 — THE SOUND WANTS A DESTINATION.** From the pneumatic tube (the capsule must ARRIVE): the whoosh is only a beat if the capsule lands somewhere at 9.5s — a departure with no arrival is a cut, not a beat. Production rule: in any travel beat, the 9.5s endpoint IS the arrival; never direct the sending without directing the landing. (Pairs with 10S-F86 — the fall wants a radius; here the journey wants an end.)

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (14:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### CHAIN 1 — from B-1043 "The Washed Mug" (the mug is washed, no machine in sight) — the machine the mug never met

1. **B-1043's washed mug → the chipped china.** Josephine Garis Cochrane's dishwasher begins as a domestic grievance: heirloom dishes chipped while being hand-washed after her dinner parties. Legend records her verdict: "If nobody else is going to invent a dishwashing machine, I'll do it myself." Fresh angle: THE CHIPPED SET — the machine was invented by the damage; the chip is the origin, not the accident. (Sources: smithsonianmag.com "This Time-Saving Patent Paved the Way for the Modern Dishwasher"; magnabureau.space inventor profile.)
2. **The chipped set → the measured dish.** Cochrane's method, recorded by the USPTO: she MEASURED THE DISHES FIRST, then built wire compartments — each designed to fit plates, cups, or saucers — set into a wheel lying flat inside a copper boiler; a motor turned the wheel while hot soapy water squirted up from the bottom and rained down. No scrubbing. US Patent 355,139, granted December 28, 1886 (filed December 31, 1885, signed "J.G. Cochran"). Fresh angle: THE MEASURED DISH — the measure precedes the attempt; the machine fits the dish, never the reverse. (Sources: Wikipedia "Josephine Cochrane"; USPTO via smithsonianmag.)
3. **The measured dish → the shed.** She built it in the shed behind her house in Shelbyville, Illinois; husband dead 1883, debts, $1,535.59 in cash; hired mechanic George Butters to build from her drawings; the machine shops "insisted on having their own way with my invention until they convinced themselves my way was the better." Fresh angle: THE SHED — the machine the factories would not build; the inventor's authority was a shed, not a shop. (Sources: popsci.com "The forgotten story of the woman who invented the dishwasher"; magnabureau.space.)
4. **The shed → the mile-wide lobby.** Hotels and restaurants bought first (the home market was too poor and too proud); her first sale was the Palmer House Hotel, Chicago, 1887. She recalled: "for a woman to cross a hotel lobby alone... the lobby seemed a mile wide. I thought I should faint at every step, but I didn't — and I got an $800 order as my reward." Fresh angle: THE MILE-WIDE LOBBY — the sale is the beat; the crossing is the pitch. (Source: popsci.com.)
5. **The lobby → the two-minute demo.** 1893, the World's Columbian Exposition, Machinery Hall: over 200 dirty dishes loaded in; two minutes later they emerged sparkling; the judges awarded the highest prize "for best mechanical construction, durability, and adaptation to its line of work" — the only device in the hall invented by a woman; she sold nine on the spot. Fresh angle: THE PERFORMING MACHINE — the machine performs; the demonstration is the advertisement. (Sources: magnabureau.space; maloriesadventures.com summary of the Exposition.)
6. **The demo → the dish pit.** The home market came later (hot water scarce, social attitudes slower); the economics of broken crockery made the machine pay for itself in hotels and restaurants. The washed mug's real home is the dish pit — the machine returns to where it was first sold. Chain closes: B-1043's mug was washed by hand; the machine that would wash it was born in a shed. Fresh angle: THE DISH PIT — the mug lives where the machine was sold first.

### CHAIN 2 — from B-1037 "The Stropped Razor" (the strop keeps the edge) — the pole that remembers blood

1. **B-1037's strop → the gripped staff.** The barber's pole originates as the rod the patient GRIPPED to dilate the veins for bloodletting; the brass ball at the top symbolizes the basin that collected the blood; the red and white stripes are the bloodied bandages washed and hung to dry on the rod, twisting in the wind into the spiral. Fresh angle: THE GRIPPED STAFF — the shop's sign is a medical instrument; the spiral is dried blood. (Sources: Wikipedia "Barber's pole"; trolleysquarebarbers.com; familytree.com.)
2. **The staff → the shop of two trades.** The barber-surgeon shaved AND bled — teeth pulled, cups applied, leeches set, fractures dressed, amputations performed; in England chartered 1462, merged with surgeons 1540 as the United Barber-Surgeons Company. Fresh angle: THE SHOP OF TWO TRADES — one chair for the shave and the surgery; the same hands. (Sources: h2g2.com "Blood, Bandages and Barber Poles"; fashionencyclopedia.com "Barbershops.")
3. **The two trades → the 1745 split.** George II's acts separated surgeons from barbers; the surgeons went on to the Royal College; the BARBERS KEPT THE POLE. Fresh angle: THE KEPT POLE — the symbol survived the trade; the pole stayed with the shavers. (Sources: h2g2.com; Wikipedia.)
4. **The kept pole → the defended symbol.** The pole is still legally fought over: in Michigan (March 2012) legislation proposed barber poles hang ONLY outside barbershops, not beauty salons; barbers and cosmetologists battle for exclusive rights to the symbol. Fresh angle: THE POLE HAS LAWYERS — the symbol needs defending; the blood is now paperwork. (Source: Wikipedia "Barber's pole.")
5. **The lawyers → the emporium.** The small-town American barbershop: an emporium where men congregated — hair cut, faces shaved, nails manicured; gossip passed, jokes shared, sports and politics debated; men read magazines and enjoyed each other's company. Fresh angle: THE SHOP AS THE WIRE — the town's news traveled through the waiting chairs. (Source: fashionencyclopedia.com.)
6. **The wire → the four-part wait.** The waiting men sang together for amusement — the trend that gave rise to the BARBERSHOP QUARTET. Fresh angle: THE FOUR-PART WAIT — the wait harmonizes; the queue is the chorus. (Source: fashionencyclopedia.com.)

### CHAIN 3 — from #160 NE-18 "The First In" (the punch at the time-clock station) — the minute that became the computer

1. **#160's punch → the bucket of brass disks.** Before the clock: bosses assigned each worker one little brass disk, and expected them to TOSS IT INTO A BUCKET every morning to mark themselves present — "sloppy. There was no accurate record of when the guy actually showed up." Fresh angle: THE TOSSED DISK — presence as a toss; the record was a bucket. (Source: 99percentinvisible.org "100 Objects #15: Bundy Clock" transcript.)
2. **The bucket → the numbered key.** 1888: Willard LeGrand Bundy patents the first employee time clock — an ornate wooden box like a grandfather clock; each worker gets his OWN KEY; insert it, turn a quarter turn, and the machine stamps the exact time onto a ribbon of paper. Fresh angle: THE QUARTER TURN — presence becomes a printed fact; the turn is the testimony. (Sources: 99percentinvisible.org; victoriancollections.net.au "Punching the Bundy"; laborhistoryin2.podbean.com.)
3. **The key → the owned minute.** "It also taught workers that the minute belonged to the machine before it belonged to the story of the day." The time recorder joined the moment, the worker, and the machine into one portable fact — a card that could be filed, totaled, shown. Fresh angle: THE OWNED MINUTE — the minute is the machine's before it is the day's. (Source: github.com/lpeasy/outsideinprint "The Clock by the Door.")
4. **The owned minute → the punch becomes the computer.** The Bundy Manufacturing Company (founded 1889 with brother Harlow) merged into the International Time Recording Company — which became part of IBM. The time card is the punch card's ancestor: the mark that counted workers became the medium that counted everything. Fresh angle: THE PUNCH BECAME THE COMPUTER — the ribbon of punched times is the first draft of the punch card. (Sources: victoriancollections.net.au; laborhistoryin2.podbean.com.)
5. **The computer → the watched bench.** Taylor's time-study men: the stopwatch on the bench, the worker watched while he works; keeping track of hours and labor costs "became an essential part of squeezing every drop of profit out of the industrial workforce." Fresh angle: THE WATCHED BENCH — the second is the unit; the watch is the work. (Source: laborhistoryin2.podbean.com.)
6. **The watched bench → the double mark.** The same mark serves power AND protection: it gives management "a daily map of the workforce" — and gives workers a record that can "survive bad memory, bad arithmetic, a payroll mistake, or a supervisor with a private interest in shaving time." Fresh angle: THE DOUBLE MARK — the punch accuses and defends; the same stamp is the foreman's and the worker's. (Source: outsideinprint "The Clock by the Door.") Lineage to #160's THE SIGN-IN AS LAW — the punch is the station's grammar; the double mark is its jurisprudence.

### PLOT RESEARCH — real broadcast and theatre practice, translated into network plots

- **THE 0048.** The BBC Shipping Forecast: broadcast since 1924 (service since 1867, after the storm that killed 800); the late forecast goes out at 00:48 PRECISELY; "Sailing By" (Ronald Binge, 1963) is played before it — not as decoration but as a BUFFER and an identification signal: "depending on when the final programme before closedown finishes, 'Sailing By' (or part of it) is played as a 'filler' as the forecast starts at 00:48hrs precisely." In the early 1990s the BBC tried to axe it; listeners revolted (Daily Mail, Daily Telegraph headlines); it stayed. The forecast is followed by the anthem and closedown; the World Service takes the frequencies after the pips at 0100. Network translation: the night desk plays one piece of music to fill the gap; it must end at the exact minute; the piece IS the identification. Staged: "The Night Piece." Premise-bank 9 ("Rituals are instructions for things that already happened") maps exactly — the 0048 happens because it happened. (Sources: Wikipedia "Sailing By"; Met Office factsheet 8; spacewar.com centenary piece.)
- **THE STANDBY FACE.** Test Card F (1967–1998): the first colour test card, the first to feature a person — eight-year-old Carole Hersee playing noughts and crosses with her clown doll Bubbles, surrounded by greyscales and colour signals. The card was shown "usually while no programmes were being broadcast"; she became "the most aired face in British television history" (~70,000 hours); paid £100; the transparency was FLIPPED because she appeared left-handed (the X painted in the left centre square had to sit in the exact middle of the screen). When the card was retired, Bubbles returned for the BBC website's error page. Network translation: when nothing is on, someone must be on; the standby face is the programme. The card's flip is the story: the image was reversed so it would read right. Staged: "The Standby Face" (lineage-flagged vs shipped B-49 "The Test Card" — B-49 is the pattern-only card; this is the card WITH the face, the off-air person). (Sources: Wikipedia "Test Card F"; Wikipedia "Carole Hersee"; ladbible.com QI piece.)
- **THE NO-WHISTLE.** Theatrical rigging descends from sailing rigging; scene changes were cued by WHISTLED codes; a stray whistle from an actor could trigger an ill-timed set change — or drop a sandbag. The rule stuck: no whistling backstage. Network translation: the cue is a rule, not a sound; the whistle that must never happen is the one the whole building listens for. Carried as lineage vs banked [READY] "The Quiet Cue" (the rope HELD, the whistle never heard) — the new item is the OPPOSITE verdict: the cue heard. Staged: "The Stray Whistle."
- **THE HALF-HOUR CALL.** The stage manager's calls — "ladies and gentlemen, this is your half-hour call," then quarter, then five. The theatre's whole evening is announced in shrinking intervals; the call is the institution's clock. Network translation: the shrinking announcement; the time to curtain is itself a performance. Un-staged — available (production-note material; background figure: THE CALLER — job = the shrinking intervals, motive = the house must be ready).

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (14:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F93 — THE MEASURE WANTS A RULER.** From Cochrane (she measured the dishes FIRST, then built the compartments): the 10s beat is legible when the STANDARD precedes the attempt — the audience reads the verdict against the measure, not against the void. Production rule: in any test/fit/check beat, stage the measure in the first 2s (the wire compartment held up, the template, the marked line) — the 9.5s endpoint is then a comparison, and comparisons read silently.
- **10S-F94 — THE BUFFER WANTS A CLOCK.** From "Sailing By" (the piece fills the gap until exactly 00:48): filler is never filler when it has a deadline — every second before the turn is the turn's antechamber. Production rule: when a take must hold time before its event (the wait, the fill, the settle), give the holding a COUNTABLE form — a filling vessel, a rising needle, a played piece with an end — so the audience feels the deadline, not the delay. (Pairs with 10S-F92 — the sound wants a destination; here the gap wants a clock.)

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (15:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### Chain 1 — the stamped ticket (start: B-1029 "The Stamped Ticket", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The stamp → the Edmondson ticket.** Thomas Edmondson's 1840s system: cardboard tickets printed and issued in serial-number order, cancelled by the dating press. The railway standardized the ticket as a DATA SYSTEM — the number, not the card, was the record; the stub kept by the company was the ledger's ancestor. Fresh angle: the ticket is only real once it has been damaged — the punch/stamp is the cancellation that completes it. Concrete link: the serial-numbered cardboard.
2. **The damage → the registered punch.** The conductor's ticket punch carried a unique die — each conductor's punch shape was registered with the railroad, so the punched mark identified WHO took the fare (an anti-fraud measure). The hole was the conductor's signature, carried as a shape in his pocket. Fresh angle: identity as a wound — the mark you leave is the proof you were there. Concrete link: the punched hole.
3. **The signature-wound → the private postmark.** The postage meter (first commercial machine, Pitney Bowes, 1922): the franking machine turned every office into its own post office — the red meter mark is a postmark printed by the sender, not the state. Fresh angle: the stamp you print yourself; the mailroom becomes a branch of the postal service by owning a machine. Concrete link: the self-printed mark.
4. **The self-printed mark → the frank.** Members of Congress frank their mail — the signature itself is the postage; the name pays the carriage. Fresh angle: the signature as currency — the most famous signature in the building costs the building nothing to send. Concrete link: the signature as the stamp.
5. **→ this:** "The Registered Punch" (the hole as signature) + "The Frank" (the office as post office).

### Chain 2 — the stacked stone (start: B-1041 "The Stacked Stone", shipped 2026-10-16 — never chained; the 14:00 run took B-1043's mug)

1. **The cairn → the inuksuk.** For centuries the Inuit have stacked rocks — sometimes into human forms — as inuksuit: "like a human" in Inuktitut. They are navigation aids and guideposts, hunting markers, messages, safe-passage signals. Fresh angle: the stack that POINTS — the cairn is not decoration, it is a direction; the human-like shape is the arrow. Concrete link: the human-shaped stack.
2. **The pointer → the logo.** The inunnguaq became the Vancouver 2010 emblem ("Ilanaaq," friend) — the waymarker turned into a brand mark, controversial among the Inuit and B.C. First Nations. Tourist regions now sprout generic inuksuit as gateways; Killarney Provincial Park issued a 2007 notice asking visitors to STOP the "invasion" of inuksuit. Fresh angle: the sign that lost its way by becoming a sign — the waymarker degrades into decoration, and the decoration degrades into noise. Concrete link: the marker-as-logo.
3. **The noise → the unbuilt marker.** Hikers' unofficial cairns confuse trail navigation; parks' leave-no-trace ethic asks walkers to dismantle unauthorized stacks — the unauthorized marker is misinformation. Fresh angle: the most honest thing you can do to a false marker is take it apart; the dismantling is the correction. Concrete link: the scattered stones.
4. **→ this:** "The Unbuilt Marker" (the dismantling as the verdict).

### Chain 3 — the bailed dinghy (start: B-1038 "The Bailed Dinghy", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The bail → the smallest possible bail.** Mary Mapes Dodge's 1865 *Hans Brinker, or The Silver Skates* popularized the little Dutch boy who plugs a leaking dike with his finger — a story-WITHIN-a-story (Hans reads it in class); it never happened, and Dodge never visited the Netherlands before publication — she wrote Holland from novels and her immigrant Dutch neighbors' accounts. Fresh angle: the smallest bail in history is imported folklore — an American's invented Holland; the network's own "the room was real, the crowd was generated" energy: the legend is generated, the myth is real. Concrete link: the finger in the dike.
2. **The generated legend → the monuments.** Harlingen's "It Jonkje" (The Little Boy) at the ferry terminal, Spaarndam, Madurodam, Holland (Michigan) — statues of a boy who never existed. Fresh angle: the monument to the generated event — the town built a statue of a story. Concrete link: the statue of the boy.
3. **The statue → the network's rhyme.** The network stages generated events as if real (the crowd was generated; the room was real). The Dutch built the boy a statue. Fresh angle: give the generated its monument ON CAMERA — the finger is the monument's whole body. Concrete link: the finger as the statue.
4. **→ this:** "The Kept Finger" (the smallest bail, staged as the monument).

### Chain 4 — plot research: the first broadcast, the interval, the door (real broadcasting/theatre institutions)

1. **The inaugural face.** 2 November 1936, Alexandra Palace: the world's first regular "high-definition" (then defined as at least 200 lines) television service — Baird's 240-line mechanical system and Marconi-EMI's 405-line all-electronic system on ALTERNATE WEEKS, each with its own studio, until 405 was chosen in 1937. Leslie Mitchell was the first announcer heard. Fresh angle: television's first face belonged to a man introducing a contest between two incompatible pictures — the service opened with an argument about what television even was. Plot translation: the announcer who opens the service by naming its own unfinishedness.
2. **The gap's entertainment.** The cinema organ (Compton/Wurlitzer) rose from the pit for the interval — the gap in the programme had its OWN show, with its own instrument and its own performer. Fresh angle: the interval is a programme wearing a gap's clothes — THE FILLER motif made flesh, rising out of the floor on hydraulics. Plot translation: the organist whose whole job is the between.
3. **The door's list.** The stage-door keeper holds the list that decides who enters the theatre — artists, crew, nobody else. The door is the institution's threshold and the keeper is its border. Fresh angle: the nod is the verdict — a whole career's worth of drama compressed into one man's small gesture at a side door. Plot translation: the keeper who admits UNC by the list.
4. **The name that must not be said.** The Scottish play — the theatre superstition that Macbeth must never be named inside a theatre. The word is theatre's own redaction: saying it summons the disaster, so the name is blacked out of the building's speech. Fresh angle: the superstition is a meme — a locked syntax (never say the name), swappable content (the play), enforced by a community. Plot translation: the poster hung blank.
5. **→ this:** "The First Announcer" (the inaugural face) + "The Interval Organist" (the filler made flesh) + "The Stage-Door Keeper" (the nod as verdict) + "The Unnamed Play" (the superstition as redaction).

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (15:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F95 — THE DISMANTLING WANTS THE BEFORE.** A beat about removal (the unbuilt marker, the scattered cairn, the peeled poster) fails if it opens on the change mid-way: the viewer must see the INTACT state first. Production note: 0–2s = the intact state as the title card (the cairn complete, the card unstamped, the room full); 4–6s = the removal; 9.5s = the aftermath. The silent-frame rule applies to destruction: the premise's "before" must read from the first frame, or the "after" reads as nothing.
- **10S-F96 — THE RISE WANTS THE PIT.** A vertical entrance — the organ rising, the stamp descending, the finger pressing — reads only against its resting state. Production note: the from-state must be visible in the first 2s (the pit empty, the hand at rest, the dike wall whole), or the motion has no "from" and the take reads as mid-action. The rise is the joke only against its absence.

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (16:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### Chain 1 — the covered statue (start: B-1030 "The Covered Statue", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The covered → the Wrapped Reichstag.** In 1995 Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the entire Reichstag in 1,076,000 square feet of fabric — a state building dressed in a drape for 14 days. Fresh angle: the largest wrapped object in modern art was a parliament — the drape turned a working institution into an object under cover. Concrete link: the monumental drape.
2. **The monumental drape → the veiled marble.** Antonio Canova's veiled busts; Giuseppe Sanmartino's *Veiled Christ* (1753) — marble carved to LOOK like a translucent veil lying over a face. Fresh angle: the veil is the statue — the stone wears cloth that is also stone; the cover is not removable. Concrete link: the carved veil.
3. **The unremovable veil → the unveiling ritual.** The draped-monument unveiling: a ceremony whose whole content is a gesture — the pull that frees the object. Ribbon-cuttings and cloth-pulls stage revelation as a civic act. Fresh angle: the premise is the pull-tab — the object is complete before the ceremony begins; only the gesture is missing. Concrete link: the pull.
4. **→ this:** "The Unveiling" (the pull that never comes) + "The Veiled Marble" (the carving that wears).

### Chain 2 — the hourglass (start: B-1035 "The Hourglass", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The glass → the ship's log glass.** A 28-second sand glass paired with the chip log: a knotted line paid out over the stern, knots counted as the glass ran — speed measured in ROPE. The word "knot" is a unit because a rope was the instrument. Fresh angle: language was tied before it was written — the knot is a word you count by hand. Concrete link: the 28-second glass.
2. **The counted rope → dead reckoning.** The ship's position as paperwork: courses and speeds logged and plotted into a chart — the voyage exists twice, once in the water and once in the ledger. Fresh angle: navigation as bookkeeping — the network's paperwork conceit at sea; the chart is the episode ledger with weather. Concrete link: the plotted chart.
3. **The chart → the guarded node.** The ship's half-hour glass (eight bells to a watch) lives on this chain — STEERED AROUND deliberately: pips/bells territory is fully mined (shipped B-333 + N-43; 12:00 dedup note). The log glass is the unmined node; the bells stay out of frame. Fresh angle: choosing the glass over the bells is the steering, not the absence.
4. **→ this:** "The Chip Log" (the rope is the speed).

### Chain 3 — the kneaded dough (start: B-1036 "The Kneaded Dough", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The dough → the baker's dozen.** Thirteen loaves for the price of twelve — a medieval practice hardened into law-adjacent custom: give the extra loaf rather than risk the short-weight fine. Fresh angle: generosity as legal insurance — the bonus loaf exists because the law counted. Concrete link: the thirteenth loaf.
2. **The counted loaf → the Assize of Bread and Ale (1266).** The English crown fixed the weight of the loaf by statute; bakers who sold short faced fines, the pillory, the stocks. Fresh angle: the loaf as a legal instrument — bread with a statute attached; the weight is the verdict. Concrete link: the regulated weight.
3. **The regulated weight → the starter mother.** Century-old levain cultures fed daily outlive the bakeries that keep them — Gold Rush starters carried across the plains in 1849, still fed generations later. Fresh angle: a living thing whose biography is a feeding schedule — the mother is older than the shop; the fed jar keeps the years. Concrete link: the fed jar.
4. **→ this:** "The Baker's Dozen" (the thirteenth loaf) + "The Mother" (the fed jar).

### Chain 4 — plot research: the off-hours, the gap's face, the face that calibrates (real broadcasting institutions)

1. **The off-hours film.** Trade test transmissions: films broadcast in daytime off-hours so television dealers could tune their display sets — programmes that existed to be calibrated to, never watched. Fresh angle: the broadcast with no audience as a professional tool — the set is the viewer. Plot translation: the dealer who tunes to a film nobody will ever see. LINEAGE: the banked 2026-10-13 [DRAFT] venture "The Trade Test" owns the trade-test node itself — this chain takes the off-hours/showroom angle, a different node of the same institution (flagged, not a collision).
2. **The gap's face.** The in-vision continuity announcer: the person whose entire job is the between — seated at the announcer's desk, bridging one programme into the next with a nod. Fresh angle: dead air as a staffed position — the bridge is a person, not a slide. LINEAGE vs shipped B-710 "The Continuity" (2026-10-13, lore THE GAP — the gap-as-programme, monitor dark; this stages the gap's FACE, a person — distinct premise, flagged) and vs [READY] "The First Announcer" (15:00 — the inaugural face; this is the recurring between) and vs "The Interval Organist" (15:00 — the programme wearing the gap; this is the gap itself, personified).
3. **The face that calibrates.** Test Card F (1967–1998): one still face aired for tens of thousands of hours to calibrate sets — the most-seen face in British television history, never moving, never speaking. Fresh angle: the standard is a person who never performs — fame without a single gesture. Plot translation: the card held to camera as the verdict of calibration.
4. **→ this:** "The Off-Hours Film" (the programme tuned to, never watched) + "The Bridge" (the between, personified) + "The Most Seen" (the standard that never speaks).

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (17:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

### Chain 1 — the washed mug (start: B-1043 "The Washed Mug", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The mug → the found object.** B-1043 washes the mug; B-797 filed it unclaimed; B-383 brewed for the next shift — the network's mug family is three deep and none of them found their owner. The mug is the found object that waits. Concrete link: the mug with no claimant.
2. **The found object → the Bureau des Objets Trouvés.** Paris, 1805: Napoleon's prefecture founded the world's oldest lost-and-found office — it still processes roughly 180,000 objects a year, shelves of bicycles, instruments, dentures, the occasional wedding dress. Fresh angle: an institution whose entire job is the waiting — the shelves are the slow queue of a city forgetting things. Concrete link: the office of the waiting.
3. **The office → the ledger nobody reads.** Every object is registered; most are never collected. The claim period expires and the unclaimed are sold — the deadline turns the lost into the sold. Fresh angle: the ledger is a diary of intentions that expired — the paperwork outlives the hope. Concrete link: the expired claim.
4. **→ this:** "The Waiting Shelf" (the waiting is the job) + lore THE CLAIM PERIOD (the deadline that turns the lost into the sold).

### Chain 2 — the split log (start: B-1040 "The Split Log", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The split → the cord.** A cord of firewood = 128 cubic feet, defined by the length of the cord wrapped around the stack to measure it. Fresh angle: the measuring rope became the unit's name — the tool is the title; the cord is a sentence about length. Concrete link: the measuring rope.
2. **The measured stack → the Holzhausen.** The roundest stack is the "wood house": a ~10-foot-diameter cylinder around a center pole, bark-shingle roof — the chimney shape draws air up the middle and dries wet splits in a single summer. The field account comes from a Canadian chimney sweep's trade notes. Fresh angle: the beehive is a machine — the stack is the season's kiln. Concrete link: the round stack.
3. **The stacked winter → the hinge.** The feller's notch and the hinge wood: the tree is persuaded, not felled — the cut steers the fall; the hinge is the argument the saw makes to the trunk. Fresh angle: the fall is negotiated before it is allowed — the notch is the sentence, the lean is the verdict. Concrete link: the steering cut.
4. **→ this:** "The Measured Cord" (the rope is the unit) + "The Hinge Cut" (the persuasion before the fall).

### Chain 3 — the turned compost (start: B-1042 "The Turned Compost", shipped 2026-10-16)

1. **The turned pile → garbology.** William Rathje's Tucson Garbage Project (1973): archaeologists excavated modern landfills and found that what people THROW AWAY is truer than what they report — the discarded is the honest survey. Fresh angle: the city throws away its autobiography — the trash is the true ledger. Concrete link: the honest bin.
2. **The honest trash → the midden.** Danish kitchen middens: 6,000-year-old shell dumps read as menus — oysters, tools, broken crockery, layered by season. Fresh angle: the dump is the diary — the layered read is the archive's oldest method. Concrete link: the layered read.
3. **The layered read → the chiffonnier.** The rag-and-bone men of Paris pushed sorted carts: bone in one pile, cloth in another, paper in a third — each pile its own market, each market its own buyer. Fresh angle: the sorter is the archivist of the thrown-away — the cart is a classification system that walks. Concrete link: the sorted cart.
4. **→ this:** "The Garbologist" (the trash is the true ledger) + "The Chiffonnier's Cart" (the walking classification).

### Chain 4 — plot research: the sweep, the certificate, the tag (real trades and their paperwork)

1. **The sweep's brush.** The chimney sweep's round: brush on rods after the 1875 Act ended the climbing boys — the flue is a room you work in standing on your knees. Fresh angle: the dirtiest room in the town is the one you clean standing inside it. Plot translation: the sweep whose workplace is the inside of the building's throat.
2. **The brush → the sold soot.** Soot was sold to farmers as nitrogen fertilizer — the sweep's bag was inventory, the dirt had a market. Fresh angle: the sweep sells what he cleans away — the product is the by-product. Plot translation: the bag weighed and sold at the gate.
3. **The sold dirt → the sweep's certificate.** Fire insurers required a signed swept certificate — the paper proving the flue was clean. Fresh angle: the signature is the product too — the paper is cleaner than the chimney. Plot translation: the certificate as the real deliverable.
4. **The certified paper → the claim tag.** The cloakroom's brass tag: the coat checked, the number kept — the tag is a loan agreement with a number instead of a name. Fresh angle: the paper stands in for the thing — the tag is the coat, legally. Plot translation: the tag that names the coat.
5. **→ this:** "The Sold Soot" (the dirt is the product) + "The Sweep's Certificate" (the paper is cleaner) + "The Numbered Coat" (the tag is the contract).

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (17:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

Production note: the counter bisects the frame; the hand sliding the object across is the 4–6s event. Without the counter the institution is just a person — the furniture is the premise.

Production note: repeat the gesture twice in frame (two brush passes, two measures) — the second proves it is a round, not a stop.

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (18:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the washed mug (start: B-1043 "The Washed Mug", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **Washed mug → the wrapped hotel glass.** Tamper-evidence as a service: the sealed plastic says nobody used this since the cleaner. The wash is not the state — the WRAP is the proof of the wash. Fresh angle: a cleaned object needs a certificate that it stayed clean.
2. **Tamper-evidence → the bill of health.** A port-of-departure document on the sanitary state of a ship (consul's handbook 1879): a *clean* bill = no disease known; a *suspected* or *touched* bill = rumors circulating, unconfirmed; a *foul* bill or no bill at all = quarantine. Fresh angle: the *suspected* grade — the rumor, unconfirmed, is itself a document class. Paperwork does not need the fact.
3. **The bill → pratique.** The port medical officer's certificate that lets the ship dock and the crew land; he is the FIRST person aboard every arriving vessel. Flag Q flown alone = "my ship is healthy and I request free pratique"; QQ = suspect; QL = infected; by night, red over white lights = "I have not free pratique." Fresh angle: arrival is not entry — a thing can be in plain sight, flag up, and still not be *in*.
4. **Owned-territory check:** "Free Pratique" (NEWS, drafted 2026-10-12) already used the Q flag + the waiting crate, and THE PRATIQUE RULE (present is not received) is banked lore. This chain steers to the two unused nodes: the SUSPECTED grade (the rumor as paperwork) and the officer himself (a background figure with a job and a motive — he wants the queue to move).

### Chain 2 — the fallen mast (start: #161 A-23 "The Mast That Fell", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **A-23's mast → the Warsaw/Konstantynów mast.** 646.38 m, the tallest structure ever built until the Burj Khalifa (2010). August 8, 1991, 16:00 UTC: during replacement of frayed guy wires, the main cable was disconnected before the two temporary cables could be connected; a gust twisted the temporarily unmoored tower and it snapped at roughly half its height. (Sources: Wikipedia Warsaw radio mast / Konstantynów; amusingplanet.)
2. **The gap → the unmoored minute.** The fall happened BETWEEN supports — not in the storm, in the handover. Fresh angle: the most dangerous state is between supports. (THE UNKEPT LOG is owned by an earlier A-23 chain — this steers to the gap itself, not the missing book.)
3. **The liability → the sentences.** The construction coordinator and the division chief were found liable and sentenced to 2.5 years in prison (one shortened to six months); the foreman kept no construction log, so the exact sequence is unknown. Fresh angle: the paperwork failure became a prison sentence — the log is structural, and its absence is a crime with a term.
4. **The staff → the mast's town.** 30 engineers, 15 administrative staff, guards hired by the Ministry of Interior from Konstantynów itself — and a block of flats built 30 km away in Sochaczew to house the crew. Fresh angle: the tallest structure ever built had its own housing block. The mast had a town.
5. **The tether → the only signal home.** The mast was the sole means for Polish expatriates to tune into homeland broadcasts; replaced at Solec Kujawski with two masts; the wreckage rusted in place until it was finally cleared in 2021 — only the concrete foundation and the helix building remain. Fresh angle: it was the tallest thing ever built; it is now a foundation.

### Chain 3 — the receiving cage (start: #159 PA-27 "The Receiving Cage", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **The cage → Unclaimed Baggage, Scottsboro, Alabama.** 1970: insurance salesman Doyle Owens hears on ham radio that Trailways buses have too much unclaimed luggage; he borrows a pickup and $300, drives to Washington D.C., sells the contents from card tables. First airline deal 1978 (Eastern). The only store of its kind in the US: 50,000 sq ft, ~7,000 new items a day, 1M+ visitors a year. (Sources: Wikipedia; Encyclopedia of Alabama; CNN.)
2. **The pipeline → the three fates.** Airlines hold bags 90–120 days while locating owners (IATA); the unsold remainder is sorted into three streams — resell, repurpose, recycle — and for every item sold, roughly one is donated. Fresh angle: the lost has exactly three fates, and the store is the court that assigns them. (Motif tie-in: THE CLASSIFIED, banked 17:00.)
3. **The finds → the mascot.** Past finds: a presidential platinum Rolex, a 5.8-carat diamond ring, a camera from the Space Shuttle (returned to NASA), an Egyptian burial mask — and the Hoggle puppet from *Labyrinth*, restored and standing in the entryway to greet guests. Fresh angle: the one lost thing that is never sold becomes the town's mascot. The kept is the kept.
4. **The 90 days → the transfer rule.** At day 90 the lost becomes the hall's. THE CLAIM PERIOD (banked 17:00) is the owner's window; this is the mirror rule — the hall's clock. Fresh angle: the deadline does not destroy the lost; it transfers it.

### Chain 4 — the punch-in (start: #160 NE-18 "The First In", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **The punched clock → the ship's bell.** Both are time-as-counting: the watch is never announced, it is counted — one bell per half-hour, struck in pairs, EIGHT BELLS = the watch is over ("Eight Bells and All Is Well"). Owned-check: NE-12/"The Relieved Watch" already banked the eighth bell as a handoff. This chain steers to the two unused nodes below.
2. **Eight bells → sixteen.** At midnight on New Year's Eve, sixteen bells are struck — eight for the old year, eight for the new. Fresh angle: the year turns by count, not by announcement.
3. **The bell → the bell as font.** Naval tradition: the inverted ship's bell is used as a baptismal font; children's names are engraved on the bell. Fresh angle: the count has a congregation — the bell holds the names of everyone it ever timed.
4. **The watch → the dog watch.** 16:00–20:00 is split into two two-hour watches so the crew's daily rotation turns AND everyone gets the evening meal. Fresh angle: the schedule is kind on purpose — the split exists so everyone eats. A plot with a want: the watch ends early because dinner does.

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (18:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F101 — the object delivers the verdict; the line only re-names it.** B-1011 shipped with the directed line weak and ~1s late and still read clean — because the sealed pipe was already the verdict by 9.5s. Production note: direct the OBJECT to complete the premise by 9.5s; the line at 7–10s may arrive late and quiet but must never BE the verdict. A take whose line carries the premise is a take that can fail on the voice axis; a take whose object carries it can only fail on the visible.
- **10S-F102 — the closing sound owns the last second.** Ship's-bell grammar: the watch ends on eight bells, never seven; a take that ends on a middle event leaves the viewer mid-watch. Production note: place the closing sound (bell, pip, stamp, seal-snap) at 8–10s — the ear files the take by its last second. Furniture-lines (the 09:00 study) land at 6–7s; the closing event owns 7–10s. (Corroborated by bank line 3040's closing-period rule — independent arrival, same rule.)

## 2026-10-16 Q0 research run (19:00 EDT) — hop chains

### Chain 1 — the read (start: #162 O-72 "The Meter Room", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **#162's meter → the five-dial watthour meter.** Read RIGHT TO LEFT; dials alternate direction (units clockwise, tens counter-clockwise, hundreds clockwise...); between numbers = record the lower; between 9 and 0 = record 9; a pointer exactly on a number is checked against the dial to its right. Fresh angle: the official reading runs BACKWARDS — the small dial is senior. (Sources: HowStuffWorks power-meter guide; SaskPower five-dial reading card; utility reading guides.)
2. **The backwards dials → the reader's round.** The meter reader walks door to door; the reading is a pointing act — the guides all say "stand directly in front of the meter." The SaskPower self-read card ("record the 5 numbers right to left starting at the far right") is paperwork: the card is the job. Fresh angle: the hand is the cursor — the reading happens where the finger points.
3. **The reader → the barograph.** The machine that reads ITSELF: partially-evacuated aneroid cells stacked in series → lever train → pen arm; the chart rides a clockwork drum rotating once per day, week, or month. The product is the barogram — the room's memory drawn as a line. Fresh angle: the weather writes itself down while nobody watches. (Sources: Wikipedia Barograph; USGS object record USGS-000242; Univ. of Reading 120-year-old barograph test.)
4. **The barogram → Cumming's barograph clock.** Alexander Cumming, watchmaker, built barometrical clocks in the 1760s — one for King George III. One surviving clock was bought by Luke Howard and used for the world's first urban climate studies; the traces were published 1847 as *Barometrographia*. A clock whose dial rotates once a YEAR, recording pressure. Fresh angle: the pressure of 1847 is still on the chart — the weather has an author.
5. **The clock → Ronalds' photographic barograph (1845, Kew Observatory).** Francis Ronalds recorded the mercury column continuously on a moving photosensitive surface — the reading made by LIGHT, not ink; used by the UK Meteorological Office for years. Fresh angle: the same measurement, three centuries of readers — dial, pen, photograph.

### Chain 2 — the sheet (start: B-1053 "The Couched Sheet", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **B-1053's sheet → laid paper.** Chain lines (wide-spaced, parallel to the shorter sides) + laid lines (fine, at right angles) — the wire grid of the mould imparted to every sheet; the fibers sink between the wires, so the paper is thinner where the mould stood proud. Fresh angle: the sheet REMEMBERS its wires — hold it to transmitted light and the grid of its birth appears. (Sources: Harvard Art Museums conservator piece; Wikipedia Laid paper; LOC Bibliomania papermaking.)
2. **The remembered grid → the moldmates.** Every mould was made by hand; no two are exactly alike. Scholars identify Rembrandt prints' moldmates by measuring chain-line spacing — the paper is fingerprinted by its mould. Fresh angle: the sheet has a birth certificate written in wire.
3. **The mould → the three hands.** The vatman dips the mould and shakes; the coucher flips the mould onto felt and hurries it back to the vat; the layer peels sheets from felt. 700–1500 sheets a day over 9–12 hour days. Fresh angle: the paper is made by PASSING — a relay of three people, one sheet.
4. **The relay → the watermark.** Silver wires twisted into a shape and woven into the mould; the paper is thinner where the wire impeded the fibers — the mill's signature IN the paper, used as authenticating branding distinguishing one company of craftsmen from another. Fresh angle: the signature you can only read against the light.
5. **The watermark → wove paper.** James Whatman, ~1756; Baskerville's 1757 Virgil — the smooth paper that FORGETS its mould. Fresh angle: laid remembers, wove forgets — the network's sheets are the remembering kind.

### Chain 3 — the seam (start: B-1052 "The Caulked Seam", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **B-1052's seam → oakum.** "Off-combings" (Old English ācumba) — old tarry ropes unraveled by hand, "picking." A prison and workhouse occupation: Tothill Fields 1862, girls under 16 picked 1 lb a day, boys 1.5 lb; Coldbath Fields men 2 lb, up to 6 on hard labour; sailors under naval punishment sentenced to pick 1 lb a day. Fresh angle: the seam is sealed with YESTERDAY'S ROPE — the old rope becomes the new seal. (Sources: Wikipedia Oakum; The Craftsman Blog oakum history.)
2. **The picked fiber → the pitch house and oakum loft.** The yard kept a building for each — Building 10 at the USS Constitution Museum site is the pitch house and oakum loft. Fresh angle: the material had an ADDRESS — pitch in one building, oakum in the other. (Source: USS Constitution Museum via the "Warship Floated on Hammered Rope Fiber" short.)
3. **The loft → paying.** "Paying" = filling a seam with caulking or pitch (French paix, pitch) — to PAY a seam is to SEAL it; money is the other meaning. Fresh angle: the seam gets its wages.
4. **The paying → the devil.** "The devil to pay (and no pitch hot)" — the devil was the longest, hardest seam; on a beached ship it was the last seam finished before the tide came back. Fresh angle: the worst job had a NAME.

### Chain 4 — the skein (start: B-1051 "The Lifted Skein", shipped 2026-10-16)
1. **B-1051's dye → mauveine.** 1856: 18-year-old William Henry Perkin, trying to synthesize quinine (malaria), oxidized aniline with potassium dichromate, washed the black sludge with alcohol — and the alcohol turned purple. Patented; dyeworks at Greenford; the first synthetic organic dye; its structure not identified until 1994. Fresh angle: the most important color of the century was a FAILED MEDICINE — the mistake was archived. (Sources: Imperial College Perkin page; Wikipedia Mauveine; ScienceBlog Easter-experiment account.)
2. **The failed medicine → Tyrian purple.** 12,000 murex snails = 1.4 grams (1908 experiment); the smell was so bad that processing centers were located downwind of populations — Martial wrote that Tyre kept a permanent fishy smell, and joked that a woman in purple liked the odor, not the color; worth its weight in silver; Nero made wearing it a capital offense; the knowledge was lost after 1453. Fresh angle: THE EXILED COLOR — the most expensive color lived outside the city because of its smell. (Sources: National Geographic; HISTORY; Chemical Processing.)
3. **The dye → the niddy-noddy.** The skein IS a measurement: winding = counting; each loop a fixed length (the classic wrap two yards; the counting rhyme "'Tis one, 'tain't two, 'twill be two by and by"); one tool does both jobs — wind the skein AND measure it. Fresh angle: the skein is a tally — yarn counted by winding. (Sources: stitchpiecenpurl; American Centuries tool demo; Maine spinning-lesson PDF.)
4. **The winding → the weasel.** The clock-like yarn weasel is set to hold a fixed yardage — when the count is complete, it POPS. Fresh angle: the count announces itself.

- **THE BACKWARD READ** — "The official reading runs backwards: the small dial is senior; between numbers, take the lower." (Chain 1.) Staged: "The Backward Read."
- **THE READER'S ROUND** — "The reader walks; the dials do not come to him." (Chain 1.) Staged: "The Backward Read" (figure: THE READER).
