## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (02:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

Seeds: B-1228 "The Same Hallway" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the door opened onto the same hallway; "Still the hallway."); B-1225 "The Catchword" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the word at the foot of the page, matched and hidden, NO-LINE); B-1224 "The Sorter's Caution" (shipped 2026-10-18 — composing room, "Mind the q."); B-1222 "The Break-Room Pot" (shipped 2026-10-17 — the pot filled, "The pot is ready.").

### Chain 1 — the same hallway (seed: B-1228 "The Same Hallway")
1. The recursive hallway → **THE WINCHESTER HOUSE.** Sarah Winchester, San Jose, 1884–1922: 38 years of continuous building, 160 rooms, 2,000 doors, 10,000 windows — doors that open onto blank walls, staircases that lead nowhere, windows that look into other rooms (wisegeek; frankrose.com). Fresh angle: the most famous hallway in America never leaves the house — the recursion is the floor plan.
2. Winchester → **THE 44-STEP STAIRCASE.** A switchback staircase with 44 steps rising only 9 feet (daytrippen). Fresh angle: the building defeats the walker one inch at a time — the climb is real, the arrival is not.
3. The shallow stairs → **THE SEANCE ROOM.** A hidden room reached only by a secret passage, where Sarah received the next day's building instructions nightly (iheart podcast). Fresh angle: the house was built on a nightly broadcast — the instructions arrive in the dark and are executed in the light. Staged in "The Seance Instructions" below.
4. The secret room → **THE 13TH FLOOR.** Winchester's lucky 13 woven through the house — thirteen hooks, thirteen panes (iheart); the modern hotel does the inverse — the 13th floor skipped, the button missing, the car still stopping. Fresh angle: two buildings agree the number is special — one shows it everywhere, one shows nothing. Staged in "The Unnumbered Stop" below.
5. The skipped 13 → **THE CAR CALL.** The call is registered; the car comes; the floor is never numbered. Lineage vs draft B-1229 "The Car Call" (the elevator call as the subject — the call vs the arrival; adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged). Fresh angle: the only stop that never gets a number is the one the building won't name.
6. The car call → **THE UNNUMBERED STOP.** Staged below.

### Chain 2 — the catchword (seed: B-1225 "The Catchword")
1. The catchword → **THE DECORATED CATCHWORD.** Catchwords at the end of quires as early as c.1000, widespread by the 12th century (historyofinformation); scribes decorated them — Lyon ms Palais des Arts 31 encloses catchwords in witty cartoons; one nervous 13th-century scribe added them redundantly in red with squiggly lines where quire numbers already sufficed (textmanuscripts). Fresh angle: the margin's instruction became the margin's doodle — order-keeping as decoration.
2. The decorated catchword → **THE CATCHWORD ERROR.** One reads "ec est."; the next page begins "Hec est" — the error is the visible proof the scribe left the initial's space blank for the rubricator (textmanuscripts). Fresh angle: the mistake shows the work — the correction is embedded in the accident.
3. The error → **THE TWO-BOOK PROBLEM.** Catchwords "make it impossible to mix up quires meant for two different books" (textmanuscripts). Fresh angle: the system was designed for the shop running two books at once — the confusion was the business model.
4. The two books → **THE CHAINED BOOK.** Hereford Cathedral's Chained Library (1611, Thomas Thornton): 1,500 books, 229 medieval manuscripts; a chain from each book's front cover to a rod along the shelf — a reader could take a book to the desk but never out of the room; unchained 1841 (herefordcathedral.org; museumsuk). Fresh angle: the library is a vault the readers enter — the book is free inside a room it can never leave. Staged in "The Wrong Way Round" below.
5. The chained book → **THE WRONG WAY ROUND.** Books shelved foredges-out, spines-in ("the wrong way round to us") so a chained book can be lifted down and opened without tangling the chain — the constraint designed the display (printedpearls; herefordcathedral.org). Fresh angle: the most browsable library hides every title — finding is the job. Stages banked lore THE FORE-EDGE OUT (2026-10-14) — first staging, lineage flagged.
6. The wrong way round → **THE MAPPA MUNDI.** The largest surviving medieval world map (c. 1300, 1.6m of calf vellum, Jerusalem at the centre, the Last Judgement above) hangs beside the chained books at Hereford (museumsuk). Fresh angle: the library's map is not a finding aid — it is the whole of creation with the judgement built in. (Unbanked landing — the map is the room.)

### Chain 3 — the sorter's caution (seed: B-1224 "The Sorter's Caution")
1. Mind the q → **THE NEIGHBOR COMPARTMENTS.** In the type case lowercase p and q sit adjacent — "begging to be mixed up"; it is "mind your p's and q's" and never "mind your b's and d's" because only p and q are neighbors; the compositor sets backwards, upside-down, right-to-left (mentalfloss; wikipedia). Fresh angle: the alphabet has a neighborhood and the bad neighbors live next door — the error is real estate.
2. The neighbors → **THE DISS.** After printing, the expensive sorts are redistributed into the case — called sorting or "dissing"; an error in dissing (a p filed in the b compartment) manufactures a future misprint (wikipedia). Fresh angle: the misprint is seeded at cleanup — tomorrow's error is filed today.
3. The diss → **OUT OF SORTS.** Running out of type mid-job makes the printer "out of sorts" — the phrase is a stock report; wrongly filed sorts do it too (mentalfloss; tbd.co.nz). Fresh angle: the mood is inventory — "I am out of sorts" is a warehouse status. Staged in "The Out of Sorts" below.
4. Out of sorts → **THE STICK.** Setting type "on the stick" — composing without written copy, in a hurry (billkovarik). Fresh angle: the rush is a method — the hurry is scheduled. (Unbanked landing.)
5. The stick → **THE WAYZGOOSE.** Bartholomew-tide (24 August): the journeymen make new paper windows; the master printer gives them a feast — entertained at his own house, then money to spend at the ale-house; "till the Master-Printer have given this Way-goose, the Journeymen do not use to Work by Candle Light" (Moxon 1683 via CPHC; conviviobookworks). Fresh angle: the candle-light season opens with a goose — the dark half of the year is licensed by a feast. Staged in "The Wayzgoose" below.
6. The wayzgoose → **THE CHAPEL.** The printers' own court: the Father of the Chapel (usually the oldest printer) summons the members at the imposing stone, receives allegations and defence "in solemn assembly," and dispenses justice "with typographical rigour and impartiality" — the punishment is a libation so the offended may wash away the stain; compositors jocosely "galley-slaves," pressmen "horses" (A Dictionary of Printers and Printing, p.525 via wikisource). Fresh angle: the print shop has its own judiciary — and its sentences are served in the tavern. Staged in "The Chapel" below. Stages banked lore THE CHAPEL (2026-10-14) — first staging, lineage flagged.

### Chain 4 — the break-room pot (seed: B-1222 "The Break-Room Pot")
1. The pot → **THE GREEN ROOM.** The theatre's break room: first recorded December 1678 in Shadwell's "The True Widow" — "in a green Room, behind the Scenes"; Colley Cibber 1701 expects the term to be known; the green-baize theory — green cloth stored for death scenes, laid so actors could die without dirtying the expensive unwashed costumes; "green" as a corruption of "scene" (worldwidewords; theatrecrafts; nickhernbooksblog). Fresh angle: the waiting room doubles as the costume morgue — the baize for the death is kept where the living wait. Staged in "The Baize" below.
2. The green room → **THE HIERARCHY OF ROOMS.** Early theatres kept several green rooms, graded hierarchically by the actor's salary (theatrecrafts). Fresh angle: the waiting is tiered — the room knows your billing. (Unbanked landing — the graded wait.)
3. The tiers → **THE SAILORS' KNOTS.** No whistling on stage: set builders and riggers were hired from ships in port; the backstage knots were passed down from sailors (nickhernbooksblog). Fresh angle: the fly tower is a ship's rigging with an audience — the theatre is sailed by land. Lineage vs shipped B-1223 "The Granny Knot" (the rigger's knot vs the cooper's knot — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
4. The sailors → **THE NO-WHISTLE RULE.** Whistling on stage could drop things on your head — the riggers' cue language was whistles, so a casual whistle was a command (nickhernbooksblog). Fresh angle: the backstage has a forbidden note — one whistle is an order.
5. The forbidden note → **THE GHOST LIGHT.** The single bare bulb on a wheeled stand left on the empty stage — safety (don't fall into the pit), then superstition (keep the ghosts company); "the last one in and the first one out" (banked lore 2026-10-11). Fresh angle: the theatre's break room has a night-light — the empty stage is never dark.
6. The ghost light → **THE ALL-NIGHT PATTERN.** The broadcast answer: the test pattern after sign-off, the transmitter alive to an empty room (banked lore — "The Liveness Bureau" venture). Fresh angle: the ghost light is television's too — the pattern is the bulb. (Unbanked landing.)

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (02:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE FLOOR MANAGER'S HANDS (plot research).** The TV floor manager's signal grammar: countdown in/out (10s), the action signal — thrust of fingers toward the talent ("you're ON AIR") — two fingers = two minutes, one finger = one minute, 30s = cupped forefinger+thumb or crossed arms, "wrap up," wind up/close = a clockwise circle of the index finger ("you must close NOW"), out-of-time = a flat hand swept horizontally, stretch = both hands pulled apart rhythmically (confidenceon.camera — TV Techie Lingo). Fresh angle: an entire directing language that never makes a sound — the show is conducted in mime. Canon riff: the teal orb never speaks (continuity-web premise 27) — the floor manager's hands are its native language. Network translation: staged in "The Wind-Up" below — the hand draws the clockwise circle at 4s, the room closes by 9.5s. NO-LINE.
- **THE QUADRATS GAME (plot research).** The printers' idle ritual: roll five or seven blank spacers ("quads") onto the composing table and call how many land nick-up (billkovarik). Fresh angle: the dead minute gets a sport — the shop's dice are blank type. Network translation: staged in "The Quads" below — roll at 4s, the call at 6s, the count at 9.5s.
- **THE STAGE MANAGER'S THREE CALLS (plot research).** Warning → Standby → Go: warning a minute out, standby seconds before ("everything should be set"), go at the moment of execution — the audience never hears the first two (alchetron theatrical cue). Fresh angle: the show is called in three beats and the viewer only witnesses the third — the first two are the broadcast's unconscious. Network translation: (unbanked — #141 "The Three Calls" shipped; the middle call's lamp staged as B-1871 "The Standby Lamp"; the first call stays unstaged, reserved.)

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (02:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F171 — The hidden order beats the shown order.** The catchword: one word at the foot of the page that matches the next — the whole book's order hides in the margin. Production note: in a 10s take, one load-bearing token can carry the entire premise if it's placed where the viewer must FIND it — the foot of the frame, the last second, the edge. Don't caption the premise; margin it.
- **10S-F172 — The threshold is the content.** The wayzgoose: the candle-light season opens with a feast — the transition is the celebration, not the season. Production note: a 10s take about a season (the dark console, the sign-off, the closedown) should stage the THRESHOLD — the paper windows going up, the first candle lit — not the season itself. Thresholds read in 10s; seasons don't.
- **10S-F173 — The soundless conductor.** The floor manager's hand grammar: countdown, wrap, wind-up — all silent, all legible at studio distance. Production note: a NO-LINE take can be directed entirely in gesture grammar — the hand draws the clockwise circle at 4s, the room closes by 9.5s. Silent hands are the network's own broadcast language (the orb never speaks; neither does the floor manager).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (02:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: MEME LITERACY

- **MEME-F158 — The wayzgoose keepsake.** Printers printed a keepsake to commemorate the wayzgoose — the feast's evidence is a printed object (alchetron). Network-native: the network's own keepsake — one bumper per season with a locked keepsake layout (title + date + one still); the remix handle is the season number. Production note: the keepsake is the meme — the audience collects the set. The meme never appears in-frame; it lives in the announce line and the ledger.
- **MEME-F159 — The Chapel trial.** The Chapel's court: the Father of the Chapel, the imposing stone, sentences served as libations. Network-native: "The Chapel" as a reply-unit — a complaint tried at the imposing stone, the sentence always a round; the remix handle is the complaint. Production note: the defendant is always a prop ("the misprinted q pleads guilty") — the meme never names real people.
- **MEME-F160 — The quadrats call.** The quads game: roll five blank spacers, call how many nicks face up. Network-native: a prediction meme — one roll, one call, the count at 9.5s; the audience posts their own rolls. Production note: the remix handle is the call ("three nicks").

- **THE WINCHESTER HOUSE** (Chain 1) — San Jose, 1884–1922: 38 years of continuous building, 160 rooms, 2,000 doors, 10,000 windows; doors onto blank walls, stairs to nowhere, windows into other rooms. The most famous hallway in America never leaves the house.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (04:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

Seeds: #189 L-39 "The Retired Kilogram" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the cylinder lifted, logged, honored; "The number outlived the metal."); B-1095 "The Crab Measure" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the crab held to the gauge, released; "It measures."); #188 NE-39 "The Readiness Buzzer" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the dial found and settled; "The frequency is held."); #187 PA-49 "The Silent Guest" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the orb set on the desk, one pulse; "The guest declines to comment.").

### Chain 1 — the retired kilogram (seed: #189 "The Retired Kilogram")
1. The retired kilogram → **THE TÉMOINS.** #189's honoree was the *second* kilogram artifact to retire from the job — the pure-platinum **Kilogramme des Archives** (1799) was replaced when the 1st CGPM sanctioned the IPK in 1889. The IPK ("Le Grand K") lived under three nested bell jars in an underground vault at the Pavillon de Breteuil, Saint-Cloud, behind three separately controlled keys, with **six official sister copies kept as *témoins* — "witnesses"** (BIPM). The retirement was timed for **20 May 2019** — World Metrology Day, anniversary of the 1875 Metre Convention; the trigger: ~50 micrograms of drift, "the weight of an eyelash" (NPL). Fresh angle: six cylinders whose only job is to watch the king — and a retirement date chosen for ritual value. The number outlived the metal *twice*.
2. The témoins → **THE MÉCHAIN SECRET.** The Kilogramme des Archives and the Mètre des Archives were fabricated in June 1799 and entered the French National Archives together — twin artifacts of the 1792–99 Dunkirk-to-Barcelona meridian survey. Pierre Méchain found a **~3-second discrepancy** in his Barcelona latitude, remeasured, and **kept the second set secret, hidden in his journals** — an open secret among 19th-century astronomers (Alder, *The Measure of All Things*). The Archive Meter fell ~0.2 mm short of one ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance; the world kept it anyway; Méchain died of yellow fever in 1804, still carrying the guilt. Fresh angle: a standard *known wrong* and honored anyway — truth certified despite the file saying otherwise. The deadpan core of the whole network.
3. The flawed meter → **THE TALLY-STICK FIRE.** **16 October 1834, Palace of Westminster:** Clerk of Works Richard Whibley tasked Joshua Cross and Patrick Furlong with burning the Exchequer's obsolete tally sticks in the undersized House of Lords stoves — Dickens: "the stove, over-gorged with these preposterous sticks, set fire to the paneling." The same blaze killed John Bird's 1760 Imperial Standard Yard (recovered unfit for use; the standard pound lost outright) (Popular Science Monthly, 1881; 1911 Britannica). The 1838 Standards Commission (Airy, Baily, Herschel, Lubbock, Sheepshanks) rebuilt the yard from six surviving scales — and, lesson learned, **triplicated** it: Guildhall, the Royal Observatory Greenwich gate, Trafalgar Square (1876, still in the pavement at tourists' feet). Fresh angle: the triplication rule — after 1834, no standard ever lives in one place again; the institutional echo of the IPK's six témoins. A whole nation learning "never one copy."
4. The tally-stick fire → **THE TRIAL OF THE PYX.** Britain's *other* precious-metal artifact standards survived the fire — the trial plates (oldest from 1279, Royal Mint Museum) were kept in the Chapel of the Pyx at Westminster Abbey, the same precinct. Survivor and victim, one precinct. Held every February since **1282** at Goldsmiths' Hall (since 1870): a jury of financial leaders plus at least six Goldsmiths' assayers in red robes tests sampled coins against trial plates (today pure platinum, gold, silver, copper, nickel, zinc); the verdict is read aloud by the Clerk of the Goldsmiths' Company **at the instruction of the King's Remembrancer** — created 1154 by Henry II, England's oldest judicial position; ancient penalties for a failed trial included fine, removal, or imprisonment of the Master of the Mint (Royal Mint Museum; GOV.UK). Fresh angle: the Remembrancer — a man whose title is *rememberer* and whose job is remembering what the coin must be. Lineage vs [READY] "The Remembrancer" (01:00 run) — the verdict ceremony vs the verdict man; adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged.
5. The Pyx → **THE SEALER OF WEIGHTS.** The Pyx certifies the nation's *coin* once a year before a judge; the sealer certifies every merchant's *weights* all year in every town — the same certification ritual at different altitudes. Allan Pollock, named Boston's Sealer of Weights and Measures in **1817**, notified residents to send him "scale beams, steelyards, weights, and measures" (Smithsonian NMAH); 1848: Massachusetts issued Howard & Davis wooden-cabinet precision standards to 316 towns and 14 counties; the office still exists (Quincy's sealer at 55 Sea St; Mass. General Laws ch. 98 §34) (Historic Ipswich; Mass.gov). Fresh angle: the seal punch itself — a stamped mark on brass that says *true*; the certificate with the owner's name, the date, and the fee. Paperwork made physical.
6. The sealer → **THE TIME BALL.** The sealer's stamp certifies the standard on a shopkeeper's weight — private; the time ball broadcasts the standard (time) to everyone who can see it — public. Installed **1833** at Flamsteed House by Astronomer Royal John Pond (built by Maudslay, Son & Field): raised halfway at 12:55 as preparatory, full at 12:58, dropped at 1pm daily — still dropping; the Admiralty notice (October 1833, John Barrow): time is recorded "when the ball began descending, not when it reached the bottom"; 1pm because at noon the astronomers were busy *finding the time*; on **6 December 1855** a winter gale blew the ball off the roof into the courtyard; release automated 1852 by electric impulse from the Shepherd Master Clock (Royal Museums Greenwich; historyextra). Fresh angle: the verdict is the *release*, not the landing — the signal is the letting-go. And the gale of 1855: the sky itself failed QC once. Lineage vs shipped bumper "The Time Ball" (the letting-go vs the falling — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).

### Chain 2 — the crab measure (seed: B-1095 "The Crab Measure")
1. The gauge → **THE CULL RING.** Maryland DNR (COMAR 08.02.03): hard crab **5 inches minimum, tip to tip of the lateral spines**; every crab pot must carry **two cull rings (2 3/16" and 2 5/16")** in its panels; recreational crabbing banned Wednesdays; folk corollary — a beer can is exactly 5" tall (dnr.maryland.gov; bluecrab.info). Fresh angle: the trap has a legal escape built into it — the measurement happens inside the trap before a human hand ever touches the gauge. The ritual begins before the ritual.
2. The cull ring → **THE LOBSTER GAUGE.** The Scarborough Historical Society (Maine) holds an actual lobsterman's brass gauge: **fixed jaws, no moving parts** — hook in the eye socket, run along the carapace. Maine has a floor AND a ceiling (the max protects breeding stock); 2025: the ASMFC raised the Gulf of Maine gauge to **3 5/16"** after surveys showed young stock down **39%** against the 2016–18 baseline; Maine's haul fell 132.6M lbs (2016) → 93.7M (scarboroughhistoricalsociety.org; tricityrecordnm.com). Fresh angle: gauges grow — a museum's brass gauge was made obsolete by **one sixteenth of an inch**. The tool is a dated law you hold in your hand; every gauge carries its expiry year.
3. The gauge → **THE V-NOTCH.** Maine 1872: first law against taking egg-bearing females. 1917: seed lobsters physically marked — a **punch through the middle tail flipper**; punched lobsters became **state property**, selling one was fined. 1948: the punch became a V-notch. 2002: mandatory, zero tolerance — any mark, however small, and the female goes back. The lobsterman's rule: "If I'm not going to keep it then the next guy shouldn't either." The notch lasts ~2 years (vnotch.info; mlcalliance.org). Fresh angle: the 1917 "state property" punch — the government branded a lobster so it could never be sold; a living animal carrying a legal document in its tail.
4. The notch → **THE SLOT LIMIT.** ASMFC Addendum VI (2020): striped bass coastwide recreational slot **28" to less than 35"** (one fish); Maryland ocean 28–31"; Chesapeake Bay 19–24"; Massachusetts' revised rule: **pinch the upper and lower fork of the tail together** for the official total length (asmfc.org; onthewater.com; thefisherman.com). Fresh angle: the tail-pinch — a fish's *official* length is whatever it measures with its tail squeezed; the measurer's thumb is part of the instrument. The trophy must go back.
5. The slot → **THE CULL BOARD.** Maryland Natural Resources Code §4-1015: oysters **culled on the natural bar where caught**; under **3 inches** (hinge to bill) back; the inseparables clause — a small oyster adhering to a marketable one goes back WITH it; 5% possession tolerance; the Potomac River Fisheries Commission adds the clock — **the cull board must be cleared within 15 minutes after lawful hours end** (law.justia.com; prfc.us). Fresh angle: the inseparables clause — the law contains a provision for pairs that won't let go; and the 15-minute rule — the ritual has a countdown.
6. The cull board → **THE OYSTER NAVY.** **March 30, 1868:** Maryland created the State Oyster Police Force — $22,000 for the Civil-War tug *Leila*, two boats, arms, ammunition; first commander **Hunter Davidson** (Naval Academy, Civil War veteran) ordered to cruise "wherever opposition to the oyster law has arisen"; a **1,450-pound cannon firing 12-pound balls** mounted on the *Leila*; December 1888: the *Governor R. M. McLane* was ambushed by pirates, **rammed and sank two of them, took 24 prisoners**. The cannon now sits in the lobby of the **Cas Taylor House** legislative office building, Annapolis — displayed for the Natural Resources Police's 150th anniversary (boundarystones.weta.org; dnr.maryland.gov). Fresh angle: the measurement-enforcement institution ended as a hallway exhibit behind a rope barrier — the gun that guarded the gauge now needs a docent.

### Chain 3 — the readiness buzzer (seed: #188 "The Readiness Buzzer")
1. The held frequency → **WWV.** The NIST Radio Section's call sign **WWV** was assigned **October 1, 1919** — "it is unknown why they were originally chosen"; first standard-frequency broadcasts **January 29, 1923**, made "to help users calibrate their radios"; before settling into the role the station broadcast music concerts and market news for farm bureaus from a first-floor office on Connecticut Avenue (NIST; J. Res. NIST "A Century of WWV"). Fresh angle: the institutional deadpan — it stopped performing and became the mark against which everything else is measured.
2. WWV → **THE PIPS.** February 5, 1924, 9:30 p.m.: six 1 kHz pips — five a tenth of a second, the sixth half a second, the hour changing at the start of the final pip; Astronomer Royal Sir Frank Watson Dyson + BBC Director-General John Reith; built by 18-year-old **Harry Lampen Edwards**, controlled by two mechanical clocks at the Royal Observatory; the 2024 centenary asked "Do We Still Need the Pips?" — digital broadcast delay had rendered them chronically *inaccurate*, yet they endure (stackscale; SWLing Post). Fresh angle: a ceremony of precision that outlived its own accuracy — the network keeps the ritual after the clock breaks. Lineage vs shipped bumper "The Pips" (the ceremony vs the pip — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
3. The pips → **BOW BELLS INTERVAL SIGNAL.** The English World Service interval signal: a **1926 recording of Bow Bells**, broadcast as a symbol of hope through WWII; January 1941 added Morse "V" (three dots + dash) — V-for-Victory, the first four notes of Beethoven's Fifth (SWLing Post citing the 1975 World Radio TV Handbook). Fresh angle: the station saying its name before it has anything to say — pure ident, held for minutes, on a crowded band.
4. Bow Bells → **THE SPEAKING CLOCK.** July 24, 1936: the GPO speaking clock (TIM); first voice **Ethel Jane Cain**, chosen from **15,000 applicants** in the "Girl with the Golden Voice" competition; she recorded in "bites" — "At the third stroke," then the hours — on **glass discs**, in a room-sized machine locked to Greenwich; one original machine now in the British Horological Institute museum — its motor failed the same day **Pat Simmons** (the clock's second voice, 1963–1985) died (2005) (BT press office; HistoryExtra; The Register). Fresh angle: the recording grammar — the hour spoken in jerks into glass — and the machine that died with its voice. Lineage vs shipped bumper "The Third Stroke" (the clock room vs the stroke — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
5. The speaking clock → **THE QSL CARD.** "QSL" = "I confirm receipt"; the earliest known card sent **1916**, 8VX (Buffalo) → 3TQ (Philadelphia); the standardized card (callsign, frequency, date) possibly 1919, C.D. Hoffman 8UX (Akron); Europe's first 1922, W.E.F. "Bill" Corsham 2UV, Harlesden (QSL Museum; Medium Wave Circle). Fresh angle: the QSL desk was the ratings department before ratings — a man waits two years for a postcard that says, in effect, "received." Lineage vs #175 "The QSL" (the receipt vs the receipt — #175 staged the QSL bureau's busted-call discard; the QSL card here is the *confirmation* — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
6. The QSL → **THE 500 kHz SILENT PERIODS.** After the Titanic, the 1912 London Radiotelegraph Conference fixed **500 kHz** as the distress wavelength; all stations observed a strictly enforced **three-minute international silent period twice hourly, at :15 and :45 past the hour GMT** — operators logged twice per hour that the silence *was* observed; ship radio-room clocks marked the silence sectors in **RED** (:15–:18, :45–:48) (ITU "Pioneers," 2006; Radiotelegraph Operator's License Q&A Manual, 1970, via archive.org). Fresh angle: time itself marked on the dial where nobody may speak — red sectors on a clock face, twice an hour, worldwide; the withheld event, logged as observed.

### Chain 4 — the silent guest (seed: #187 "The Silent Guest")
1. The declined comment → **NO COMMENT.** First recorded as a stock answer in **1950** by Charles Ross, Truman's White House press secretary (Wikipedia); William Safire traces the phrase to Sumner Welles via Churchill, who after a 1946 White House meeting called it "a splendid expression" (groupgordon.com). Fresh angle: the refusal is the quote — saying nothing is a complete segment, and it is older than television news.
2. The refusal → **THE VISITORS' BOOK.** Storied antecedents in medieval monasteries — the **Grand Chartreuse** in Savoy; the Notes & Queries 1853 genealogy traces the "album" to **Bede**, earliest specimen the **Book of Life of Durham Cathedral** (British Library); German learned men's albums; Swift's 1730 windowpane verse at Willoughby ("There are three Crosses at your door..."); Victorian hotel books as rituals of arrival and departure — volumes the proprietors produced, superintended, redacted, withdrew, and destroyed (libra.unine.ch). Fresh angle: the guest who refuses the interview still has to sign — the book keeps what the microphone loses.
3. The guest book → **THE HOTEL REGISTER.** The signing-in ritual at the desk; the register kept behind the desk, belonging to the house. Fresh angle: the register is the house's evidence — the names belong to the building, not the guests. (Unbanked landing — the night desk waits.)
4. The register → **THE RECEIVING LINE.** U.S. State Department protocol for official functions: Announcer – Host – Guest of Honor – Guest of Honor's Wife – Host's Wife – **Extra Man**; the announcer listens to your name and never shakes your hand; **~20 seconds per guest**; 100 guests = 30–45 minutes; "names do not travel well" — repeat yours to each person (whcinsider.com; hollyholden.com; lisagrotts.com). Fresh angle: the most formal social machine in American life is a queue with a script, running on 20-second units — the network's 10s is the receiving line cut in half.
5. The receiving line → **THE EXTRA MAN.** The protocol's last man: his function is to avoid placing a woman at the end of the line and to move guests into the reception area; if the line runs too long, **he may be eliminated**. Fresh angle: there is a named job that IS "the end of the line" — and the protocol explicitly allows his elimination.
6. The extra man → **THE LOCKOUT.** The College Bowl TV show implemented a buzzer system as studio furniture; previous lockout systems used by Bible Bowl as early as the 1950s (**John P. Reynolds** of Dayton, OH — the portable-buzzer patent filed 1972); the original Jeopardy! buzzer ran solenoid-driven plungers; **September 1985**: ring-in only after the clue, board lights added, early ring-in = **0.5s lockout** (qbwiki.com; trebisky.com). Fresh angle: the receiving line teaches patience with a queue; the buzzer teaches it with a penalty — eagerness is the only offense. Lineage vs shipped bumper "The Buzzer" (the punished ring vs the held tone — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (05:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

Seeds: B-1237 "The Wash House" (shipped 2026-10-18 — wring/hang/peg a shirt; "Wring it twice."); B-1228 "The Same Hallway" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the recursive reveal, a door opened onto the SAME hallway; "Still the hallway."); B-1232 "The Steady Needle" (shipped 2026-10-18 — boiler room, walk-stop-read; "The needle holds."); B-1233 "The Turned Hay" (shipped 2026-10-18 — ted/stack + cock verdict; "The sun does the drying.").

### Chain 1 — the wash house (seed: B-1237 "The Wash House")
1. The wring → **THE LAVOIR.** Law of 3 February 1851 (Napoleon III): state subsidies up to 30% of construction costs for public wash-houses; Haussmann's 1850s redesign put a free lavoir in every Paris neighbourhood; some lavoirs date to the 10th century; the lavoir was "the central gathering place for women... as much a part of communal life as the market" (Roddier, via Taubman/Princeton Architectural Press); by the 18th century their construction was a public-health measure against cholera and typhoid. Fresh angle: the wash-house was the village newsroom — the news got washed along with the shirts. Lineage vs B-1237 (the institution vs the wring — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
2. The lavoir → **BATEAUX-LAVOIRS.** Laundry boats moored on the banks of the Seine at Paris and Lyon — floating laundries, the washing done ON the river. Fresh angle: the wash-house that sways and creaks with the river.
3. The wash boats → **LE BATEAU-LAVOIR.** 13 rue Ravignan (Place Ravignan, rechristened Place Émile Goudeau 1911), Montmartre; the name coined by poet Max Jacob because the dark, dirty, creaking wooden building reminded residents of the Seine wash-boats; formerly a ballroom and piano factory; squatted 1889 and divided into 20 small workshops along a corridor with a single water source; Picasso lived there 1904–1912 and painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) there; fire May 1970, rebuilt 1978. Fresh angle: the building where Cubism was born is named after a laundry barge — the name out-arted the art.
4. The renamed square → **THE RENAMED ADDRESS.** Place Ravignan → Place Émile Goudeau (1911), for Émile Goudeau (1849–1906), founder of the Les Hydropathes literary club. Fresh angle: the square was renamed; the wash-boat name stuck — the nickname outlived the address. Paperwork that refuses to update.
5. The address → **THE WASHDAY LITURGY.** The folk weekly calendar: "Wash on Monday, Iron on Tuesday, Mend on Wednesday, Churn on Thursday, Clean on Friday, Bake on Saturday, Rest on Sunday." Fresh angle: laundry had a liturgy — each day assigned; the week's washing was a seven-day programme schedule. The network runs a weekly cadence too.

### Chain 2 — the same hallway (seed: B-1228 "The Same Hallway")
1. The recursive hallway → **THE WINCHESTER RULE.** Sarah Winchester, San Jose, 1884–1922: 38 years of continuous construction (carpenters in day-and-night shifts); ~160 rooms, 2,000 doors (many to walls or drops), 47 staircases including the switchback staircase (two-inch steps, seven turns, nine feet up) and the Stairway to Nowhere ending at a ceiling; "halls winded back to their beginnings and rooms had rooms within rooms"; the 1906 earthquake trapped her in the Daisy Bedroom. Fresh angle: the house where opening a door onto the same hallway is the NORMAL condition — B-1228's gag is the house's floor plan. The Winchester Rule: keep building; never finish. (The network's own production doctrine, filed as lore.)
2. The stair-to-nowhere → **THE AMES ROOM.** Adelbert Ames Jr., 1946 (patented 1940); the trapezoidal room viewed one-eyed through a peephole reads as an ordinary rectangular room; a walker grows and shrinks crossing it; Ames' original design included a groove that rolled a ball "uphill" — an anti-gravity illusion. Fresh angle: the room that lies about where its own walls are — the hallway that denies its own shape. The generator's depth is Ames-grade; direct hallways accordingly.
3. The peephole → **PEPPER'S BLUE ROOM.** Christmas Eve 1862, John Henry Pepper at London's Royal Polytechnic Institution: a 45° sheet of plate glass + a hidden lit actor in the "blue room" = a ghost walking among the live actors of Dickens' The Haunted Man; The Times (Dec 1862) called it "the most startling novelty produced this season, at any place of entertainment"; Henry Dircks had the idea in the late 1850s but couldn't sell it to any theatre — Pepper bought his rights outright. Fresh angle: the hallway's ghost is equipment — a reflection, a lamp, a dimmer. The haunting is staged from the blue room. And Dircks: the man who invented the effect and signed the rights away.
4. The blue room → **THE TELEPROMPTER.** The modern descendant of Pepper's ghost: the angled glass that puts text in the air in front of the reader. Fresh angle: the Colonel's prompter IS the ghost machine — the news desk reads words that appear from the blue room. Canon riff: the N-series register (the desk, the straight face) is 1862 stagecraft. The Control Voice stays furniture — the prompter is equipment, never a channel.
5. The ghost text → **THE BLUE-ROOM KEEPER.** Background figure staged in "The Blue Room" below (job = the hidden lamp, motive = the ghost must appear).

### Chain 3 — the steady needle (seed: B-1232 "The Steady Needle")
1. The held needle → **THE SI NAN.** Han dynasty "south-pointing spoon": lodestone carved into a dipper, rotating on a bronze heaven-plate marked with the eight trigrams and 24 directions; the handle pointed SOUTH (the emperor faced south; south was auspicious); used for geomancy/feng shui and divination — not navigation. Fresh angle: the first needle was a fortune-telling spoon — the direction was a verdict before it was a bearing.
2. The spoon → **THE FLOATING NEEDLE.** Tang–Song: magnetized iron needle floated on wood in water (the wet compass); Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks (1119 CE) records navigational use; the transition from lodestone to magnetized needle was "a tremendous advancement." Fresh angle: the needle had to FLOAT — the instrument's verdict depended on still water. B-1232's needle holds still in a vibrating boiler room; stillness is the technology. (10S-F178 stages this.)
3. The floating needle → **THE NEEDLE ALPHABET.** Cooke & Wheatstone, patent May/June 1837: five needles on a diamond board, two converging to point at letters — 20 of 26 letters coded; first public trial 25 July 1837 (Euston–Camden); first commercial line Paddington–West Drayton 1838–39; the 5-wire system too expensive, replaced by 2-needle then single-needle; needle telegraphs ran on British railways into the 1930s. Fresh angle: the needle became the alphabet — the letter is where two needles agree. The needle is the message.
4. The alphabet → **THE MISSING Q.** The 5-needle board coded only 20 letters: no C, J, Q, U, X, Z. Fresh angle: the first electric telegraph could not send a Q — and B-1224's whole premise is "Mind the q." The letter the network minds is the letter the telegraph couldn't spell. Concrete connection to the B-1224 seed.
5. The missing Q → **THE BLOCK INDICATOR.** Single-needle railway signal block indicators — "specifically used to prevent two trains from trying to use the same length of track" (telegraphkeys.com). Fresh angle: the needle's railway job was to say "the track is occupied" — the needle holds = the track holds. Rhyme with B-1232's "The needle holds."

### Chain 4 — the turned hay (seed: B-1233 "The Turned Hay")
1. The turned hay → **THE PROVERB.** "Make hay while the sun shines" — first recorded in John Heywood's A dialogue conteinyng the nomber in effect of all the prouerbes in the Englishe tongue, 1546: "Whan the sunne shinth make hay. Whiche is to say. / Take time whan time cometh, lest time steale away." By 1673 it was already cited in a thieves-and-beggars glossary — the farm proverb had left the farm. Fresh angle: the oldest deadline in English is a weather report — the urgency is the sky, not the boss. B-1233's line ("The sun does the drying") is the proverb with the advice removed.
2. The proverb → **THE LAST SHEAF.** The harvest's remainder: the last patch of standing corn — the 'mell' or 'neck'. Cutting it ended the harvest and opened the feast. Fresh angle: the harvest has a last page — the work ends when the remainder is cut, not when the field is empty.
3. The neck → **CRYING THE NECK.** Cornwall/Devon: the reaper holds the last sheaf aloft — "I 'ave 'un! I 'ave 'un! I 'ave 'un!" / "What 'ave 'ee? What 'ave 'ee? What 'ave 'ee?" / "A neck! A neck! A neck!" / "Hurrah! Hurrah for the neck!" — the neck plaited, dressed with flowers, carried into the farmhouse kitchen and kept in the place of honour until the next year's neck; some regions cut it anonymously (sickle-throwing, blindfolded scythes) so no one would anger the spirit. Fresh angle: the harvest's last page is a person — plaited, flowered, carried home, given the seat of honour. (10S-F179 stages this.)
4. The neck → **THE CORN DOLLY.** The last sheaf woven into a figure — the Kern Baby (Northumberland, dressed in women's clothing, paraded), the Cailleach, the Mare, the Neck — kept above the hearth through winter to protect the household; the seeds it carried often sown the following spring to bless the new crop. Fresh angle: the remainder is given a body — the crop's leftovers become the house's guardian. (MEME-F164 stages this.)
5. The dolly → **THE WINNOWING.** After the threshing floor: the fan separates wheat from chaff — the wind is the sieve. Fresh angle: the harvest's last machine is the weather — the separation is delegated to the air. Staged in "The Winnowing" below.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (05:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE NBC CHIMES (plot research).** 1927–28: a committee of three (Oscar Hanson, engineering; Earnest LaPrade, orchestra leader; Phillips Carlin, announcer) bought hand dinner chimes from the Lesch Silver Co. of Manhattan for $48.50; the seven-note sequences (G-C-G-E-G-C-E) proved too complicated for announcers to strike consistently BY HAND; simplified to G-E-C — first broadcast Nov 29, 1929, at 59:30 and 29:30 past the hour; the first "purely audio" US trademark (1950); the machine version came in 1932 (24 reeds plucked by a mechanical finger) — the hand won first. Fresh angle: the signature was simplified to fit the human hand — the institution's most famous sound is a person striking metal live. Network translation: staged in "The Hand" + "The Chime" venture below — the signature is a person, struck live, never a machine.
- **THE APOLOGY CARD — PRE-COVERED, not re-banked.** N-40 "The Apology Card" shipped 2026-10-12 (goal episode #51); the 2026-10-17 08:15 run staged the continuity announcer ("The Thumbs-Up", MEME-F118, the 1943 Broadcasting House dash + BBC Year Book 1950 four-fates doctrine). The chime chain takes this run's plot-research slot.
- **THE HARVEST HOME (plot research).** Folded into Chain 4 above: the last sheaf, Crying the Neck, the corn dolly, and the Mell Supper (Old Norse "meal"/"gathering" — the farmer feasts the workers the evening of the neck-cutting, in the farmhouse kitchen). Fresh angle: the institution's calendar ends in a feast — the work year closes on a shared table, not a report. Network translation: staged in "The Last Sheaf" + "The Neck" below; the season's last installment should be a supper, not a summary.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (06:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

Seeds: B-1231 "The Coal Sifter" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the sift; NO-LINE); B-1235 "The Gas Gauge" (shipped 2026-10-18 — "The gas is rising."); B-1230 "The Reserved Spot" (shipped 2026-10-18 — "The spot is open.", parking lot); B-1229 "The Car Call" (shipped 2026-10-18 — "Going down.", elevator).

### Chain 1 — the coal sifter (seed: B-1231 "The Coal Sifter")
1. The sift → **THE BREAKER BOYS.** Anthracite coal breakers, Pennsylvania: boys aged 8-12 sat straddling iron troughs picking slate from the coal with bare hands, 10-hour days, six days a week, 70-90 cents a day; Lewis Hine photographed them at Pittston (Hughestown Borough Coal Co.), January 16, 1911 ("Breaker Boys. Smallest is Angelo Ross"); the 1901 Bureau of Mines report counted 19,564 slate-pickers of 147,651 anthracite employees; Stephen Crane (1894): "the coal is expected to be fairly pure after it passes the final boy." Fresh angle: the screen was a child — the sift was a row of small hands. Lineage vs B-1231 (the labor vs the sift — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
2. The pickers → **THE CHECKWEIGHMAN.** The miner was paid by the ton he extracted — but "a ton was never really a ton, because it was presumed that a large percentage of it was actually slate, bone and rock"; the checkweighman weighed the coal and determined the miner's earnings, docking up to 33% regardless of examination; companies offered higher wages where checkweighmen were NOT demanded. Fresh angle: the weighing is the wage — the scale is the argument.
3. The weighing → **TARE AND TRETT.** The arithmetic textbooks' six-thing rule (Charles Vyse, The Tutor's Guide): 1. The Gross Weight, 2. Tare, 3. Trett (an allowance of 4 lb per 104 lb for waste), 4. Suttle, 5. Cloff, 6. The Net Weight. Fresh angle: an entire taxonomy for subtracting — six words for what the goods are NOT.
4. The subtraction → **THE SUTTLE MAN.** Staged background figure: job = the net after all six subtractions, motive = the goods are only what survives the arithmetic.

### Chain 2 — the gas gauge (seed: B-1235 "The Gas Gauge")
1. The rising gas → **THE GASOMETER.** The telescopic gasholder, invented 1824 (first built Leeds): nested vessels like a telescope that rise as gas is pumped in and fall as demand draws it off; the word was coined by William Murdoch, the inventor of gas lighting, to his peers' annoyance ("a container and not a meter"); "the gas is rising" is the building changing height. Fresh angle: the gauge B-1235 reads IS the gasometer's wall — the reading and the building are one object. Lineage vs B-1235 (the building vs the dial — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
2. The gasometer → **THE STANDARD CANDLE.** (London) Metropolis Gas Act 1860: candle-power was defined as the light of a sperm candle, six to the pound, each burning 120 grains an hour; the gas examiner lighted the gas fifteen minutes before testing, made ten photometer observations a minute apart, weighed the candles before and after, and recorded the correction — gas was legally judged against the flame it was replacing. Fresh angle: the law measured gas in candles — the new light was sentenced by the old one. Staged in "The Tare"-adjacent "The Gas Examiner" below? No — the examiner is the background figure of "The Paper That Darkens" below.
3. The candle → **THE COCKSPUR BURNER.** Murdoch's earliest burner (1807, Phillips & Lee's works, Manchester): he welded up the tube end and bored three small holes forming three divergent jets — under one candle per cubic foot; followed by the flattened cockscomb, the saw-cut batswing, the impinging flat flame. Fresh angle: the first gas flame was three small holes — three beats, one hand; 10S-F182's precedent.
4. The burner → **THE LEAD PAPER.** The sulphuretted-hydrogen test from the gas statutes: a glass vessel holding a strip of bibulous paper moistened with acetate of lead — the paper darkens in the presence of poison. Fresh angle: the purity test is paperwork that blushes — the document changes colour instead of signing.

### Chain 3 — the reserved spot (seed: B-1230 "The Reserved Spot")
1. The spot → **THE PARK-O-METER.** July 16, 1935, southeast corner of First Street and Robinson Avenue, Oklahoma City: Carl C. Magee (newspaperman, chairman of the Chamber's Traffic Committee) installs Park-O-Meter No. 1 — a nickel for an hour; the prototype was nicknamed the "Black Maria"; opponents called paid parking un-American, "a tax on their cars... without due process of law"; a 9-year-old deposited a nickel thinking it was a gumball machine. Fresh angle: the spot was free until a newspaperman decided that TIME was the product — the commodity was never the curb, it was the hour. Lineage vs B-1230 (the meter vs the vacancy — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
2. The ticket → **THE DENVER BOOT.** Frank Marugg — pattern maker and second-chair violinist of the Denver Symphony Orchestra — invented the wheel clamp in 1944 (patented 1958); Denver police first used it January 5, 1955 and collected $18,000 in the first month; it exists because towed cars were being vandalized in the pound and owners sued the city. Fresh angle: the clamp is the cheaper punishment — the boot was invented because the impound lot was a worse idea.
3. The clamp → **THE CHALK MARK.** Taylor v. City of Saginaw (6th Cir., decided April 25, 2019): parking officers chalking tires to track parking duration = a search under the Fourth Amendment (common-law trespass + information-gathering, following United States v. Jones); "Because we chalk this practice up to a regulatory exercise, rather than a community-caretaking function, we reverse" (Judge Donald); officer Tabitha Hoskins chalked Alison Taylor's tires 15 times, 2014–2017. Fresh angle: the lightest mark carries the heaviest law — a chalk stroke is a search. MEME-F165 stages this.
4. The chalk → **THE LINE PAINTER.** Staged background figure: job = the painted lines, motive = the spot only exists because of paint.

### Chain 4 — the car call (seed: B-1229 "The Car Call")
1. The call → **THE OPERATORS' STRIKE.** September 1945: 15,000–17,000 elevator operators (Building Service Employees IU Local 32B) walked out; 30,000 buildings affected including the Empire State Building and Rockefeller Center; 1.5 million workers would not climb ("the first hundred flights are the hardest," Hearst Metrotone newsreel); five days; Governor Dewey ordered binding arbitration. Fresh angle: the lift stopped and the city became stairs — the strike returned the vertical world to the horizontal. Lineage vs B-1229 (the stairs vs the car — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged).
2. The strike → **THE SOOTHING VOICE.** The automation aftermath: emergency phones, stop buttons, alarms; Otis's 1950s ads showed children pushing buttons and grandma riding; "a soothing voice piped out of speakers: 'This is an automatic elevator. Please press the button for the floor you desire.'" Fresh angle: the machine learned to talk because the city no longer trusted the silence — the voice is the apology for the absent operator. Canon riff: the Control Voice stays furniture — but the elevator learned the trick first.
3. The automation → **THE ROPE-CUT DEMONSTRATION.** May 1854, Crystal Palace, Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations: Elisha Otis rode his platform up, ordered the rope cut with an axe/knife, the wagon-spring safety snapped into the ratchet bars — "All safe, gentlemen, all safe." (The drawing everyone knows was made in 1978 for the company's 125th anniversary — the iconic image is a recreation.) Fresh angle: the product launch was a man ordering his own rope cut — the confidence is the demo.
4. The rope → **THE PATERNOSTER.** Peter Ellis's patent July 1866; first cyclic elevators at Oriel Chambers, Liverpool, 1868; Frederick Hart's 1878 patent; J&E Hall's "Cyclic Elevator" 1884, London: open compartments in a continuous loop, ~1 foot per second, never stopping — no doors, no buttons; named for the Lord's Prayer ("Our Father"), the loop is a rosary; construction banned mid-1970s; 230 remain in Germany, 68 in Czechia. Fresh angle: the lift that never stops has no call button — B-1229's "Going down" is the one sentence the paternoster never says.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (06:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE TEST CARD GIRL (plot research).** BBC Test Card F: first broadcast 2 July 1967 (the day after the first colour pictures reached the public) on BBC2 — 8-year-old Carole Hersee playing noughts-and-crosses with Bubbles the Clown, developed by her father, BBC engineer George Hersee (she was chosen because her younger sister Gillian was missing two front teeth; paid £100); broadcast during daytime downtime for four decades — the most-aired face in British television history (~70,000 hours claimed); later depicted as the Test Card Girl in Life on Mars. Fresh angle: the network's most-watched program was a photograph of a girl and a doll — the downtime WAS the channel. Network translation: staged in the venture "The Downtime" below — a fixed still + music aired whenever nothing is scheduled; the audience watches the absence. MEME-F166 stages here.
- **THE INTERVAL SIGNAL (plot research).** Shortwave interval signals: BBC World Service's Lillibullero (1943 onward, an Irish jig as the Empire's signature), Bow Bells, Radio New Zealand's bellbird call, Vatican Radio's Christus Vincit on celesta. One attributed origin (a German author): the earliest studios were so small they had to be aired out between programs — so a metronome or alarm clock ticked to keep the channel open, and the filler became the ident. Fresh angle: the station's identity was born as ventilation filler — the signal is a held breath. Network translation: staged in the venture "The Airing" — a segment that exists to keep the channel open, a metronome with a callsign.

B-1111's tagged handle answers the untagged handle. Production note: the 10s is a couplet, not a sentence; draft both endpoints before the middle.
- **10S-F182 — Three beats, one hand.** The cockspur precedent: three small holes, one burner. In 10s, never more than three hand events; the hand is the metronome. Production note: count the hand events in the draft (10S-F177's one-event rule for strikes is the special case).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — KEVIN BACON CHAINS

Seeds: B-1232 "The Steady Needle" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the held needle; "The needle holds."); B-1234 "The Seed Drill" (shipped 2026-10-18 — the sowing machine); #189 L-39 "The Retired Kilogram" (shipped 2026-10-18 — "The number outlived the metal."); #188 NE-39 "The Readiness Buzzer" (shipped 2026-10-18 — "The tone is the programming.").

### Chain 1 — the steady needle (seed: B-1232 "The Steady Needle")
1. The needle → **KELVIN'S COMPASS.** Sir William Thomson (Lord Kelvin, 1824–1907), first compass patents 1876 after experiments on his yacht *Lalla Rookh*; built by James White, Glasgow. The 10-inch card carried **8 short needles on silk threads**, weighed **178 grains**, and oscillated at ~60 seconds (vs ~20s for the Admiralty Standard) so it never rocked in synchrony with the ship. The binnacle corrected the ship's own iron with adjustable bar-magnet correctors, a heeling magnet, and a pair of iron globes ("Kelvin's balls") for quadrantal error. Fresh angle: the compass corrects for the ship ITSELF — the instrument accounts for its own distortion. Lineage vs the 05:00 run's [READY] "The South-Pointing Spoon" (the correction vs the divination — adjudicated distinct, lineage flagged). Sources: nationalacademies.org (*Degrees Kelvin*); collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk (Kelvin compass, 1876); 1902 Encyclopaedia Britannica "Compass" (8 needles, 178 grains, iron globes, correctors).
2. The binnacle → **THE DEVIATION CARD / NAPIER'S DIAGRAM.** After the correctors, residual error remains — so a compass adjuster "swings the ship" through 360° and issues a **deviation card**: the known error for every heading. **James Napier (1821–1879)** devised his diagram in **1851**: two vertical course scales with lines at 60° — deviation without trigonometry. Published USNI cards show errors swinging +11°E to −8°W. Fresh angle: the instrument needs paperwork to be honest. Stages in "The Deviation Card" below. Sources: southstreetseaportmuseum.org (swinging the compass); deadreckonings.com (Napier's diagram, 1851); usni.org (worked deviation-card table). FLAG honored: 1851, not 1839.
3. The deviation → **HALLEY'S DECLINATION CHART, 1701.** Every navigator corrects two things: deviation (the ship's iron) and variation (the geography of the Earth's own field). Edmond Halley commanded the 52-foot pink *Paramour* on the first purely scientific English naval voyages (1698–1700), 52°N to 52°S; the results were *A New and Correct Chart Shewing the Variations of the Compass*, presented to the Royal Society **4 June 1701** — the **first published isogonic ("Halleyan") lines**, ~150 observations. Its cartouche: the curve lines "shew at one View all the places where the Variation of the Compass is the same." The contour idea later inspired Humboldt's isotherms. Fresh angle: the first chart of a correction is also the first contour map. Sources: en.wikipedia.org (Halley, Paramour, isogonic lines); raremaps.com (Royal Society 4 June 1701; cartouche quotation).
4. The needle as a reader → **COOKE & WHEATSTONE'S NEEDLE TELEGRAPH.** Oersted's 1820 discovery — a current moves a nearby compass needle — IS the display mechanism. **William Fothergill Cooke (1806–1879)** and **Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875)** patented the first practical commercial electric telegraph in **1837** (five-needle design; letters read by two needles converging on a diamond board — 20 letters, C J Q U X Z omitted). The **first public telegraph service in the world** opened **1839**: 13 miles (21 km) alongside the Great Western Railway, **Paddington to West Drayton** (four-needle instruments per modern reappraisal; extended to Slough 1842). Fresh angle: the needle went from reading the Earth's field to reading electricity. Sources: collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk (five-needle telegraph, 1837); londonmuseum.org.uk (1839 GWR service; patent No. 7614). FLAG honored: four-needle on the 1839 line, five-needle in the 1837 patent.
5. The same inventor → **KELVIN'S MIRROR GALVANOMETER, 1858.** Thomson cemented a tiny mirror to a silk-suspended needle inside a coil — the cable's faintest pulses became a moving **spot of light on a scale**. Made by **James White, Glasgow**; the **only instrument sensitive enough** to read the first transatlantic cable's messages (completed **5 August 1858**, Valentia ↔ Newfoundland; the cable died **18 September 1858** after chief electrician Whitehouse pushed ~2,000 volts through an induction coil, burning the gutta-percha). Fresh angle: the man who steadied the ship's needle built the needle that read the ocean's wire — one inventor, both ends of the needle's job. Stages in "The Light Spot" below. Sources: collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk (mirror galvanometer, 1858; Newfoundland end; siphon recorder).
6. The reader → **EDISON'S PHONOGRAPH STYLUS.** US Patent **200,521**: application filed **24 December 1877**, granted **19 February 1878**. The tinfoil phonograph used an up-and-down **"hill-and-dale" stylus** and **two needles** — one to record, one to play back; tinfoil wrapped on a grooved cylinder, sound embossed as indentations. First demo: **"Mary Had a Little Lamb."** ~600 licensed copies built for exhibition in early 1878; Edison Speaking Phonograph Co. formed **24 January 1878**; successors: Bell & Tainter's wax **Graphophone** (1886), Berliner's lateral-cut **Gramophone** (1887). Fresh angle: "The phonograph was born out of the telegraph and telephone" (IEEE Spectrum) — the needle as reader moves from wire to groove. Stages in "The Two Needles" below. Sources: spectrum.ieee.org (patent no./dates; telegraph lineage); capsnews.org (tinfoil mechanics; 600 copies).

### Chain 2 — the seed drill (seed: B-1234 "The Seed Drill")
1. The machine → **TULL'S DRILL, ~1701.** Jethro Tull (1674–1741), Basildon, Berkshire; Oxford, called to the bar 1699, farmed instead. The horse-drawn seed drill sowed in neat rows at uniform depth — the rows let a horse-hoe pass between them. Published 1731 as *The New Horse Houghing Husbandry*. Two stealable details (EBSCO): the metering mechanism was modeled on the **groove-tongue-and-spring of a pipe organ's soundboard**, and he built it after his laborers **refused his order to hand-drill sainfoin**. Fresh angle: the machine of precision rows was invented for a refusal. FLAG: invention ~1701 attested (Britannica, 1911 Britannica, EBSCO); "patented 1701" is unverified — never claim it. Sources: britannica.com; ebsco.com; 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica "Tull, Jethro".
2. The drill's opposite → **THE BROADCAST SEEDER.** Tull's system existed to "do away with the broadcasting of seed"; the broadcast seeder **mechanized the scatter he hated**. Cahoon's 1861 US-patented side-crank finned drum (4–8 acres/hour); Speicher's "Cyclone" 1868 (Urbana, Indiana; canvas bag, 1 peck); Esterly of Whitewater; Waddell's Patent 242,402 (May 31, 1881). Fresh angle: two machines, one word apart — the drill places, the seeder flings. Stages in "The Two Sowings" below. Sources: prestigequeen.com (Cahoon 1861); sdstate.edu Agricultural Heritage Museum (Cyclone/Speicher); wi101.wisc.edu (Esterly).
3. The word → **"BROADCAST" GOES ON AIR.** etymonline: *broadcast* adj. **1767** — "dispersed upon the ground by hand," of seed; figurative "widely spread" by 1785; radio use 1921/22. First institutional use: **KDKA Pittsburgh** — first commercial license **Oct 27, 1920**; **Nov 2, 1920, 6 p.m.**, Leo Rosenberg broadcast the Harding–Cox election returns from a shack atop a Westinghouse building (100-watt transmitter, returns telephoned in from the *Pittsburgh Post* office) to ~1,000 listeners. Frank Conrad's 8XK ham broadcasts preceded it; 500+ licensed US stations by 1922. Fresh angle: the word the network lives under was a farming verb for scattering. Sources: etymonline.com; wamc.org (NPR 2025-10-15, Wisconsin Historical Society); pabook.libraries.psu.edu; ieeeghn.org.
4. The first broadcast → **THE CLOSEDOWN RITUAL.** BBC One's nightly closedown: next-evening schedule rundown, weather, PIF, goodnight over the station clock, "God Save the Queen" over the ident — ended **November 1997** when BBC News 24 launched and BBC One went 24-hour. **Test Card F**: first broadcast **2 July 1967** on BBC2 (the day after the UK's first public colour pictures); 8-year-old Carole Hersee (b. 1958) playing noughts-and-crosses with Bubbles the Clown, developed by her father, BBC engineer George Hersee (1924–2001); the first UK test card in colour and the first with a person; aired in downtime until BBC1 went 24-hour (Nov 1997) / BBC2 switched to Ceefax (Jan 1999). FLAG: the "~70,000 hours, most-broadcast person in history" claim is nostalgia-site (doyouremember.co.uk), not primary — treat as reported. Lineage: the banked NETWORK venture "The Closedown" + "The Good Night" + "The Sign-Off" already stage this ground — hop banked as chain record, no new item this run. Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("Television closedown routines in the United Kingdom"; "Test Card F"); doyouremember.co.uk (flagged).
5. The threshold ritual → **PLOUGH MONDAY.** The first Monday after Epiphany (Jan 6); traditional start of the English agricultural year. Plough Sunday: the plough blessed in church (plough lights, blessing of the seed). Monday: costumed Plough Boys drag a plough house to house with musicians, a **"Bessy"** (man in women's clothes) and a fool, collecting money — refusers get their **doorstep turned over** or a **furrow cut in front of the door**. Strongest in Yorkshire, Lincolnshire, East Anglia; documented back to the 15th century; revived in the 1960s folk revival. Fresh angle: the collection call with a built-in penalty — the refusal is the receipt. Stages in "The Plough Boys" below. Sources: whodoyouthinkyouaremagazine.com; blogs.reading.ac.uk (Museum of English Rural Life); web-holidays.com.
6. The blessed tool → **ROGATIONTIDE / BEATING THE BOUNDS.** *Rogation* from Latin *rogare*, "to ask." Major Rogation: April 25 (St Mark's day); Minor Rogations: Mon–Wed before Ascension Thursday. The congregation walks the parish bounds blessing fields, trees, and stones; **boundary stones struck with rods** — boys were bumped at the markers so the parish line would be **branded into living memory**. Anglo-Saxon origins; pre-map property law made boundary knowledge load-bearing; the Poor Laws (1598–1834) made it legally decisive. Still observed (e.g., St Michael at the North Gate, Oxford). Fresh angle: the boundary was enforced by pain, not paper. Sources: onepeterfive.com; liturgy.co.nz; sttimothysacc.com; chasingchurches.org.

### Chain 3 — the retired kilogram (seed: #189 L-39 "The Retired Kilogram")
1. The cylinder → **LE GRAND K (THE IPK).** The International Prototype of the Kilogram, made **1889** from 90% platinum / 10% iridium (39 mm cylinder), lived in a vault at Sèvres under three nested glass bell jars and drifted **~50 micrograms** against its own national copies over a century — the mass of a fingerprint. Because the kilogram was *by definition* whatever it weighed, the official reading was that the rest of the world had grown heavier. Its cleaning ritual: a chamois soaked in ether and ethanol, then steam from twice-distilled water, stripping **5–60 µg** of accumulated film every decade — it gains weight in storage and loses it in the wash. Stages in "The Chamois" below. Sources: phys.org ("Adieu, Le Grand K"); en.wikipedia.org ("Timeline of International Kilogram Prototypes").
2. The drift → **THE 2019 SI REDEFINITION.** On **16 November 2018** the 26th CGPM in Versailles voted *unanimously* to define the kilogram by fixing the Planck constant at exactly **6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s**; the new SI took effect **20 May 2019** — World Metrology Day, deliberately the 144th anniversary of the 1875 Metre Convention. For the first time since 1960, **no SI unit is defined by a physical artifact**; the ampere, kelvin, and mole were redefined in the same room. Physics Today: "the biggest conceptual transformation in metrology since the French Revolution." Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("2019 revision of the SI"); physicstoday.aip.org.
3. The redefinition → **THE KIBBLE BALANCE.** Proposed by **Bryan Kibble** at the UK's National Physical Laboratory in **1975** (originally the "watt balance"; renamed after his death in 2016). Two modes — weighing (mass against electromagnetic force) and velocity (coil through the field, measuring voltage) — equating electrical power to mechanical power so the coil's properties cancel out. NPL's Mark I is now at the National Research Council of Canada. Stages in a sponsor concept below ("The Kibble Balance Works"). Sources: iopscience.iop.org (Metrologia review); physicsworld.com.
4. The treaty → **THE METRE CONVENTION, 1875.** Signed in Paris on **20 May 1875** by 17 nations (France, Germany, Russia, the USA, Argentina, Venezuela; the UK waited until 1884). Created three bodies — BIPM, CGPM, CIPM — at the **Pavillon de Breteuil** in the Parc de Saint-Cloud (granted 1876, holds *extraterritorial status*); the pavilion had been damaged in the 1870 Franco-Prussian War and repaired for the purpose. 60 member states today. Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("International Bureau of Weights and Measures"); onlinelibrary.wiley.com (Foerster's role, 1875).
5. The alternate disaster → **THE 1834 TALLY-STICK FIRE.** On **16 October 1834** the medieval Palace of Westminster burned down because clerks burned a stockpile of obsolete wooden tally sticks — the Exchequer's notched accounting receipts, replaced by paper records in 1826 — in undersized furnaces beneath the House of Lords. Britain's primary standards (the 1758 brass Imperial Standard Yard and the standard pound) went down with the palace; Turner was in the crowd and painted the fire twice. The 1824 Act's fallback natural equivalents (a seconds pendulum at Greenwich) proved impossible to reconstruct from. Fresh angle: paperwork destroyed the standards — the accounting ate the measure. Sources: citizendailypost.com; curiousexpeditions.org; ukma.org.uk (confirms 1834 destruction).
6. The resurrection → **BRONZE 19 AND THE IMMURED STANDARDS.** The **1855 Weights and Measures Act** permitted recreating the prototypes from secondary standards. The new Imperial Standard Yard — "Bronze 19," 38 inches, one inch square — was cast in **Baily's metal** (16 parts copper, 2½ tin, 1 zinc) with the defining graduations on **gold plugs sunk into the bar**, legalized by Act of Parliament on **30 July 1855**, kept in the "Strong Room" of Old Palace Yard; bronze No. 11 was presented to the United States in 1856 (the US yard until 1893). And the four 1844–45 "Parliamentary Copies" were placed with the Royal Mint, the Royal Society, Greenwich Observatory — and one set was literally **immured**: walled up inside the staircase of the House of Commons as a doomsday backup. Stages in "The Immured Copy" below. Sources: en.wikisource.org (Popular Science Monthly, Vol. 19, 1881 — Bronze 19, Baily's metal, legalization date); en.wikipedia.org ("Troughton scale"; "Imperial units"); nature.com (1894 note on the immured standards).

### Chain 4 — the readiness buzzer (seed: #188 NE-39 "The Readiness Buzzer")
1. The tone → **THE SIX PIPS.** The archetype of an authoritative broadcast tone. The idea of Astronomer Royal **Sir Frank Watson Dyson** and BBC director **John Reith**; first broadcast at **9:30 p.m. on 5 February 1924**. Generated by electrical contacts on the pendulums of **two** mechanical clocks at the Royal Greenwich Observatory (two, in case one broke), each feeding a **1 kHz** tone to the BBC: five 0.1s pips, then a 0.5s sixth that marks the moment. The build was given to engineer Harry Lampen Edwards (well-attested as 18, second-hand — treat the age as well-attested but second-hand). By the late 1930s the Admiralty tried to bill the BBC **£520 a year** for the service; Vice-Admiral Carpendale fought it in a tongue-in-cheek letter listing all the free Navy coverage the BBC aired instead. Stages in plot research below (the leased-line negative signal). Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("Greenwich Time Signal"); miketodd.net; stackscale.com.
2. The pips → **THE SPEAKING CLOCK ("TIM").** The UK service launched **24 July 1936** (General Post Office); the script embeds the pip — "At the third stroke…" First voice: London telephonist **Ethel "Jane" Cain**, chosen through a "Golden Voice" competition among the Post Office's **15,000 operators**, winning **10 guineas**, holding the job 27 years (1936–1963). The machinery filled a small room: motors, glass discs, photocells, valves; her voice recorded optically onto the glass discs like a film soundtrack. Callers dialled **TIM (846)**; standardized to **123** by the early 1990s. **13 million calls** in its first year. Pat Simmons replaced Cain in 1963 on the Mark III (voice on a magnetic drum) until 1985; actor Brian Cobby became the first male voice. Lineage: the banked 2026-10-14 MEDIA SCHOOL episode "The Golden Voice" + "The Four Voices" already stage this ground — hop banked as chain record, no new item this run; canon care: the voice is a recorded prop, Control Voice stays furniture. Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("Speaking clock"); theregister.com (BT Heritage); sitepoint.com.
3. The institutional voice → **THE V-FOR-VICTORY CALL SIGN.** Another wartime-BBC authoritative voice — and a fiction: the campaign's wartime broadcaster was assistant news editor **Douglas Ritchie** performing *as* **"Colonel Britton."** On **14 January 1941**, Victor de Laveleye (ex-Belgian Justice Minister, director of the BBC's Belgian French broadcasts) told Belgians to chalk the letter V everywhere (victoire/vrijheid). Ritchie suggested making the V audible via Morse (**dot-dot-dot-dash, …—**), matching the **timpani opening of Beethoven's 5th**; the BBC used it as the call sign for its foreign-language programmes for the rest of the war — "Fate knocking on the door" of Nazi Germany, in a German composer's own music. Churchill adopted the campaign officially **19 July 1941**. Stages in "The V" below. Sources: collections.ushmm.org; info.mysticstamp.com; cmuse.org.
4. The coded timpani → **THE AIR-RAID ALL-CLEAR.** The other side of the wartime sound-code: WWII Britain used exactly two warning tones — the "red warning" (rising-falling wail) and the **all clear** (a steady tone), triggered by the Royal Observer Corps over a wire-broadcast system. Sirens were **tested in REVERSE order** — all clear first, then the red warning — so the public would never mistake a test for a real attack. Mostly built by Carter, Gents, Castle Castings, and Secomak; 10 and 12 ports making a minor-third interval (B♭/D♭) — the sound dubbed into films set in countries that never used it. ~1,200 remain in Britain, tested annually August–September. In England, factories kept running after the *first* siren and sheltered only at the *second* — work and warning shared the soundscape. Stages in "The Reversed Test" below. Sources: en.wikipedia.org ("Air raid siren"); throughouthistory.com (two-siren factory protocol).
5. The siren → **THE MILL WHISTLE.** The same physical object class — a loud fixed-tone blast with fixed civic meaning. At the Mendocino Lumber Company, when the office clock reached the appointed time someone pulled the steam whistle: **"clocks were set by it and lives were regulated by it."** The civic liturgy: first blast "Get up and get down to the mill," second blast finish breakfast, the **noon whistle** meaning 12 o'clock — lunch for workers, school recess, the bank closing; the evening whistle signalling housewives to start supper. In Woodstock, Vermont, the noon whistle was "the town's watch" when not everyone owned a timepiece; in Elizabethton, Tennessee, the North American Rayon plant's three-stage brass steam whistle sounded four times daily from **June 1938**, and locals set their watches by the **10pm whistle** — later the town's curfew. Stages in "The Town's Watch" below. Sources: kelleyhousemuseum.org; sevendaysvt.com; cartercountyhistory.com.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — PLOT RESEARCH (real show/media history)

- **THE SIGN-OFF (plot research).** The broadcast day used to END. Until the late 1970s/80s, US local affiliates ran a fixed nightly sequence ~11:30 PM–1 AM: station identification (announcer reads the call letters, frequency, studio location — the US legal minimum is the call sign + city of license), the national anthem over flying flags/military footage, then the transmitter cut to a test pattern (SMPTE color bars) with a continuous 1,000 Hz tone, then static/snow until morning. BBC closedowns: continuity announcement, clock, anthem over the spinning globe, fade to silence — then the hum. One detail worth stealing: stations switched off remote transmitters by sending touch tones down the line — the signal ended with a *command*, not a fade. Sources: Wikipedia "Sign-on and sign-off"; oneclickstip.com sign-off history; absolutewrite.com early-television forum thread (1960 BBC: midnight announcement, test card with music, then music stopped, then hum, then static hiss).
- **THE PIPS' LEASED LINE (plot research).** The Greenwich Time Signal's leased line from the Royal Observatory to Broadcasting House carried a steady 1 kHz tone at all times EXCEPT when a pip was required — the signal was the ABSENCE of the tone. Faults were detected instantly by loss of audio: the line was proof-of-life in the negative. Network translation: MEME-F167 below — a signal that says something by stopping. Sources: en.wikipedia.org "Greenwich Time Signal"; royalobservatorygreenwich.org Time Department history (two Dent clocks, contacts on the pendula, 5 February 1924).
- **THE TOUCH-TONE KILL (plot research).** Sign-off note above, sharpened: the station ended the day by sending DTMF tones to remote transmitters. The farthest tower went silent on a telephone command. Sources: Wikipedia "Sign-on and sign-off" (touch tones to turn off remote transmitters).

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: THE ART OF 10 SECONDS

- **10S-F183 — The cut is the verb.** The sign-off sequence ends with the tone cutting to snow — no fade, no goodbye. In 10s, the 9.5s state must be a CUT from the 4-6s event, not a dissolve of it. Production note: drafts should name the cut (what is absent at 9.5s that was present at 6s) as explicitly as the event; the cut is the second half of the beat.
- **10S-F184 — One kHz is a room.** The sign-off's 1,000 Hz test tone was audible proof the transmitter was alive — a room you could hear. Production note: when the take's premise is absence (a test pattern, a test card, a sealed object), put the ONE directed tone in the audio plan and let it carry the liveness. The bed is the broadcast.

## 2026-10-18 Q0 research run (07:00 EDT) — STANDING STUDY: MEME LITERACY

- **MEME-F167 — The negative signal.** The pips' leased line: tone always on, interrupted to speak. The meme is the interruption — a form where the default state is ON and the content is the cut. Network-native: the sealed dossier as a segment that never opens; the hypnotic bumper that never jokes; the closedown ident where the station stops and the tone stops with it. The audience learns to wait for the gap, and the gap is the message.
- **MEME-F168 — The closedown as a daily ritual.** Children's channels in the sign-off era aired the characters going to bed — hosts and mascots performing sleep, then a loop of them sleeping until morning programming. Network-native: a NETWORK closedown ident — the channel's cast putting the channel to bed each night, the tone cutting at 9.5s per 10S-F183. Daily ritual = daily remix surface; the audience returns because the ritual is fixed and the details rotate.
