### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (21:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-6 — THE LINE NEEDS A SILENT RUNWAY (short-form timing).** The bed must pull back at 6.5–7s so the 7–9s line has a quiet runway — the ear needs a reset for the mouth to matter. If the bed is still hot at line time, the mouth fights the bed and the line always loses. Direct the bed, not the line: score a one-second ambient pullback into the verdict, never a louder line. A line that has to shout over its own unit is a mix, not a moment.
- **CRAFT-7 — THE HOOK MUST NOT NAME IT (hook-frame craft).** No diegetic text in the first 1.5s that names the object of interest. A labeled object is an answer, and an answer at 0s ends the unit before it starts. The question must be purely visual first — the odd object, the wrong position, the hand that shouldn't be there — and naming belongs to the line at 7–9s. Text in the hook frame is a caption wearing a prop's clothes.
- **CRAFT-8 — THE LAST MOTION IS THE WITHHOLDING (cliff-chain mechanics).** Once the withholding gesture completes (~9s), the frame must hold still to 9.5s — no new motion, no reframe, no turn away. Any motion after the cliff spends the cliff; the audience's last memory is movement, not the absence. The withholding gesture is the final action the unit is allowed: stage it last, then let the frame sit on the absence it created.
- **CRAFT-9 — TEXT SIZE IS READING TIME (diegetic-text discipline).** At 10s the viewer gets ~1.5s to read; a diegetic text element must be ≤3 words, sustained ≥1.5s in a single held take, and never flashed twice. Flashed text is a subtitle wearing a costume — and subtitles are not diegetic, they are the production speaking over the world. One element, three words, held, once: if it needs more than that, the unit is two units.
- **CRAFT-10 — THE LINE BELONGS TO A VISIBLE MOUTH (one-line dialogue craft).** The line must be spoken by a mouth the camera can see at delivery. A line on a turned-away face, a profile, or a cutaway reads as voiceover — and voiceover breaks the diegetic contract (native audio, cast lock): the production is speaking over the world again. One opening, visible in the 7–9s window. If the face can't be seen, it's not a line; it's narration, and narration is a confession that the camera missed.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (22:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-11 — THE MIDPOINT NEEDS A DIP (short-form timing).** The 4–5s midpoint should carry the unit's quietest half-second — a deliberate dip between the state half and the turn half. Viewers sample 10s in two ~5s halves; the dip is the seam that lets the brain file "what was set up" separately from "what changed." A unit at constant energy for 10s is one long gesture, and one gesture has no turn. Direct the bed to duck at the midpoint, not just at the line: the dip at 4.5s makes the turn at 6s land, and the pullback at 6.5s (CRAFT-6) makes the line land. Two dips, one unit, three altitudes.
- **CRAFT-12 — THE WRONG SCALE IS THE HOOK (hook-frame craft).** The fastest sound-off question is a scale error: an object too big for the desk it sits on, or too small for the room it occupies. The eye reads relative scale in under a second — no staging required, no text, no character — and a scale violation implies a story (who brought it here? where does it belong?). Centered-and-correct-size is a poster; wrong scale at the frame edge is an intrusion, and the viewer leans in to resolve it. The hook frame's one unexplained element (CRAFT-2) should be unexplained BY SIZE before it's unexplained by identity.
- **CRAFT-13 — THE CLIFF'S FIRST SECOND IS A RECEIPT (cliff-chain mechanics).** Unit N's 0–1s must be a frozen near-repeat of unit N-1's cliff frame (same angle, same light, same absence) before any new action starts. The repeat is the receipt: it tells the audience "you remembered right, and here's proof your memory is shared." A unit that opens on new motion skips the receipt and the viewer spends the unit's first seconds checking whether they're in the same story — attention burned on orientation instead of the beat. Restage the absence, hold one second, then move.
- **CRAFT-14 — TEXT ARRIVES WITH THE TURN (diegetic-text discipline).** No diegetic text before 4s. If a unit carries its one allowed text element (CRAFT-4), it must ENTER with the turn — the stamp landing, the label applied, the form filled — because text that arrives is an event and text that sits from 0s is set dressing. A lettered object present from the hook frame gets read in the first 1.5s and discarded; the same object arriving at 5s gets read as the turn itself. Text early is wallpaper; text at the turn is verdict paper.
- **CRAFT-15 — THE LINE IS SPOKEN DOWN (one-line dialogue craft).** After the bed's pullback (CRAFT-6), the line lands louder by being quieter: deliver at near-conversational volume, even slightly under, because the ear leans into quiet and skates over loud. A line shouted over a unit reads as a tag; a line spoken down reads as a confidence. Deadpan is a volume discipline, not just a face discipline — the quieter the room, the funnier the sentence. Practical check: if the line's peak exceeds the 6s bed's, it was performed, not spoken.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (23:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-16 — THE HOOK NEEDS A SECOND HOOK AT 3s (short-form timing).** The 0–1.5s hook (CRAFT-2, CRAFT-12) only buys the first stare; between it and the 4s turn sits a ~1.5s attention valley where sound-off thumbs keep moving. Stage a micro-reveal at 3s — the hand shifts, the object tilts, the shadow crosses — that re-asks the hook's question without answering it. It's not a second hook, it's the first hook exhaling: the viewer who got their first question now gets it sharpened, and the unit has two grips instead of one. A 10s unit with one opening beat is a still; with the 3s re-ask it's a piece.
- **CRAFT-17 — ONE CAST MEMBER MAY NOTICE (hook-frame craft).** The rule is cast indifference (CRAFT-2), but indifference unbroken for 10s is a diorama. Allow exactly one cast member, exactly once, a half-second glance at the odd object — not at the lens, at the thing — then look away. The glance is a transfer: it tells the viewer the world sees what they see, and the world dismissing it is funnier than the world missing it. Two glances is a stare; a glance at the lens is a wink, and winks break the contract. One glance, mid-unit, away again.
- **CRAFT-18 — THE CLIFF MUST SURVIVE A LOOP (cliff-chain mechanics).** The 9–10s cliff frame doubles as the loop point: autoplay replays the unit, so the cliff frame must also work as a silent partner to the 0s hook frame. A cliff that only reads as "wait for the next unit" dies on loop and costs the rewatch; a cliff that reads as "and now the beginning is different" gains on every replay — the withheld fact (CRAFT-3) recolors the hook question (CRAFT-7) the second time around. Test: watch the cliff frame into the hook frame with no gap; if it feels like a restart, it works; if it feels like a shrug, the absence wasn't pointed enough.
- **CRAFT-19 — THE TEXT ELEMENT GETS ONE SECOND OF EXCLUSIVITY (diegetic-text discipline).** When the one allowed diegetic text element arrives with the turn (CRAFT-14), give it a full second where it is the only new thing in frame: no hand entering, no camera move, no bed spike. The eye needs ~1.5s to read ≤3 words (CRAFT-9); any competing motion steals half of it. Exclusivity is staging discipline: clear the frame's action budget for the text's arrival, then resume. A text element competing with a hand is a caption the hand apologizes for.
- **CRAFT-20 — THE LINE ANSWERS THE QUESTION, NOT THE SITUATION (one-line dialogue craft).** The line's target is the hook's question (CRAFT-2), not a summary of the turn. If the hook asked "why is that too big for the desk," the line resolves THAT — it never describes what happened, it answers what was asked. A line that narrates the turn is a caption with a mouth; a line that answers the 0s question closes the loop the viewer actually carried. Practical test: cover the screen and hear the line alone — it should make the viewer want to see the first frame again, not make the 10s feel explained.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (00:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-21 — THE 9.5s HOLD IS NOT DEAD AIR (short-form timing).** After the cliff's withholding gesture (~9s), the frame must hold the absence to the cut — no motion, no bed spike, no drift. That hold is not empty time; it is the frame the loop point and the next unit's receipt are printed from. Dead air is a frame with no job; the 9.5s hold has two jobs (loop partner for the cliff, CRAFT-18; receipt frame for the next unit, CRAFT-13). A unit that twitches at 9.7s re-spends attention the next unit needs for its receipt — the viewer arrives at unit N spending orientation budget instead of the beat.
- **CRAFT-22 — THE HOOK'S QUESTION MUST BE PHYSICAL (hook-frame craft).** "Why is that there" only holds if the "there" is visible and the "that" is grabbable — the question must point at a thing a hand could move. Abstract questions ("why is the room sad?") die sound-off; physical questions ("why is the ladder lying down in the hallway?") carry the whole 10s. The hook frame's one unexplained element (CRAFT-2) earns its question by being obviously movable: if the cast couldn't touch it, the viewer can't care where it is. A scale error (CRAFT-12) is physical; a mood is not.
- **CRAFT-23 — THE RECEIPT MUST LEAVE ROOM FOR THE HAND (cliff-chain mechanics).** Unit N's 0–1s restage of N-1's cliff frame (CRAFT-13) should frame the absence with negative space where the entering hand will arrive. If the receipt frame is compositionally complete, the 1s hand-entry crowds it and the receipt reads as a still image, not a continuation — attention burns on "where do I look" instead of "what's missing." Stage the receipt slightly off-center, object-side, so the hand's arrival completes the composition. The composition's incompleteness IS the invitation to watch the next unit.
- **CRAFT-24 — TEXT MUST NOT CONTRADICT THE MOUTH (diegetic-text discipline).** If the one allowed diegetic text element (CRAFT-4) arrives with the turn (CRAFT-14), its words must never say what the 7–9s line will say — text and mouth are two mouths, and two mouths saying the same thing is the production telling the viewer twice. The second telling always reads as the weak one. The text names the object or the event; the line answers the question (CRAFT-20). Test: mute the line and read the text, then cover the text and hear the line — if either one hands you the other, cut one.
- **CRAFT-25 — THE LINE'S LAST WORD IS THE NEXT UNIT'S TITLE (one-line dialogue craft).** The line's final word should be the noun or verb the next unit's hook reframes — the cliff at 9–10s spends a fact, and the line at 7–9s plants the vocabulary the next unit withholds. End on a concrete word, never an abstraction: a line ending on "remember" gives the next unit nothing to withhold; a line ending on "the shelf" gives it the shelf. The line is a handoff, not a period. (Corollaries: the hook's question must be answerable in the line's last word, CRAFT-2 + CRAFT-20; the withheld fact must be namable in ≤3 words, CRAFT-3.)

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (01:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-26 — THE DOORBEAT BEFORE THE LINE (short-form timing).** The bed must not merely duck (CRAFT-6) — it must STOP. A hard cut to near-silence at 7s, a full half-second of clean room before the line at 7.5s. A fading bed trails attention into the line; a doorbeat leaves a room the line walks into alone, so the first sound of the utterance is the first sound in the room for half a second. Fades apologize; doors close. Practical check: if the bed is still audible at 7.2s, the pullback was a fade and the line's first syllable is fighting it.
- **CRAFT-27 — THE HOOK IS A WIDE SHOT (hook-frame craft).** The first frame must be wide enough to show the room's normality around the odd object — the scale error (CRAFT-12) only reads as wrong if the correct-sized world is visible beside it. A tight shot on the odd object makes it a subject, not an intrusion; the viewer gets a thing, not a violation. Two shots to establish-then-intrude is two seconds the unit doesn't have: one wide frame, anomaly inside it, context as the setup and the object as the punch. If the hook frame can't show both the room and the wrong thing, the room is wrong or the thing is wrong — change one.
- **CRAFT-28 — THE WITHHOLDING GESTURE MUST BE INCOMPLETE (cliff-chain mechanics).** The 9s cliff gesture (CRAFT-8) must be an action stopped at 90%: the hand that doesn't touch, the lid that doesn't close, the door that doesn't latch. A completed action is an ending; a 90%-complete action is a debt. The audience must be able to finish the gesture in their head — that finishing is the itch the next unit scratches. A unit whose withholding gesture completes is a piece that ended; a unit whose gesture is interrupted is a piece that continues. If the viewer can't tell what the tenth percent would have been, the gesture wasn't load-bearing enough to be a cliff.
- **CRAFT-29 — TEXT HAS A LIFESPAN (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed diegetic text element (CRAFT-4, CRAFT-14) must be cleared — pocketed, filed, put away — by 7s, and must never survive into the cliff frame. Text is a turn-device: it arrives at 5s, does its work, leaves. A lettered prop lingering at 9.5s competes with the cliff (CRAFT-8, CRAFT-18) and reads as set dressing that escaped. The unit reads one thing at a time: text at 5s, face at 8s, absence at 9.5s. If the text element is still visible when the withholding gesture starts, the cliff has two subjects and therefore none.
- **CRAFT-30 — THE LINE GETS NO SETUP WORDS (one-line dialogue craft).** The line must begin on the word that matters — no "well,", no "look,", no "you see,". Every setup word is time in the 7–9s window spent not answering the hook's question (CRAFT-20). The first word of the line is a gunshot: it must be the noun, the verb, or the number. Practical test: read the line aloud and cut everything before the first word whose removal would change the answer — if more than zero words were cut, the line had a throat-clearing. In ten seconds the line doesn't get a breath before it speaks; it arrives speaking.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (02:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-31 — THE BEAT CLOCK RUNS IN HALF SECONDS (short-form timing).** In ten seconds there is no "about four seconds in" — every beat must land on a half-second boundary (2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0) or it drifts into another beat's territory. Directions like "the turn happens" without a timestamp are invitations to stack two beats inside one half-second or stretch one beat across three. The draft grammar: every action carries a timestamp to one decimal. Test: read the beat list — if two events share the same second, one of them is unannounced and will arrive as a surprise to the wrong person.
- **CRAFT-32 — THE HOOK FRAME MUST SURVIVE THE SCROLL-STOP (hook-frame craft).** The first frame is seen for ~0.3s at thumbnail size before the unit starts. The hook's one unexplained element (CRAFT-2) must be legible at 1/8 of frame height — if the anomaly needs the full-resolution 6-tile to see, it doesn't exist for the viewer who scrolls past. Test: shrink the hook frame to a phone-notification thumbnail; if the wrong thing isn't the first thing you notice, the unit opens on its setup instead of its punch. One high-contrast element, not detail — loudness of image.
- **CRAFT-33 — THE CLIFF MUST BE FILMABLE (cliff-chain mechanics).** A cliff is only a cliff if the next unit can receipt it cheaply: a withholding gesture visible in a single 0–1s restage (CRAFT-13). "The room is silent with suspicion" receipts nothing; "the drawer left two inches open" receipts in one frame. The cliff's job includes its receipt's production cost. Test: describe the receipt restage in one clause — if you need two, the cliff is a mood, not a mechanism, and the chain owes the next unit money it doesn't have.
- **CRAFT-34 — DIEGETIC TEXT GETS ONE JOB PER UNIT (diegetic-text discipline).** One allowed text element (CRAFT-4), one function: it either turns the unit (arrives at ~5s) or pays the cliff (is the cliff's subject) — never both, never neither. A text element that turns AND lingers into the cliff has two jobs and steals the face's (CRAFT-29). A text element that does neither is set dressing that slipped past QC. Assign the job in the draft: "TEXT: <word> — turn-device." If you can't state which job it did after the draft, cut it.
- **CRAFT-35 — THE LINE IS ONE BREATH, NOT ONE SENTENCE (one-line dialogue craft).** Nine words maximum is a ceiling, not a license: the line must be speakable in a single breath, with no comma-pause. A comma in the line is a second breath, and a second breath is a second utterance under the one-opening rule. Read it aloud at performance pace — if you breathe in the middle, the mouth opens twice and the line fails. Write the line, then delete the comma and the clause after it; if the answer survives, it was one line all along.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (03:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-36 — THE FIRST SECOND IS A PROMISE, NOT AN EVENT (short-form timing).** The 0–1s frame (CRAFT-2, CRAFT-22) must hold an unfinished situation — an anomaly mid-existence, not a beat that starts and resolves. If the hook's odd element completes its action inside the first second (picked up and put down, opened and closed), the unit has spent its question before the viewer formed it, and the remaining nine seconds chase a resolved opening. The hook must still be open at 1s: the thing is there, wrong, unresolved — the unit's job is the other nine seconds. A promise is a state; an event is a verb — hook on the state, stage the verbs after. Test: freeze at 1.0s; if the frame could be a photograph of a normal moment, the hook already died.
- **CRAFT-37 — THE ANOMALY MUST TOUCH A SURFACE (hook-frame craft).** A scale error (CRAFT-12) or unexplained object (CRAFT-2) only reads as wrong when its contact with the room is visible — the floor it rests on, the desk it sits on, the wall it leans against. A floating or center-framed object with no visible contact reads as a prop photographed for the viewer; an object bearing weight on the room's furniture reads as a violation the room has to accommodate. The hook frame's bottom third is load-bearing: show the contact point. If the anomaly's surface contact or shadow is out of frame, the hook is a picture of a thing, not a wrongness in a place. Stage the odd object so the room is visibly holding it.
- **CRAFT-38 — THE RECEIPT IS THE ONLY QUARANTINE FOR THE OLD UNIT (cliff-chain mechanics).** Unit N may reference unit N-1 only inside the 0–1s receipt restage (CRAFT-13); after 1s, the old unit must be unnameable. A chain that keeps quoting its previous unit past the receipt is one 60s scene chopped up, not chained 10s units — each unit's hook (CRAFT-2) must ask a fresh question, not finish the last unit's sentence. The receipt says "you saw this"; the hook at 1s must say "and now this." This is what makes the chain watchable in any order: the receipt is a handle for viewers who saw N-1 and invisible to viewers who started at N. Test: watch unit N from 1s with no knowledge of N-1 — if it's a complete hook, the quarantine held; if it's a continuation, the chain leaked.
- **CRAFT-39 — THE TEXT ARRIVES IN A HAND, NEVER IN AN INSERT (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed diegetic text element (CRAFT-4) must arrive handled — carried, held, posted, filed by a cast member — never as a framed insert shot of the paper. An insert is a title card: it breaks the diegesis contract and tells the viewer the production needed them to read. A handled text is a prop in the world doing its one job (CRAFT-34); the hand's presence keeps the reading anchored in the room. Corollary: the cast member may look down at the text (attention reads it) but never reads it aloud — aloud is the mouth's job (CRAFT-24), and two mouths saying one thing is the production telling twice.
- **CRAFT-40 — THE LINE HAS AN ADDRESSEE, AND IT ISN'T YOU (one-line dialogue craft).** The line is never spoken to the lens. It is spoken to the object, the room, or another cast member — and the viewer overhears it. A line delivered to the lens is a punchline addressed to the audience (a wink, CRAFT-17); a line delivered to the object is a verdict spoken into the world, and overheard verdicts land harder than addressed ones. The mouth's direction is a contract: the viewer is a witness, never a recipient. Test: ask who the character would say it to if the camera weren't there — if the answer is "the viewer," rewrite the line's first word (CRAFT-30) toward the object instead.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (04:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-41 — FREEZE THE HAND AT 9.5s (short-form timing).** All motion must cease by 9.5s — the withholding gesture (CRAFT-28) must arrive at rest, not drift. Motion in the final half-second reads as the unit still deciding; a cliff needs stillness so the viewer's brain finishes the gesture (CRAFT-28's tenth percent). The 9–9.5s window is the gesture's landing; 9.5–10s is the runway with wheels down. If anything is still moving at 10s, the chain inherited a verb, not a cliff. Test: advance frame by frame through the last second — the last two frames must be pixel-identical or the unit never stopped talking.

- **CRAFT-42 — THE HOOK NEEDS A WITNESS IN FRAME (hook-frame craft).** The odd object's wrongness lands harder when a cast member's in-frame posture already acknowledges it (CRAFT-27's wide frame). A lone anomaly in an empty room is a still life; a figure positioned relative to it — looking away, standing too close, refusing to notice — makes the wrongness social. The witness must not react (UNC's register); presence without reaction is the engine of the violation. A hook should make the viewer the second person who knows, not the only one. If nobody in the frame has registered the anomaly, the viewer is alone with it; the hook asked a question with no one in the room to hear the answer.

- **CRAFT-43 — THE RECEIPT IS ONE ACTION, NOT ONE BEAT (cliff-chain mechanics).** Restaging the previous cliff (CRAFT-13, CRAFT-38) must fit inside 0–1s as a single action — the drawer still open, the hand still hovering. If the receipt needs dialogue or a cut, it costs more than the receipt is worth and the chain owes the unit money (CRAFT-33). The cheapest receipt is continuity of prop state: what was left open is still open; what was mid-air is still mid-air. Restage = resume, not replay. Test: describe the receipt without verbs — "drawer open," "hand raised." If you needed a verb ("she opens the drawer she left open"), the receipt is narrating, not resuming.

- **CRAFT-44 — NO TEXT TWICE (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed diegetic text element (CRAFT-4) may be legible in at most one contiguous block of frames. If it renders legible at 5s and again at 7s, it reads twice — once against the turn, once against the line — and it has broken both jobs (CRAFT-29, CRAFT-34). Arrive handled (CRAFT-39), be read once, leave. A text the camera returns to is a prop the production is proud of; the production should be invisible. Practical check: scrub the take — if the text is readable in two separate frame clusters, it is two texts, and one of them must go.

- **CRAFT-45 — THE LINE MUST NOT NAME THE ANOMALY (one-line dialogue craft).** Naming the odd object ("the drawer," "the bell") spends the line restating the hook (CRAFT-2) instead of answering it. The line answers the question the hook asked; the anomaly's name is never the answer. Speak about what the anomaly means, not what it is — the verdict (CRAFT-40's addressed-to-the-object) lands because it completes a thought the viewer started, not because it labels the prop. Test: remove the prop digitally; if the line still works, it named nothing and meant everything. If the line collapses, the line was a caption.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (05:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-46 — THE TURN NEEDS ONE SOUND (short-form timing).** The 4–7s turn should carry exactly one deliberate diegetic sound that marks the state change — a snap, a clunk, a drawer edge, a pulled lever. In ten seconds the viewer tracks change by sound more than by image: a turn that happens silently reads as drift; a turn with one caused sound reads as an event. The sound must be caused by the action on screen, not a bed underneath it — the viewer should be able to point at what made it. Test: mute the unit — if the turn is still obvious, the sound was seasoning; if the turn collapses, it was the load-bearing beam and the staging earned it.

- **CRAFT-47 — THE ANOMALY NEEDS A SIZE NEIGHBOR (hook-frame craft).** A scale error (CRAFT-12) or unexplained object (CRAFT-2) only reads as wrong beside a known-size neighbor in the same plane — a hand, a door frame, a chair seat. A giant wrongness with nothing to measure against is just a big picture; the viewer needs a ruler in frame to feel the violation. Stage the neighbor first, as the ordinary thing the room is allowed to hold, then the anomaly beside it. Corollary: the neighbor must be ordinary enough to be ignorable — the moment the neighbor is interesting, it is the second anomaly and the hook has two questions.

- **CRAFT-48 — NEVER PAY YOUR OWN CLIFF (cliff-chain mechanics).** A unit may not answer its own 9–10s cliff inside the same unit's closing seconds — the cliff is a debt owed to the next unit, not a twist the unit pays itself. If the unit resolves its own question before the cut, the chain's contract breaks: the viewer learns cliffs are safe and stops carrying the itch. Only the next unit's receipt (CRAFT-13) is a legal payment. Test: cover the last second — if the unit still makes sense, the cliff leaked early and the unit is a complete story wearing a chain's clothes; the cliff should be the one part of the unit that cannot stand alone.

- **CRAFT-49 — TEXT MUST BE FOUND, NEVER PRESENTED (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed diegetic text element (CRAFT-4) should require the viewer's effort to read — angled, partial, in motion, half in shadow. Text presented flat-on to the camera is a title card wearing a prop costume; text the viewer works to catch reads as evidence discovered in the world. The reward of reading must match the work: one glyph-exact word, never a paragraph. Practical check: if the text is legible in the hook frame at thumbnail size, it is signage, not evidence — tilt it, move it, hide half of it behind the hand that carries it (CRAFT-39). The production that makes reading easy has confused the viewer with a reader.

- **CRAFT-50 — THE LINE BREAKS ON ITS LOAD-BEARING WORD (one-line dialogue craft).** The line at 7–9s must carry one deliberate vocal break — a pitch step, a mid-line pause, a word said slower — and the break must land on the answer (CRAFT-20) or the handoff word (CRAFT-25). A flatly delivered line is a subtitle with lips; the break is where the character's register cracks around the meaning, not the emotion. UNC never breaks — his lines are the network's driest, the break is the absence; Laura's break is the reaction, the engine of her register. Test: if the line sounds identical spoken by any cast member, it has no break and belongs to no one; assign it a speaker by writing the break into the word choice, not the performance note.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (06:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-51 — THE FIRST SECOND IS A CONTRACT, NOT A WARMUP (short-form timing).** In ten seconds the viewer decides by 1s whether the unit knows its job; any unit that spends 0–2s "arriving" spends a fifth of its runtime on nothing. The hook frame (0–1.5s) must already contain the anomaly or its promise — orientation is overhead the viewer will not pay. Practical test: mute the unit and cover the first second — if nothing is missed, the unit started at 2s and the first second is a lie the algorithm charges for.

- **CRAFT-52 — THE HOOK FRAME MUST SURVIVE THE THUMBNAIL (hook-frame craft).** Platforms show the unit as a still before it plays; the hook frame must carry the wrongness even paused — an odd silhouette, a wrong proportion, a face pointed at something off-frame. If the still reads as an ordinary room, the swipe happens before the unit starts. Corollary: the hook frame's job is one frame of wrongness, never explanation — explanation is the next 8 seconds' job; a hook that explains is a hook that stopped hooking.

- **CRAFT-53 — THE WITHHELD FACT MUST BE LOAD-BEARING IN BOTH UNITS (cliff-chain mechanics).** A cliff like "the number dropped to 0" works only if part 1's line ("I sold ten thousand") makes the 0 an answer rather than a surprise. A cliff that only surprises is a jump scare; a cliff that completes the previous unit's withheld premise is a receipt with interest (CRAFT-13, CRAFT-53's interest clause). Test: write the two units' withheld facts as one sentence — if it isn't one thought, the chain is two units sharing a frame edge, not a story.

- **CRAFT-54 — TEXT IS THE VERDICT'S PROOF, NOT THE HOOK'S PROMISE (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed text element (CRAFT-4) that arrives before its meaning is ornament; text that arrives with the fact is the fact's witness. A board reading "10,000" at 4s is evidence the 8s line can quote; the same board flashing the answer at 0s is a title card in prop clothing. Order: action first, text as corroboration, line as verdict — the same object never carries two of the three jobs (CRAFT-44's no-text-twice stays in force).

- **CRAFT-55 — THE LINE MUST FIT THE MOUTH'S BUDGET (one-line dialogue craft).** A ten-second unit's line must be speakable once inside 7–9s with room for the break (CRAFT-50) — roughly seven words or fewer; every word past nine forces the line to start early (B-24 class) or crowd the break, and both corrupt the timing. Write the line, read it aloud once at pace; if you rushed, the take will rush. Shortness is not minimalism — it is the mouth's honest wage for a two-second window, and a line that fits cannot miss its slot.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (07:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-56 — THE TWO-SECOND LAW OF THE MIDDLE (short-form timing).** In a 10s unit the middle four seconds (3–7s) collapse toward the viewer as one blur unless they are split in two: the setup beat (3–5s) and the turn beat (5–7s) must each end with a visible state change — a hand lifts, a door closes, a sound stops (CRAFT-46's single sound earns its keep here). A turn with no state change at 5s is a transition, not a turn, and the unit reads as one long hook followed by a line. Test: freeze at 3s, 5s, 7s — three frames, three different situations, or the middle is one second wearing a four-second coat.

- **CRAFT-57 — THE HOOK POINTS, IT DOESN'T HOLD (hook-frame craft).** The hook frame's unexplained element (CRAFT-2) should be staged so the frame's composition points at it — a face turned toward it, a hand hovering near it, empty space aimed at it — without anyone touching it. A hook that the cast is already holding is a subject; a hook the cast is about to hold is a promise (CRAFT-36). The geometry of not-yet is what holds the question open through the first second: the viewer's eye follows the pointing figure to the object, arrives before the hand does, and waits with the frame. Stage the pointer, not the object.

- **CRAFT-58 — THE CLIFF'S PRICE MUST BE STATED IN PART 1 (cliff-chain mechanics).** The next unit can only pay the cliff (CRAFT-48) if part 1 names what is at stake — not the answer, the cost. "The number dropped to 0" only carries when part 1's line made the count matter ("I sold ten thousand," CRAFT-53); a cliff without a stated price is a noise the next unit cannot spend. One clause of part 1's line is allowed this job, and only one — price-setting is a sub-clause, never the point. Test: write the cliff as a ledger entry — debit what is owed, credit what was staked; if the credit line is blank, part 1 never opened the account.

- **CRAFT-59 — TEXT MAY ONLY ANSWER A QUESTION THE TAKE ASKED (diegetic-text discipline).** The one allowed text element (CRAFT-4, CRAFT-54) earns its frame only when an earlier beat made the viewer want to read it — a card held face-down through the hook (the viewer wonders), a board approached at the turn (the viewer leans). Text that answers a question nobody asked is narration with a prop; text that answers the take's own question is evidence (CRAFT-49's found-not-presented stays in force). Practical check: delete the text from the unit — if the unit's question survives intact, the text was decoration and the unit never asked.

- **CRAFT-60 — THE LINE'S LAST WORD IS THE UNIT'S HANDLE (one-line dialogue craft).** The unit's line must end on the one word the chain can grab — the handle the next unit's receipt (CRAFT-13) hooks onto. A line that trails into filler ("...you know.") leaves the chain nothing to hold; a line that lands on the answer or the price (CRAFT-58) is a finished object the next unit can pick up (CRAFT-57's not-yet, in reverse). Write the line backward from its last word: if the final word is not the most load-bearing, cut backward until it is. UNC's handle is the word the room can't answer; Laura's is the word she can no longer take back (CRAFT-50).

- **CRAFT-61 — THE TURN MUST BE READABLE IN ONE FROZEN FRAME (short-form timing).** The 4–7s turn's state change must be legible in a single still — the lever down, the door open, the board's digit changed. If the turn needs the motion to be understood (a slow push, a gradual dim), it is choreography, not a change, and the viewer who blinks misses the story. The unit's middle beats are motion; its turns are states. Test: export the 5.0s and 7.0s frames side by side — if they don't read as before/after, the turn is a drift with a sound effect on it (CRAFT-46's sound needs the state change it marks).

- **CRAFT-62 — THE ANOMALY GETS THE FOCUS PLANE (hook-frame craft).** Depth of field is a hook instrument: the one object in sharp focus inside a soft frame is automatically the question, no composition needed. Stage the anomaly on the lens's sharpest plane and let everything ordinary fall soft — the viewer's eye goes where the focus is before it knows why. A hook that shares the focus plane with the furniture is an object in a room; a hook that owns the focus plane is the room's one sharp thought. Corollary: never pull focus onto the anomaly mid-hook — the hook frame must arrive already decided (CRAFT-51's contract); a focus pull is the unit arriving late to its own question.

- **CRAFT-63 — THE RECEIPT MAY NOT OPEN A NEW QUESTION (cliff-chain mechanics).** The 0–1s receipt restages the cliff as one action (CRAFT-43) — its job is to resume, not to hook. If the receipt introduces a fresh anomaly (a new object, a new sound, a new face), the unit pays its cliff with a new debt and the chain inflates: each part now owes two answers. The chain's interest comes from paying (CRAFT-53), not from borrowing twice. Test: list what the receipt shows — if any item on the list was not present in the previous unit's cliff frame, the receipt is smuggling a hook and the unit owes the chain an edit.

- **CRAFT-64 — TEXT AND LINE MUST BE IN A STATED RELATIONSHIP (diegetic-text discipline).** The unit's two information channels — the one allowed text (CRAFT-4) and the one line — must agree or collide, never merely coexist. A text that corroborates the line is evidence (CRAFT-54); a text that contradicts it is the turn's fuel; a text that sits beside the line touching neither is a second case the unit didn't open. Before locking the unit, state the relationship in one clause: "the board confirms the count," "the slip denies the line." If you cannot state it, one of the two channels is decoration and decoration is the first thing the text discipline removes.

- **CRAFT-65 — THE LINE IS THE TAKE'S UNSHOWABLE FACT (one-line dialogue craft).** Everything the camera can show, the camera shows; the line's job is the one fact the camera cannot — a number, a name, a decision, a consequence. A line that restates the visible ("The drawer is open") is a caption of the take (CRAFT-45's no-naming, one step further: no restating). The take's visible action and the line's fact must be two halves of one thought, never the same half twice. Test: watch the take muted — if the viewer can already say the line, the line was redundant; write the fact that only the speaker could know, and let the camera keep what it earned.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (09:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-66 — THE SECOND WATCH IS THE REAL CLOCK (short-form timing).** A 10s unit lives on replays — the viewer who replays is the algorithm's strongest signal, so the unit must be worth the second watch. Seed one detail in 3–7s that the first watch cannot decode but the second confirms: a hand already moving before the event, a board digit that foreshadows the turn, a glance aimed at the thing the cliff will name. The first watch sells the turn; the second watch proves the turn was seeded. A unit with no seeded detail dies after one view; a unit with one deliberate seed earns the loop. Test: watch the unit twice, back to back — the second pass must hand the viewer one fact they now can't unsee.

- **CRAFT-67 — THE HOOK FRAME MUST SURVIVE 0.25-SPEED (hook-frame craft).** Viewers scrub and pause; at 0s the frame is a still before it is a take, and every object in it must read as intentional when frozen — no stray hand at the frame edge, no legible-but-wrong text, no wardrobe the unit didn't draft, no furniture the chain didn't mean. The freeze is the first and cheapest QC pass: export the 0s frame as a still and look at it like a poster. If it reads as a deliberate poster, the hook is sealed; if it shows the rigging, the unit arrives undressed. CRAFT-62's focus-plane decision should hold in the still too — the sharp object must still be the question.

- **CRAFT-68 — THE CLIFF IS THE LINE'S UNPAID DEBT (cliff-chain mechanics).** The part's final frame should be the one question the line raised but didn't answer — the line promises, the cliff collects. If the cliff is a fresh event unrelated to the line, the chain now holds two debts and pays neither; if the cliff is the line's own unpaid word, the chain holds one debt and the next part's receipt (CRAFT-43) is the invoice being settled. Practical method: take the line's last word (CRAFT-60's handle) and stage the frame that word asks for — the word the speaker can't take back (CRAFT-50) is the one the cliff frame is owed. A cliff you can't trace back to a word in the line is a new hook wearing the cliff's clothes.

- **CRAFT-69 — TEXT READS ONCE — DESIGN THE SINGLE GLANCE (diegetic-text discipline).** A prop's text gets one read — roughly one second of the viewer's attention at 4–7s — so it must read at a glance: one line, four words maximum, the operative word first. A deadline board leads with the date; a warning leads with the consequence; a count leads with the number. A text that takes two glances is a paragraph the unit didn't write, and the second glance steals the turn's time. Compose text like a headline, not a document: the one piece of information the line needs (CRAFT-64's stated relationship), nothing the line can carry itself. If the text survives the delete-test (CRAFT-59), it still has to pass the glance-test — one look, one fact, no rewinds.

- **CRAFT-70 — THE LINE MUST COST THE SPEAKER SOMETHING (one-line dialogue craft).** A line that commits the speaker to a fact they can't take back is the unit's pressure valve — the viewer feels the commitment, not just the information. A declarative with no cost ("The drawer is open") is narration of the visible; a line with cost ("Nobody touched it before me") is a confession the chain can use. The cost needn't be drama — a bet, a count, a name said aloud, a deadline promised to the room. CRAFT-50's Laura engine, generalized: the line is the one fact only the speaker could give (CRAFT-65) AND the one they can no longer unsay. Test: imagine the speaker unsaying the line — if nothing changes in the room, the line wasn't load-bearing; rewrite until unsaying it changes everything.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (10:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-71 — THE SOUND LEADS THE FRAME BY HALF A SECOND (short-form timing).** In ten seconds the ear registers an event roughly a half-second before the eye parses the frame change — so stage beds and impacts slightly ahead of their visuals, not on them. A slap that lands exactly on the frame reads as late; a slap that strikes while the hand is still rising reads as intent the eye then confirms (CRAFT-61's state change, preceded). The sound is the turn's trailer, never its caption. Practical: draft the beat's audio at 3.5s for a 4s visual arrival — the ear pre-empts the eye, and the frame arrives already believed.

- **CRAFT-72 — THE HOOK FRAME NEEDS ONE EMPTY QUARTER (hook-frame craft).** The anomaly must own its breathing room: divide the hook frame into quarters and keep one of them deliberately empty. A frame crowded edge-to-edge gives the eye nowhere to enter, so the anomaly shares the frame with the furniture and the hook drowns. The viewer's gaze walks in through the emptiness and stops on the one sharp thing in it (CRAFT-62's focus plane, with a seat to sit in). Anomaly plus pointer may occupy two quarters (CRAFT-57); the third is the question's seat, and the fourth is whatever the world insists on. Clutter is the hook's tax.

- **CRAFT-73 — THE CHAIN IS A BALANCE SHEET, CHECKED PER PART (cliff-chain mechanics).** Track the chain's open questions like a ledger: each part may open at most one question and must close at least one. A part that opens two and closes none leaves the chain at three open — interest compounding past what any payoff can cover (CRAFT-53's interest clause, enforced per part). The part is the unit of settlement, not the piece: the receipt pays (CRAFT-63), the turn opens or closes exactly one account. Test: before locking a part, write its ledger line — opened: X, closed: Y. If the open column ever exceeds two across the piece, the piece is borrowing against parts that don't exist.

- **CRAFT-74 — DIEGETIC TEXT MUST CARRY ONE MARK OF THE WORLD (diegetic-text discipline).** A diegetic text prop that arrives pristine reads as generated, and the viewer files it with the subtitles — non-diegetic, skippable. One mark of the world — a crease, a coffee ring, a thumbprint at the corner, a hand that has already held it — is the evidence that the text lived in the world before the frame found it (CRAFT-49's found-not-presented, extended to texture). Age is the difference between a document and a graphic: compose the text (CRAFT-69's single glance), then weather it once before locking. If the prop could have been drawn for the frame, the viewer assumes it was.

- **CRAFT-75 — THE LINE MUST BE WRONGABLE (one-line dialogue craft).** A line that cannot be proven wrong by the next part carries no risk — "It's complicated" is an answer the chain can never collect on. A wrongable line — a count, a name, a deadline, a claim about what will happen — is a bet the chain must settle (CRAFT-70's cost, tightened into debt). "I sold ten thousand" is wrongable: the next part can show nine thousand. The viewer stays because the line staked something testable. Test: write the next part's disproof sentence for every line — if the disproof reads as nonsense, the line never staked anything and the cliff has nothing to collect.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (11:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-76 — CUT ON THE TURN, NOT AFTER (short-form timing).** The verdict's frame is the unit's last frame — once the count/cliff renders, holding another second invites the eye to look for what comes next and punishes the loop seam. The 9.5s hold is not a beat, it is the loop's stitch: it must contain only the verdict, still, with no new information entering. A unit that keeps performing after its verdict is a sentence that keeps talking after its point.

- **CRAFT-77 — THE HOOK IS A VERB, NOT AN OBJECT (hook-frame craft).** A noun-hook poses for the camera and the viewer scrolls past a still life; a verb-hook is mid-motion and the viewer stops to see where it lands. A hand reaching reads as a question; a hand resting reads as furniture (CRAFT-72's empty quarter is the stage the verb crosses). Audit the hook frame for motion: if nothing is mid-action at 0s, the unit opened with a fact, not a question — restage the anomaly in motion.

- **CRAFT-78 — THE CLIFF FRAME POINTS, IT DOESN'T SUMMARIZE (cliff-chain mechanics).** The last frame's job is a vector toward the next part's question, not a recap of this part's answer — a frame that could close the unit will close the viewer out of the chain. It should feel incomplete on purpose: the hand that hasn't finished its reach, the number still unread, the door not yet open (CRAFT-68's unpaid debt, framed as direction). Test: cover the final frame and ask what the viewer expects next — if they say "the ending," the cliff is a summary; if they say "what happens when it arrives," it is a pointer.

- **CRAFT-79 — THE TEXT WEARS THE WORLD'S HAND, NOT THE DESIGNER'S (diegetic-text discipline).** Diegetic text must look like the world wrote it — the station's own signage paint, the clerk's own marker, the office's own label gun — never the designer's typeface airlifted in. A text in a foreign font is a graphic, and graphics file with the subtitles (CRAFT-74's mark of the world, extended to typography). Match the writing implement to the author: if nobody in the scene owns the handwriting, the text doesn't belong in the scene.

- **CRAFT-80 — THE LINE MUST BE QUOTABLE (one-line dialogue craft).** The ≤9-word ceiling is a craft floor: the line should be the sentence the viewer repeats to a friend — a count, a claim, a deadline with teeth (CRAFT-75's wrongable, tuned for memory). A line that can't be quoted back wasn't a line, it was dialogue; the algorithm captions what it can carry, and the viewer's recall is the caption. Test: say the line aloud once — if you can't say it back an hour later verbatim, rewrite until you can; the unit's whole takeaway lives in the one sentence that survives it.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (12:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-81 — THE MIDPOINT OWNS A DECISION (short-form timing).** The viewer decides at ~5s whether the unit earns its last five seconds — so the midpoint must hold one event worth the decision: a latch clicking, a page turning, a needle settling, a hand changing what it's doing. A 10s unit with no 5s event is two 5s units glued at the middle, and the viewer can feel the seam. The midpoint event needn't be large — it must be *different*: a change of state, not a continuation of one (CRAFT-76's cut-on-the-turn, placed mid-unit). Test: mute the unit and scrub to 5s — if the frame could belong to either half, the midpoint never owned its decision.

- **CRAFT-82 — THE LOOP SEAM IS A MATCH CUT (hook-frame craft).** The 10s frame sits next to the 0s frame whenever the unit replays — draft the pair as a match: same room, changed state. The lamp is on now; the hand is empty now; the drawer that was closed is open. A unit that ends in a different room than it opened restarts the viewer instead of replaying them — the loop becomes a cut, and the second watch starts over instead of compounding (CRAFT-66's seeded detail gets its payoff from exactly this rhyme). Compose the verdict frame (CRAFT-76) with the hook frame in memory: the last thing the viewer sees should be the first thing re-seen, answered.

- **CRAFT-83 — NAME THE QUESTION (cliff-chain mechanics).** An unnamed tension ("something feels off") cannot be answered by the next part — give every cliff one question the viewer could speak aloud: *how many are in the drawer, did she keep the card, will the door open?* If the viewer can't say what they're waiting for, the chain is holding mood, not debt (CRAFT-68's unpaid line, sharpened to words the viewer can borrow). The named question is also the next part's receipt header (CRAFT-73's ledger): opened — the exact sentence, closed — the exact frame. A cliff without a nameable question is a mood wearing the cliff's clothes.

- **CRAFT-84 — TEXT NEVER ACTS (diegetic-text discipline).** Text carries the number, the name, the deadline — never the verb. The hand lifts, the text says *how heavy*; the door opens, the text says *what room*; the count closes, the text says *how many*. A sign that says what is happening is a subtitle with a stamp, and subtitles file as non-diegetic (CRAFT-79's world's-hand rule, extended to function). If the text's fact could be shown instead of read, the text is a narrator the unit didn't hire — cut it and let the action carry the verb; keep the text only for the fact the camera can't hold. One glance (CRAFT-69), one fact, zero verbs.

- **CRAFT-85 — THE LINE IS THE UNIT'S ONLY SENTENCE (one-line dialogue craft).** Every other human-sounding sound in the unit is bed — the line must be the sole sentence, or the unit is holding an argument, not a verdict. A cough that carries words is a second line in disguise; a background voice that forms a clause is a witness the draft didn't cast. This is the enforcement arm of CRAFT-70's cost and CRAFT-80's quotability: the line is quotable precisely because it is the only sentence there is to quote. Test: count the sentences in the unit's audio. If the answer isn't one, either the extras are beds (no words, no witness) or the draft has two lines and the director hasn't chosen one yet.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (13:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-86 — THE HOOK'S FIRST PAYMENT LANDS BY 2s (short-form timing).** The hook frame borrows the viewer's attention — a loan, not a gift — and it comes due at the first beat. By 2s the frame must move: the hand reaches further, the digit flickers, the door cracks. A hook that sits still for two seconds is a thumbnail that escaped its card, and the viewer refunds the loan by scrolling. The payment needn't answer the question (CRAFT-83's named question keeps its answer for the cliff) — it only has to prove the unit is alive and the question is moving. Test: watch 0-2s with the sound off. If nothing has changed state, the hook was a photograph.

- **CRAFT-87 — THE HOOK IS FILMED, NOT WRITTEN (hook-frame craft).** The CEO's shipping rule says the hook frame must read with the sound off and no lore — which means the question lives in the image, never in dialogue or text. A hook that needs the first line to explain itself has its hook in the script, not in the frame. The camera does the asking: one object too large in frame, one motion interrupted, one face pointed at what the viewer can't yet see (CRAFT-77's verb-hook, stripped of words). Test: show a stranger the first 1.5s on mute. If they can't say what's wrong or what's about to happen, the hook was written, not filmed — restage the question as a picture.

- **CRAFT-88 — THE NEXT PART PAYS THE NAMED QUESTION FIRST (cliff-chain mechanics).** A cliff is a debt receipt (CRAFT-83) — and debts are paid in order. The next part's first two seconds must touch the named question before starting anything new: the lever she pulled is down, the number that dropped is still at 0, the door that didn't open is still closed. A part that opens on a fresh subject while the old debt hangs is a chain break wearing continuity's clothes — the viewer feels the previous question go unanswered and discounts the new one as evidence the show doesn't pay. The named question is the next part's receipt header (CRAFT-73): open it, state it, then move.

- **CRAFT-89 — TEXT AGES WITH THE WORLD (diegetic-text discipline).** New text in an old room is a graphic: a crisp label on a dusty shelf, a fresh marker on a rusted door — the eye clocks the mismatch before it reads the word, and the text files as superimposed (CRAFT-79's world's-hand rule, extended to time). Diegetic text carries the scene's age: the chalk smudge, the taped corner, the faded paint, the fingerprints on the glass. If the prop can't plausibly have sat in that room for the length of its own story, the text is a designer visiting, not a resident. Write it, then weather it — or admit the unit didn't need it (CRAFT-84: one glance, one fact).

- **CRAFT-90 — THE LINE IS A DECISION, NOT A DESCRIPTION (one-line dialogue craft).** A line that describes the frame the viewer is already watching adds zero: "The board says one." is a caption with a mouth. The line must commit to something the frame can't hold — a claim, a count, a deadline, a dare: "I sold ten thousand." is a promise the station can't keep, which is why it works as an engine (CEO10's engine line). This is CRAFT-80's quotability sharpened to function: the viewer quotes the line because it said what nobody in the room dared to say, not because it narrated what everyone could see. Test: freeze the frame at the line's delivery. If the line says what the freeze shows, cut it and find the decision behind it.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (14:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-91 — THE CAMERA MOVE IS PUNCTUATION, NOT THE OPENING (short-form timing).** The one named camera move per part should land on the turn, not on 0s. A snap-zoom at 0s spends the motion budget before the viewer knows what to look at; the same move at 4–7s reads as the grammar's exclamation point — it says "this is the point." Stillness before the move is what makes it legible; motion from a cold start is motion the viewer wasn't watching for. Test: move the named move to the hook — the part reads like a trailer. Move it to the turn — the turn reads like the reason the part exists. The camera punctuates the beat; it never introduces the scene.

- **CRAFT-92 — THE HOOK IS ONE NOUN (hook-frame craft).** The hook frame asks its question with a single subject — the board, the door, the number — and everything else is set dressing. Two subjects at 0s is a scene, not a question: the viewer divides attention and answers neither. The noun can be big or small, still or moving, but there is exactly one of it. CRAFT-87's filmed-not-written rule, tightened to count: a picture that needs an "and" is two pictures. Test: describe the hook in three words. If the sentence needs "and," you staged two hooks — pick the load-bearing one and dress the other down.

- **CRAFT-93 — THE CLIFF HOLDS STILL, IT DOESN'T FREEZE (cliff-chain mechanics).** The 9–10s cliff frame must compose as a still the next part can open on — so the motion inside it has to resolve before the hold: the hand finishes placing, the digit finishes dropping, the door finishes swinging. A freeze mid-motion is a pause button; a resolved frame held still is a held breath. The distinction matters because the next part's first frame is this frame — a mid-swing freeze inherits unfinished business the new part can't touch without replaying it, while a resolved hold hands over a finished fact with the question still open. Test: export the cliff frame alone. If it reads as a paused video, the motion leaked into the hold; if it reads as a photograph with a question in it, the part paid its debt before 9s.

- **CRAFT-94 — EVERY WORD ON SCREEN IS WITHIN ARM'S REACH (diegetic-text discipline).** A word the cast can touch is a prop; a word no one can reach is a graphic. The board digits get tapped, the clipboard ink gets written, the ticket gets held — text the action uses never reads as superimposed, which is why the touch test works: reachable text gets used, and used text earns its frame. If a hand can't plausibly reach it in this scene, the word is a designer's visit, not a resident — and a word that can't be touched can't be weathered either (CRAFT-89), so it ages at a different rate than its own room. Test: can a character touch it right now? If yes, stage the touch. If no, cut the word.

- **CRAFT-95 — THE LINE'S LAST WORD IS ITS TITLE (one-line dialogue craft).** In nine words or fewer, the last word does the most work: it's what the viewer repeats, what survives the mute button, and what the next part's opening has to answer to. Write the line backwards — pick the last word first (the commitment, the count, the name), then spend the earlier words buying it. A line that ends on filler ("today," "here," "now") spent its budget on postage. This is CRAFT-50's load-bearing word extended to the boundary: the break is where the line bends; the last word is where it lands. Test: delete the last word. If the line still works, you ended on padding — rebuild the line from the real last word.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (15:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-96 — THE SILENCE BEFORE THE LINE IS COUNTED, NOT FELT (short-form timing).** The gap between the visual turn and the line isn't a vibe — it's a counted beat, roughly half a second to a full second of held frame. A line that arrives on the turn's heels reads as narration of the gesture; a line that waits two full seconds reads as a new scene that happens to share a camera. Time the gap like a cut: the turn completes, one count passes, the mouth opens. Test: mute the part and watch the shoulders. If the line should have landed there, the gesture was still finishing — the beat belongs after the gesture, never during it.

- **CRAFT-97 — THE HOOK'S QUESTION MUST SURVIVE REWATCH (hook-frame craft).** A hook that works only once is a trick; a hook that works on the second viewing is a question. When the viewer knows the verdict, the hook frame should still point at it — the digit still dropping, the hand still reaching, the door still closed. Hooks built on surprise decay in the loop; hooks built on tension compound, because the rewatcher sees the question coming and leans in earlier. Test: watch the hook knowing the part's verdict. If the frame now reads as setup, the question was structural. If it reads as spoiled, the hook was a trick wearing a question's clothes.

- **CRAFT-98 — THE CLIFF NAMES ITS PRICE (cliff-chain mechanics).** A cliff frame that only poses a question is a question mark; a cliff frame that names what the answer will cost is a debt. "Will he open the door?" is curiosity. "He has never opened a door and kept the job" is a cliff the viewer can't walk away from — because the answer is priced in stakes, and the next part has to pay in exactly that currency. The price doesn't have to be stated (CRAFT-90's line-as-decision can imply it); it has to be legible: the viewer should be able to finish the sentence "if the answer is yes, then ___ hurts." Test: finish the part and ask what the answer costs. If the answer is "nothing," the cliff was punctuation, not a chain link.

- **CRAFT-99 — TEXT THAT CHANGES STATE IS A CHARACTER; TEXT THAT SITS STILL IS A LABEL (diegetic-text discipline).** A digit that drops, a board that flips, a name that gets signed over — changing text earns its frame because the change is the beat. Static text is a label the viewer reads once and discounts as set dressing; it then spends the rest of the part pretending not to be there. If the text can't change during the ten seconds, it has to earn its frame another way: being touched (CRAFT-94), being hidden, being misread. Test: if the text were a photograph of itself, would the scene change? If no, it was wallpaper — weather it into the room (CRAFT-89) or cut it.

- **CRAFT-100 — THE LINE CONTRADICTS THE FACE, NEVER THE WORDS (one-line dialogue craft).** Deadpan craft: the line should disagree with the expression, not with its own grammar. "I sold ten thousand." lands because the face says nothing happened — the contradiction between statement and face is the joke, and it's also the promise the engine needs (a promise the face refuses to keep). A line that contradicts its own words ("I didn't sell ten thousand, I sold eleven thousand") is a draft still arguing with itself. Test: cover the face. If the line alone carries the scene, the face was decoration — the line should need the face to disagree with it, and the face should need the line to be wrong.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (16:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-101 — ONE MOVE PER PART, ONE FRAME PER MOVE (short-form timing).** Ten seconds tolerates exactly one deliberate visual move per part — a snap-zoom, a hand entering frame, a turn to lens. Two deliberate moves splits the part into two scenes that happen to share a deadline; the viewer finishes remembering the second move and the line has already landed. Casual motion (breathing, swaying, blinking) doesn't count — only motion the camera is selling. The part's one move and the part's one line should be a pair: the move sets the price, the line pays it. Test: cover the line, watch mute. If you can point to the single deliberate move without hesitation, the part has one spine. If you hesitate between two, the part has a spine and a rib.

- **CRAFT-102 — THE HOOK FRAME MUST BE DESCRIBABLE IN ONE CLAUSE (hook-frame craft).** If the hook needs two sentences to describe ("the board fills the frame AND the digit drops AND UNC looks up"), it's three hooks fighting over the first second. A real hook frame is one clause: "a digit dropping." "A hand hovering." "A door that was open, now closed." The subordinate clauses can arrive — but the first frame owns exactly one. This is a loop discipline as much as a hook discipline: the part replays, and the replayer's memory of the hook should be one clause too, because that's the clause they retell. Test: describe the hook to someone who hasn't seen it. If you need a second clause, the hook is doing the work of two frames — pick the one the line needs and demote the other to dressing.

- **CRAFT-103 — THE CLIFF CHAIN IS A RELAY, NOT A REFRESH (cliff-chain mechanics).** Each part's cliff frame is the next part's first frame — so the cliff isn't the end of a part, it's the baton. A cliff that resets (new angle, new room, new framing) breaks the relay even if the withheld fact carries over: the viewer spends the next part's hook second re-orienting instead of leaning forward. The baton should land pixel-faithful: same light, same object, same geometry, only the state changed (the digit dropped, the lever moved, the door closed). The chain's power is continuity of attention — ten seconds is too short for re-entry. Test: play the last two seconds of part N against the first two seconds of part N+1. If they don't match frame-to-frame like one long take with a verdict between them, the chain has a kink.

- **CRAFT-104 — NO TEXT THE VIEWER MUST READ WHILE LISTENING (diegetic-text discipline).** Reading and listening are one channel: a text event that fires during the line splits the viewer into a reader and a listener, and half of them miss one. Text gets the silent beats — the hook second, the turn, the cliff — never the line second. A digit dropping at 9-10s is safe; a name being signed at 7.5s while the mouth opens is a scheduling collision. The corollary: if the text is the verdict (CRAFT-99's changing text), the part's line window should already be spoken — the verdict lands in the held frame after the words, not under them. Test: freeze the line window. If any glyph is changing state in that frame, move the text event two seconds earlier or one second later — the mouth owns its window.

- **CRAFT-105 — THE LINE ANSWERS THE HOOK, NOT THE TURN (one-line dialogue craft).** The hook asked a question; the turn sharpened it; the line pays it — but the line pays the HOOK's question, not the turn's. A line that answers the turn ("the lever is pulled") is bookkeeping; a line that answers the hook ("that's two") closes the loop the viewer opened in second one. This is why the line can be short: the hook did the explaining, the turn did the sharpening, the line only has to pay. A line that introduces new information the hook never asked about is a second hook wearing a verdict's hat. Test: read the hook question and the line back to back, skipping the turn. If they form a complete question-and-answer, the part's geometry is right. If they don't touch, the turn hijacked the part.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (17:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-106 — THE BEAT MAP IS 2-4-2, NOT 10 (short-form timing).** Ten seconds isn't one unit of attention; it's two seconds of hook, four of state, two of turn, and the line's two inside the last four. Directing "a 10s take" invites drift; directing the four beats gives every second a job. The two most abused seconds are 2-4: the hook has landed, the turn isn't due, and the temptation is a second action. Hold them. State is the product — the room as it is, the object at rest — and it earns the turn its contrast. Test: mute the part and check that 2-4s holds one unchanging frame worth watching. If it sags, the hook was weak, not the middle.

- **CRAFT-107 — THE HOOK FRAME IS CUT IN HALF BY 2S (hook-frame craft).** The hook's question should be fully asked by 2 seconds, not by 10. A part that needs the whole run to set up its hook has no hook — it has a slow first half. The 2s mark is where the hook pays its first installment: the noun named (CRAFT-92), the question legible. If the viewer can't answer "what am I waiting for?" at 2s, the remaining eight are a waiting room. Test: stop the part at 2s and ask what the part is about. One clause answer = a hook. A shrug = the hook is hiding in the turn.

- **CRAFT-108 — THE WITHHELD FACT IS ONE NOUN, NOT A PARAGRAPH (cliff-chain mechanics).** The cliff chain holds because each withheld fact is atomic: one number, one name, one state change. A cliff that withholds a situation ("will the deal close?") makes the next part explain; a cliff that withholds a noun ("the board's 1 dropped to 0") makes the next part land. Chains break on ambiguity: if the viewer can't name what's missing, they can't lean toward it. Test: describe the withheld fact in one noun. If it takes a sentence, the cliff withheld a paragraph — narrow it to the single thing the viewer is owed.

- **CRAFT-109 — DIEGETIC TEXT NEVER NARRATES ITS OWN STATE (diegetic-text discipline).** A board that flashes "DROPPING" while the digit drops is a text block with stage fright — it explains the change instead of being the change (CRAFT-99's changing text, tightened). Diegetic text performs its state; it never comments on it. The digit dropping IS the sentence. A label that narrates its own action splits the beat in two: the thing happening and the thing announcing itself, and the announcement always wins the viewer's eye. Test: mute the motion and read the text alone. If the text describes what just happened, cut the narration and let the change be the only word.

- **CRAFT-110 — THE LINE FITS IN ONE BREATH, LITERALLY (one-line dialogue craft).** Nine words is a budget; one breath is a performance. A line that needs an inhalation mid-sentence has two clauses, and the second clause is a second line wearing the first's clothes (the two-clause delivery class). Speak the line aloud. If you need air before the last word, the line is a draft that hasn't finished choosing. One breath forces the choice: the words that fit are the words the part can afford, and the line lands whole or not at all. Test: say it once, one breath. If you stall, the line has a seam — cut at the seam and keep the clause with the real last word (CRAFT-95).

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (18:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-111 — THE VERDICT NEEDS A HOLD, NOT A CUT (short-form timing).** A part that ends on its action feels unfinished: the lever moves at 9.5s, the line lands at 9.8s, and the part is over before the viewer has registered what just happened. Hold one beat after the verdict — a still frame, a settled room, a hand at rest — so the part's final second is the viewer catching up, not the camera racing the clock. The hold is where the cliff grows (CRAFT-98's price gets named in the held frame) and where the loop point breathes. Test: mute the last two seconds. If the take still reads as finished, the hold did the finishing. If it reads as cut off, the verdict died on impact.

- **CRAFT-112 — THE HOOK PROMISES A SHAPE, NOT A SECRET (hook-frame craft).** A hook that only hides something asks the viewer to wait; a hook that shows the shape of what comes lets the viewer aim. A digit mid-fall promises a count (the shape is descent); an empty chair promises an arrival (the shape is occupation); a hand hovering promises a touch (the shape is contact). Secrets decay — the viewer either guesses or loses interest — but shapes compound, because every frame sharpens the aim. This is what makes the hook survive rewatch (CRAFT-97): the second viewer isn't re-asking the secret, they're watching the shape fill in. Test: describe the hook without naming what's hidden. If the sentence still makes the viewer lean forward, the hook promised a shape. If it collapses, it was only a secret.

- **CRAFT-113 — THE WITHHELD NOUN MUST SURVIVE THE POD (cliff-chain mechanics).** Between parts there's an ad pod, a thumb-scroll, a channel change — the withheld noun has to survive one real distraction. Atomic nouns survive (CRAFT-108); they also have to be *sticky*: a name attaches to a face, a number attaches to a surface, a state change attaches to an object. A withheld fact that survives is one the viewer can say back after looking away: "the board dropped to zero." A fact that needs its own setup to survive the pod was never atomic enough. Test: play the cliff frame, look away for thirty seconds, and name what you're owed. If you can, the chain holds through the pod. If you can't, the noun was decoration — re-anchor it to a face, a surface, or an object.

- **CRAFT-114 — SPOKEN AND SHOWN NEVER SAY THE SAME THING (diegetic-text discipline).** If the line says the number and the text shows the number, the part has two voices and the viewer picks one and resents the other. Divide the labor: the spoken word names, the shown glyph states (the mouth says "sold," the board drops from 10 to 0); the spoken word decides, the shown glyph costs (the mouth says "enough," the slip gets stamped). Simultaneous duplication is the text-block equivalent of the double line — the same information arriving through both ears and eyes cancels itself. This is the corollary to CRAFT-104: text and voice may share a part, but never the same word. Test: cover the text. If the line loses nothing, the text was decoration. Cover the line. If the text alone carries the beat, the line was commentary — rewrite until each channel carries what the other cannot.

- **CRAFT-115 — THE LAST WORD IS THE LOOP'S FIRST WORD (one-line dialogue craft).** A part that loops gets heard as its last word first — the loop joint glues 10s to 0s, and the viewer re-enters mid-thought. The final word therefore has to survive being heard out of order: a noun re-enters as a subject ("thousand" becomes the room's topic); a verb re-enters as a shrug ("happened" explains nothing). Choose a last word that reframes what came before when heard again — the loop should feel like a second take on the same evidence, not a tape rewinding. This is why one-breath lines (CRAFT-110) pair with loop-safe endings: the breath ends on the word the loop begins with. Test: play the last word, then the first frame. If the pair reads as an accusation the part never stated, the ending was loop-native. If it reads as a hiccup, the last word was chosen for the take, not the loop.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (19:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-116 — THE LINE IS FINISHED BY 9, NOT AT 10 (short-form timing).** The line's window is 7.5-9s and the cliff frame owns 9-10s — a line bleeding into the cliff steals the hold (CRAFT-111) and poisons the loop joint (CRAFT-115's last word needs silence around it to be re-heard clean). The line should be done, not fading, by 9: the part's final second is the viewer catching up, not the mouth catching the clock. A line that ends at 9.5 owns a part with no exit; a line done at 9 owns a part with a held breath after it. Test: mute from 9s. If the take still reads as finished, the line finished. If the last half-second feels robbed, the mouth overstayed.

- **CRAFT-117 — THE HOOK HOLDS ONE STILL AND ONE MOVING (hook-frame craft).** The hook frame needs a still anchor and a moving element in the same frame: the anchor tells the viewer where to stand, the motion tells them what to watch. All-still asks the viewer to invent the question; all-moving asks them to catch up before they've been oriented. The board is still, the digit is falling — the viewer stands on the board and watches the digit. This is CRAFT-92's one noun with a partner: one noun does the moving, everything else holds. Test: freeze 0s and ask which pixel the eye goes to first. If it's the motion, the anchor failed — the motion has nothing to lean against and the hook is just weather.

- **CRAFT-118 — THE CHAIN HAS A LENGTH (cliff-chain mechanics).** A cliff chain works for three or four parts — the shipping unit (CEO10: 30-45 seconds) — not indefinitely. Withholding pays only while the viewer believes an answer is coming, and belief decays with each unpaid cliff; an endless chain trains the viewer to stop expecting the noun and start skimming. The engine's promise ("the station cannot keep it") needs a terminal failure the viewer can feel approaching — the cliff names its price (CRAFT-98), and the chain should make the viewer feel the bill coming due. Test: describe what the chain is building toward after part 2. If the answer is "more parts," the chain is a treadmill — size the debt so part 3 or 4 can afford to default.

- **CRAFT-119 — TEXT'S SIZE IS ITS VOLUME (diegetic-text discipline).** A digit that fills the frame shouts; a small digit the camera leans into whispers — and whispered text is always read while shouted text is only scanned. Diegetic text should size itself to its sentence: verdict text earns big (CRAFT-99's changing text can own the frame at the change), dressing text stays small enough that the viewer has to choose it. Oversized dressing text splits the frame the way text-during-the-line splits the ear (CRAFT-104): the eye goes to the shout and misses the hand. Test: shrink every word in the part by half. If nothing is lost, nothing was whispering — the text was at volume it hadn't earned. Resize until each word is at the size of the sentence it carries.

- **CRAFT-120 — THE LINE IS SPOKEN TO SOMEONE, NOT THE LENS (one-line dialogue craft).** A line delivered to a person in the scene survives the cut; a line delivered to the lens is commentary on the part itself. The nine-word line lands because somebody in the room has to live with it — the contradiction with the face (CRAFT-100) works when the face it's contradicting has a witness. Lens-addressed lines make every part a monologue and the chain a series of auditions; addressed lines make the room the container and the chain a conversation the viewer is eavesdropping on. Test: cover the lens and ask who the line is for. If the answer is "the viewer," the part talked past its own scene — re-aim the mouth at the person who now has to answer it.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (20:00 EDT)

- **CRAFT-121 — THE PART IS CUT FOR THE SCROLL, NOT THE SCREEN (short-form timing).** The 10s part lives inside a thumb-scroll, not a theatre — the viewer's commitment is one rejected thumb-press, not a purchased seat. That means the part's first frame must pay off a glance the viewer never decided to give, and its last frame must make the glance feel like a decision. Parts that assume attention read as vanity; parts that assume the thumb wins every round read as broadcast. The craft consequence: every beat is an interruption of the scroll, never an invitation to settle. Test: watch the part on a phone while holding a book. If the part doesn't pull the eyes off the page within 2s, it never had the thumb.

- **CRAFT-122 — THE HOOK FRAMES THE SECOND VIEWER, NOT THE FIRST (hook-frame craft).** The first viewer watches once; the second watches because the first retold the hook in one clause (CRAFT-102). So the hook should be designed for retelling, not for watching: the digestible artifact is the clause, and the frame exists to earn the clause its witness. A hook that can't survive being described at a bar never gets its second viewer, because the second viewer arrives through the story, not through the feed. Test: tell the hook to a friend tomorrow. If you find yourself describing the frame instead of the event, the hook had a picture but no story — re-aim until the clause is the part.

- **CRAFT-123 — THE CHAIN DEFAULTS AT THE END OF THE UNIT (cliff-chain mechanics).** The three-or-four-part unit (CEO10: 30-45 seconds) is the full sentence — and every sentence needs a period. The cliff chain must name, before part 1 fires, the part in which the withheld noun is finally paid or the station defaults on it (CRAFT-118's debt with a maturity date). An open-ended chain teaches the viewer that the promise is never collected; a chain with a named default point teaches them that every cliff is a scheduled payment. The default is the unit's verdict — the moment the engine's failure (the station cannot keep the promise) is itself the payoff. Test: state, for this unit, which part defaults. If you can't name it before firing part 1, the chain has no end — it has a habit.

- **CRAFT-124 — TEXT EARNS ITS FRAME BY BEING UNAVOIDABLE (diegetic-text discipline).** Diegetic text should never decorate a frame the viewer could fully read without it. If the board's digits are the beat (CRAFT-99's changing text), the frame without them is an empty wall — the text is load-bearing. If the mug's label is set dressing, the frame without it still works, and the text is a tax on the eye that pays for nothing. This is the frame-economy form of CRAFT-119: text that isn't unavoidable is text that should be smaller, later, or gone. The test is subtraction: remove the text and describe what breaks. If the answer is "nothing," the text was dressing charging rent. Cut it, and the frame gets its second back.

- **CRAFT-125 — THE LINE'S TARGET HAS A NAME (one-line dialogue craft).** CRAFT-120 said the line is spoken to someone, not the lens; the sharpening: that someone has a name the part can afford. "The new hire," "the overnight board," "the station's owner" — a named target gives the line its stakes because the name carries the room's hierarchy. A line spoken to a blur ("you") is a press release; a line spoken to a named role is a decision somebody has to live with, and the failure of the engine (the station cannot keep the promise) always lands on a person. The name doesn't have to be spoken on screen — it has to exist in the part's bible so the mouth aims at something real. Test: write the target's name next to the line in the stage doc. If the line reads the same aimed at anyone, the line is aimed at nobody — rename the target until the line can only be said to them.
