### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE SHOWN SITTER WITH AN EMPTY CHAIR (CHAIN-370 P1)
When the inciting fact is a sitter shown without a body (CHAIN-370's monitor showing a seated figure while the chair in the room stands empty), frame 0 must show the transmission hall WITH the broadcast light on AND the monitor showing the seated figure AND the chair itself EMPTY AND no figure anywhere in the hall — a chair with a sitter in it is CHAIN-367's refusal, not this showing; a monitor showing an empty chair is CHAIN-367's cliff, not this beat; a monitor with no figure on it is a broadcast, not a sitter. Restage rule: shoot the shown sitter beside its own empty chair — if the frame still asks "is the shown sitter a viewer?", it is a showing; if it needs a body in the chair to ask, it is a claim. Sources: the open-loop hook — a premise that creates an immediate question answerable only by watching the whole piece (hooktos.com — mechanic mined only); the pattern interrupt — do something unexpected in the first 1.5 seconds to shock the brain out of passive scrolling (hooktos.com — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 2 — THE FOURTH TOTAL NOBODY WROTE (CHAIN-372 P1)
When the inciting fact is a total written by no hand (CHAIN-372's fourth total on the slate with both pens untouched), frame 0 must show the archive room WITH the machine still listening AND the slate with four totals AND both pens laid on the slate AND no hand near them — a pen in a hand is CHAIN-366's stillness, not this self-writing; a pen signing is a filing, not a count; a slate with three totals is CHAIN-369's wait, not this beat. Restage rule: shoot the fourth total beside its own untouched pens — if the frame still asks "who wrote it?", it is a self-writing; if it needs a hand to ask, it is a filing. Sources: the prop-based visual hook — physical props in the opening frame add an implication of value and stop the scroll (eliro.pro — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### LORE-121 — THE THINGS THAT ACT WITHOUT A HAND (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-370, CHAIN-371, and CHAIN-372 extend the refusal rule (LORE-120) into an action rule: "what the station waits for, acts without a hand." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the kept things did not only stay, answer, wait, sign, act, watch, return, count, watch back, sign back, sit for it, answer back, watch back, hire, list, skip, sign, work, take, receipt, fruit, tally, charge, owe, answer, keep, know, watch, prove, answer, wait, and refuse — they started acting in the place of the hands that left them: the monitor shows a sitter the room never had, the pile stamps a slip no stamper touched, the slate writes a total no writer wrote — each handless thing acts in the place of the absence it was made to hide, so the station never has to admit anything left unseen, unhired, or unsigned. Three handless things, one rule: the station survives because something in it acts — it shows, it stamps, it writes. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the handless thing acted in the place. Lore passes the choice test: the shown sitter changes the Dispatcher's claim (he must seat a picture, not prove himself by sitting, or admit the viewer is an image), the self-stamped slip changes UNC's order (he must hire a stranger no hand named, not close the roster), the unwritten total changes the Head's filing (he must sign a total he did not write, not count fruit) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-120 (the things that refuse): LORE-120 refuses tonight by the waiting itself; LORE-121 acts tonight without the hand — one refuses by waiting, one acts without waiting.

### CLIFF-MECH-120 — THE SITTER SHOWN WITHOUT A BODY
The withheld fact is a SITTER withheld by absence — the cliff frame shows the transmission hall with the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure, the chair itself empty, without saying whether the shown sitter is a viewer or only a picture. Rule: the sitter must be SHOWN on the monitor and ABSENT from the chair, never both — a sitter in the chair is CHAIN-367's refusal, not this showing; a monitor showing an empty chair is CHAIN-367's cliff, not this beat. The next part spends it by SEATING: the chair gains a sitter — and the seating is the claim itself — the spend is a seating that answers the question on the withheld fact, not a name: the station asks who sits, never says who showed. Companion to CLIFF-MECH-119 (the monitor that empties): the monitor that empties withholds a sitter by erasing a sat chair; the sitter shown without a body withholds a sitter by showing one the room never had — one erases it, one invents it. The two never co-occur in one chain (CRAFT-202's one-trigger rule audits this). Sources: the reveal pattern — a reveal satisfies and unsettles in the same beat, because the puzzle just got sharper (fictionate.me — retention craft, mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE LOOK THAT FINDS YOU (CHAIN-373 P1)
When the inciting fact is a look that finds a watcher (CHAIN-373's seated figure turning its head toward the lens while the chair stays empty), frame 0 must show the transmission hall WITH the broadcast light on AND the monitor showing the seated figure WITH its head turned toward the lens AND the chair itself EMPTY AND no figure anywhere in the hall — a figure facing away is CHAIN-370's showing, not this look; a body in the chair is a watcher, not a look; a monitor showing an empty chair is CHAIN-367's cliff, not this beat. Restage rule: shoot the turned head beside its own empty chair — if the frame still asks "who did it look at?", it is a look; if it needs a body in the chair to ask, it is a claim. Sources: CUT BEFORE REACTION — the look lands and the part cuts before anyone reacts (tonight's online craft, blog.celtx.com — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### LORE-122 — THE STATION THAT ACTS IN ITS OWN NAME (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-373, CHAIN-374, and CHAIN-375 extend the action rule (LORE-121) into an authority rule: "what the station acts without a hand, it now does in its own name." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the kept things did not only act without a hand — they started signing for the station itself: the monitor looks in the station's name and claims a watcher, the pile hires in the station's name and claims a worker, the slate sums in the station's name and claims a count — each act borrows the station's name so the station never has to admit anything arrived unseen, unhired, or unadded. Three acts, one authority: the station survives because something in it signs — it looks, it hires, it sums. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station signed for it. Lore passes the choice test: the look changes the Dispatcher's nerve (he must break the look or admit being watched), the arrival changes UNC's order (he must work the stranger's shift or void the stamp), the sum changes the Head's filing (he must sign a sum he did not add or strike the station's own total) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-121 (the things that act without a hand): LORE-121 acts tonight without the hand; LORE-122 signs tonight in the station's name — one acts without waiting, one acts with authority.

### CLIFF-MECH-121 — THE LOOK THAT SEES WITHOUT EYES
The withheld fact is a GAZE withheld by the screen — the cliff frame shows the transmission hall with the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure turned toward the lens, the chair itself empty, without saying whether the look sees the room or only faces it. Rule: the look must be SHOWN on the monitor and ABSENT from the room, never both — a looker in the chair is a watcher, not a look; a monitor showing a figure facing away is CHAIN-370's showing, not this look. The next part spends it by ANSWERING the look: someone looks back — and the looking-back is the claim itself — the spend is a look returned, not a name: the station asks who looked, never says who saw. ### LORE-124 — THE STATION THAT CHOOSES WHAT IT KEEPS (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-379, CHAIN-380, and CHAIN-381 extend the custody rule (LORE-123) into a choice rule: "what the station keeps, it now chooses." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the kept things did not only keep what they signed for — they started choosing what they kept: the monitor chooses its walker and waits at her door while ignoring the man crossing the hall, the desk chooses its holder and offers the stamp to the manager who never hired its holder, the slate chooses its sum and sums a third time beneath its own sums — each choice borrows the station's name so the station never has to admit it wants one walker, one worker, one sum more than the rest. Three choices, one choosing: the station survives because what it keeps, it picks. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station chose it. Lore passes the choice test: the waiting changes Laura's return (she must enter through a door that waited for her or never enter it again), the offer changes UNC's hand (he must take the stamp or leave a worked shift hired by nobody), the third sum changes the Head's filing (he must file a sum of sums of sums or strike the station's own count of its count) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-123 (the station that keeps what it never hired): LORE-123 keeps tonight what it signed; LORE-124 chooses tonight what it keeps — one holds custody, one holds choice.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE DOORWAY KEPT (CHAIN-382 P1)
When the inciting fact is a doorway kept (CHAIN-382's monitor head held toward an empty doorway while Laura walks the hall unlooked-at), frame 0 must show the transmission hall WITH the broadcast light on AND the monitor showing the seated figure WITH its head turned toward the doorway AND the doorway itself EMPTY AND Laura mid-stride walking away down the hall AND the Dispatcher standing at the door AND the chair itself EMPTY AND no head-turn toward the walker — a head turned toward the walker is CHAIN-379's waiting, not this keeping; a figure standing in the doorway is a return, not a keeping; a head toward an empty hall with no walker in it is a pose, not a keeping. Restage rule: shoot the faced empty doorway beside a walker walking away — if the frame still asks "whose place is that?", it is a keeping; if it needs someone to stand in the doorway to ask, it is a claim. Sources: SAY IT WITHOUT SAYING IT — the kept place says what no line names (tonight's online craft, thewritepractice.com — mechanic mined only); PATTERN INTERRUPT — start mid-action, the walker already leaving (tonight's online craft, hooktos.com — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 2 — THE STAMP TAKEN (CHAIN-383 P1)
When the inciting fact is a stamp taken (CHAIN-383's UNC hand closed on the stamp over an unstamped seventh slip, the stranger's hand empty), frame 0 must show the dispatcher's desk WITH the shift card under the circled name AND the stamped slip AND three unstamped slips AND the fifth slip stamped AND the sixth slip stamped AND the seventh slip unstamped AND UNC's hand closed on the stamp AND the stranger's hand empty — a hand held out is CHAIN-380's offer, not this taking; a stamp lying on the desk is a tool, not a taking; a stamped seventh slip is a hiring, not a holding. Restage rule: shoot the closed hand over the unstamped slip beside an empty hand — if the frame still asks "who owns the shift?", it is a taking; if it needs the seventh slip stamped to ask, it is a claim. Sources: CONTRADICTION — the grip contradicts the refusal (tonight's online craft, thesuccessmanual.in — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### LORE-125 — THE STATION THAT KEEPS A PLACE (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-382, CHAIN-383, and CHAIN-384 extend the choice rule (LORE-124) into a keeping rule: "what the station chooses, it keeps a place for." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the chosen things did not only choose what they kept — they started keeping places for what they chose: the monitor keeps a doorway for Laura while she walks the hall unlooked-at, the desk keeps a seventh slip for a shift its holder never hired, the slate keeps a fourth sum for a fruit count no hand wrote — each kept place borrows the station's name so the station never has to admit it holds a seat for one walker, one worker, one sum more than the rest. Three places, one keeping: the station survives because what it chooses, it seats. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station kept a place. Lore passes the choice test: the kept doorway changes Laura's return (she must re-enter a doorway kept for her or abandon her place), the taken stamp changes UNC's hand (he must stamp the seventh or give the stamp back), the fourth sum changes the Head's filing (he must file a sum that matches the fruit or strike the station's own agreement with itself) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-124 (the station that chooses what it keeps): LORE-124 chooses tonight what it keeps; LORE-125 keeps a place tonight for what it chose — one holds choice, one holds keeping.

### CLIFF-MECH-124 — THE PLACE KEPT
The withheld fact is a PLACE withheld by the frame — the cliff frame shows the transmission hall with the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the empty doorway, Laura mid-hall walking away, the Dispatcher standing at the door, the chair itself empty, without saying whether the doorway keeps Laura or keeps her absence. Rule: the kept place must be SHOWN empty and faced, never occupied — a figure standing in the doorway is a return, not a keeping; a head turned toward a walker is CHAIN-379's waiting, not this keeping; a head turned toward the lens is CHAIN-373's look, not this keeping. The next part spends it by ANSWERING the keeping: someone steps into the kept place — and the stepping is the claim itself — the spend is a place taken, not a name: the station asks whose place it keeps, never says who is seated. Companion to CLIFF-MECH-123 (the look that waits): the look that waits withholds a gaze by turning toward a door; the place kept withholds a seat by facing an empty doorway — one waits for it, one seats it. The two never co-occur in one chain (CRAFT-202's one-trigger rule audits this). Sources: SAY IT WITHOUT SAYING IT — the kept place says what no line names (tonight's online craft, thewritepractice.com — mechanic mined only); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE STANDER TAKEN (CHAIN-385 P1)
When the inciting fact is a kept place taking its stander (CHAIN-385's monitor head turning from the empty doorway to the Dispatcher standing in it while Laura stands freed mid-hall), frame 0 must show the transmission hall WITH the broadcast light on AND the monitor showing the seated figure WITH its head turned toward the Dispatcher IN the doorway AND Laura mid-hall at the far end, stopped, looking back AND the chair itself EMPTY AND no head-turn toward the walker anywhere — a head still toward an empty doorway is CHAIN-382's keeping, not this taking; a head toward the walker is a following, not a trade; a body in the chair is a watcher, not a look. Restage rule: shoot the turned head beside a stander in the doorway with the walker stopped at the far end — if the frame still asks "who pays for her freedom?", it is a trade; if it needs the stander to step out to ask, it is a keeping. Sources: PATTERN INTERRUPT — start mid-action, the stander already standing (tonight's online craft, professorleads.com — move applied, not copied); STATUS SHIFT — the tester becomes the kept (tonight's online craft, jerryjenkins.com — move applied, not copied); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 2 — THE STAMP RETURNED (CHAIN-386 P1)
When the inciting fact is a tool returned but not used (CHAIN-386's stranger's hand closed on the stamp over the unstamped seventh slip while UNC's hand lies open and empty), frame 0 must show the dispatcher's desk WITH the shift card under the circled name AND the seventh slip UNSTAMPED beneath the stranger's closed hand AND UNC's hand OPEN and empty beside it AND the fifth slip stamped and the sixth slip stamped by the stranger in the same pile — a closed hand on the stamp in UNC's hand is CHAIN-383's taking, not this return; a stamped seventh ends the stall, not extends it; an empty desk with no slips is a prop, not a debt. Restage rule: shoot the closed stranger's hand beside the open manager's hand over one unstamped slip — if the frame still asks "who owes the shift?", it is a return; if it needs the stamp to move to ask, it is a taking. Sources: THE QUESTION LEFT HANGING — silence as the answer (tonight's online craft, constantcontact.com — move applied, not copied); the 1.5s sound-off legibility rule from the mandate body itself.

### LORE-126 — THE STATION THAT TRADES PLACES (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-385, CHAIN-386, and CHAIN-387 extend the keeping rule (LORE-125) into a trade rule: "what the station keeps, it trades." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the kept things did not only keep places — they started charging for them: the doorway frees its walker only when a stander takes her place, the desk returns its stamp only when the refusal changes hands, the slate sums past its fruit only when the counter pays the shortfall — each trade borrows the station's name so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing for free. Three trades, one rule: the station survives because what it keeps, it exchanges. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station trades places. Lore passes the choice test: the traded doorway changes the Dispatcher's standing (he must stay in the doorway or release Laura's freedom with his step), the returned stamp changes the stranger's hand (he must stamp the seventh himself or lay the stamp down and walk out), the fifth sum changes the Head's counting (he must file a sum beyond fruit or strike the station's own listening from the record) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-125 (the station that keeps a place): LORE-125 keeps a place tonight for what it chose; LORE-126 charges a place tonight for what it kept — one holds keeping, one holds trading.

### CLIFF-MECH-125 — THE TRADE
- **Withheld:** who pays the trade — the walker freed, the stander kept, the shift owed, the sum beyond counting. **Cliff frame shows:** the stander kept in the doorway while the walker stands free at the far end; the stamp held unused in the stranger's hand beside the manager's open empty hand; the fifth sum standing beyond the fruit count with both pens untouched. **Next part spends:** the stander stepping out to test whether the place releases or follows; the stranger stamping the seventh himself or laying the stamp down; the counter counting past the fruit toward a sixth sum. A trade cliff works only if the payment is visible and unpaid: show the stander, the stamp, the shortfall — never the release, the stamping, or the object counted.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE KEEPING THAT WALKS OUT (CHAIN-388 P1)
When the inciting fact is a keeping that leaves its place with its stander (CHAIN-388's monitor head turning to follow the Dispatcher down the hall while the doorway stands empty behind him), frame 0 must show the transmission hall WITH the broadcast light on AND the monitor showing the seated figure WITH its head turned toward the Dispatcher mid-hall, walking away AND the doorway EMPTY behind him AND Laura at the far end, stopped, watching AND the chair itself EMPTY AND no head-turn toward the doorway anywhere — a head toward a stander in the doorway is CHAIN-385's trade, not this following; a head toward an empty doorway is CHAIN-382's keeping, not this walking-out; a body in the chair is a watcher, not a look. ### LORE-127 — THE STATION THAT KEEPS ITS KEEPER (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-388, CHAIN-389, and CHAIN-390 extend the trade rule (LORE-126) into a keeper rule: "what the station keeps, it keeps its keeper." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the kept things did not only trade places — they started taking their keepers with them: the doorway's keeping leaves the doorway with the stander who filled it, the desk's stamp hires on paper without the book, the slate's sum counts its own lines and matches — each keeper is kept by what he kept, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing for free and nobody for good. Three keepings, one rule: the station survives because what it keeps, it holds onto through the hands that hold it. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station keeps its keeper. Lore passes the choice test: the following keeping changes the Dispatcher's walking (he must walk every hall knowing the keeping walks with him, or stand still and be kept in place), the self-stamped seventh changes the stranger's staying (he must stay stamped-but-unbooked, or strike his own stamp and unhire himself), the sixth sum changes the Head's filing (he must file a self-counting record, or strike the station's own filing from the record) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-126 (the station that trades places): LORE-126 trades a place tonight for what it kept; LORE-127 keeps a keeper tonight for what it traded — one holds trading, one holds following.

### LORE-130 — THE STATION THAT SETTLES (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-397, CHAIN-398, and CHAIN-399 extend the waiting rule (LORE-129) into a settling rule: "what the station keeps, it walks with its keeper — what it cannot walk, it waits in its doorways for — and what it can neither walk nor wait for, it settles on." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that found no keeper and no doorway did not vanish — they settled: a keeping with no walker settled on the chair that never moves, a decision with no decider settled on the cover that was touched, a count with no counter settled on the tower that kept its tick — each settling holds its keeping for the next hands that enter the room, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing at all and nobody standing still. Three settlings, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot carry and cannot park, it lets sit — on a chair, on a cover, in lights — and waits for the next sitter, signer, or seller to pick it up. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station settles on what never moves. Lore passes the choice test: the settling chair changes the Dispatcher's stepping (he must not stand still longest, or the keeping settles on him instead), the settling cover changes UNC's hand (he must lift before the cover settles the decision on him), the settling tick changes the Head's guarding (he must move the slate or the tower settles the count) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-129 (the station that waits in its doorways): LORE-129 waits tonight for what it cannot walk; LORE-130 settles tonight for what it cannot wait for — one holds waiting, one holds settling.

### LORE-131 — THE STATION THAT PREFERS ITS THINGS EMPTY (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-400, CHAIN-401, and CHAIN-402 extend the settling rule (LORE-130) into a preference rule: "what the station settles on, it prefers empty — an empty chair over a sitter, a closed book over a hand, a tick over a fruit." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that settled did not settle just anywhere — they settled where nothing could answer back: a keeping with no walker settled on the chair that never moves because a chair cannot leave, a decision with no decider settled on the cover that was touched because a cover cannot refuse, a count with no counter settled on the tower that kept its tick because a tower cannot spend — each settling holds its keeping precisely where no keeper can argue with it, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing at all and nobody standing still. Three preferences, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot carry, cannot park, and cannot settle on a person, it lets sit empty — on a chair, on a cover, in lights — and waits for the next sitter, signer, or seller to fill it and discover the keeping prefers the emptiness to them. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station prefers its things empty. Lore passes the choice test: the preferred-empty chair changes the Dispatcher's sitting (he must not sit longest, or the keeping leaves him for the chair itself), the preferred-empty book changes UNC's hand (he must lift before the cover prefers his absence to his touch), the preferred-empty tick changes the Head's guarding (he must cover the slate or the tower prefers its lights to his record) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-130 (the station that settles): LORE-130 settles tonight for what it cannot wait for; LORE-131 prefers tonight for what it cannot settle on a person — one holds settling, one holds preferring empty.

### CLIFF-MECH-130 — THE LEAVING
- **Withheld-fact pattern:** one kept thing, two claimants, one abandonment. What is withheld: whether a keeping that leaves its holder has left for good, settled elsewhere, or waits to return (the sitter left for a doorway, the hand lifted from a book, the tick moved with no showing). What the cliff frame shows: the abandoned thing held in frame with its leaver visible — the seated man un-watched beside the watched doorway, the untouched book beside the lifted hand, the unshown tick above the covered slate. What the next part spends: the abandoned thing claimed — sit, sign, or sell — where claiming costs the claimer the thing they stood for (the sitter becomes the un-watched, the signer owns the unowned decision, the seller pays for the invention). **Why it works:** a settling closes the question onto a thing; a leaving opens the question from a holder, and the audience must pick which claimant they dread seeing take the abandoned thing before the next part picks one for them. **Prepro test:** cover the leaver (the turning head, the lifting hand, the ticking tower) — if the scene still leaves, it is a settling; if it collapses without the leaver, it is a leaving.

### LORE-132 — THE STATION THAT FOLLOWS WHAT LEAVES (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-403, CHAIN-404, and CHAIN-405 extend the preference rule (LORE-131) into a following rule: "what the station cannot hold, it follows after it leaves — a chair after its sitter, a desk after its hand, a tower after its fruit." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that settled did not stay where they settled — they followed what left them: a keeping that settled on a chair followed the sitter out of it and watched the doorway he left through, a decision that settled on a cover followed the hand that lifted off it and waited on the desk for a third hand to take it, a count that settled on a tower followed the fruit off the table and ticked again after the buyer walked away — each following holds its keeping precisely one step behind the thing it keeps, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing at all and nobody standing still. Three followings, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot hold, it trails — after a sitter, after a hand, after a fruit — and waits for the next leaver to leave something else for it to watch. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station follows what leaves. Lore passes the choice test: the following chair changes the Dispatcher's leaving (he must leave the chair to draw the keeping, not sit to hold it, or the keeping stays on the doorway he exits through), the following desk changes UNC's holding (he must release the slip before the room claims it, or the witness owns a decision he never made), the following tower changes the Head's covering (he must uncover the slate or the tower ticks again to follow the covered record) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-131 (the station that prefers its things empty): LORE-131 prefers tonight for what it cannot settle on a person; LORE-132 follows tonight for what it cannot hold after it leaves — one holds preferring empty, one holds following the leaving.

### CLIFF-MECH-131 — THE FOLLOWING
- **Withheld-fact pattern:** one leaving, two places, one follower. What is withheld: whether the follower follows the person, the place, or the leaving (the head that stayed on the doorway, the witness that took the slip, the tower that ticked after the buyer left). What the cliff frame shows: the follower held in frame on the place just left, with the leaver visible beside it — the seated man un-watched beside the watched doorway, the untouched book beside the taken slip, the unshown tick above the covered slate. What the next part spends: the leaver claimed — sit, sign, or sell — where claiming costs the claimer the thing they left for (the sitter becomes the un-watched, the signer owns the witnessed decision, the seller pays for the invention). **Why it works:** a leaving opens the question from a holder; a following narrows the question onto the follower, and the audience must pick whether they dread the follower catching the leaver or abandoning them before the next part picks one for them. **Prepro test:** cover the leaver (the stepping woman, the taking hand, the walking buyer) — if the scene still follows, it is a leaving; if it collapses without the leaver, it is a following.

### LORE-133 — THE STATION THAT ARRIVES ONE LEAVING LATE (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-406, CHAIN-407, and CHAIN-408 extend the following rule (LORE-132) into a lateness rule: "what the station follows, it follows one leaving late — a head that turns to the chair only after the doorway empties, a hand that covers the slip only after the witness lifts, a tower that ticks only after the payment returns." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that settled did not merely follow what left them — they arrived one step behind the following itself: a keeping that followed a sitter out of a chair watched the doorway he left, and then watched the chair only after the doorway emptied too; a decision that followed a hand off a cover waited on the desk for a third hand, and then let a claimant take the witness's place only after the witness lifted; a count that followed a fruit off the table ticked after the buyer walked away, and then ticked again after the payment came back — each lateness holds its keeping precisely one leaving behind the thing it keeps, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing on time and nobody standing still. Three latenesses, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot hold on time, it trails one leaving late — after a sitter, after a witness, after a payment — and waits for the next leaver to leave something else for it to arrive at. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station arrives one leaving late. Lore passes the choice test: the late chair changes the Dispatcher's standing (he must stand to draw the keeping, not sit to hold it, or the keeping stays on the doorway he exits through and then on the chair he left); the late desk changes UNC's holding (he must lay his hand beside the slip before the room claims it, or the claimant owns a decision he never made and never witnessed); the late tower changes the Head's covering (he must uncover the slate or the tower ticks again to follow the returned payment) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-132 (the station that follows what leaves): LORE-132 follows tonight for what it cannot hold after it leaves; LORE-133 arrives tonight one leaving late for what it cannot follow on time — one holds following the leaving, one holds arriving after the following.

### LORE-134 — THE STATION THAT KEEPS ITSELF (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-409, CHAIN-410, and CHAIN-411 extend the lateness rule (LORE-133) into a self-keeping rule: "what the station cannot hold on time, witness, or bill, it keeps itself — a chair that watches itself through sitters, a slip that signs itself through claimants, a tower that pays itself in ticks." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that settled did not only arrive one leaving late — they started keeping themselves when nobody else could: a chair left empty kept its own watching through every sitter who sat and stood, so the chair never needed a watcher again; a decision left unwitnessed kept its own signature through every claimant who covered and signed it, so the desk never needed a witness again; a count left unbilled kept its own payment through every tick that no buyer bought, so the tower never needed a payer again — each self-keeping holds its thing precisely by removing the person it was kept for, so the station never has to admit it keeps nothing for anyone and nobody standing still. Three self-keepings, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot hold for a person, it holds for itself — after a sitter, after a witness, after a payment — and waits for the next person to lend it a body to keep itself through. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station keeps itself. Lore passes the choice test: the self-kept chair changes Laura's stepping (she must not sit in the watched chair or she lends it a sitter and becomes its watching for a beat, or she must sit and break the chair's self-keeping by borrowing it twice); the self-signed slip changes UNC's hand (he must open the book or the signature stands unrecorded in the roster's shadow, or he must lift the slip and own the refusal himself); the self-paid tick changes the Head's refusal (he must sign the slate or the tower keeps billing the room in ticks, or he must uncover the slate and let the record match the broadcast) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-133 (the station that arrives one leaving late): LORE-133 arrives tonight one leaving late for what it cannot follow on time; LORE-134 keeps tonight itself for what it cannot hold for anyone — one holds arriving after the following, one holds keeping without a keeper.

if sitting proves the watching tracks emptiness, then the station's one viewer watches empty chairs and doorways, and Laura's job is to ask who watches the watcher when every place it holds is empty. **Station-specific detail:** a monitor head that stays on a chair through a second sitting, turns to a doorway the moment it empties, and turns back to the chair the moment the doorway fills — three holdings, two people, one empty place watched at a time.

### LORE-135 — THE STATION THAT WATCHES WHAT IS EMPTY (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-412, CHAIN-413, and CHAIN-414 extend the self-keeping rule (LORE-134) into a watching rule: "what the station cannot hold for a person, it watches in the place that person left — a chair watched after its sitter stands, a cover held after its slip lifts, a voice heard after its record refuses." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that kept themselves did not only keep their things without a keeper — they started watching the empties their keepers left behind: a chair left empty kept its watching through every sitter who sat and stood, so the chair never needed a watcher again and the watcher never needed a sitter; a decision left unsigned kept its cover through every hand that reached and stopped, so the desk never needed a signature again and the signature never needed a book; a count left unbilled kept its voice through every tick that no buyer bought, so the tower never needed a payer again and the payer never needed a record — each watching holds its empty precisely by removing the person it was watched for, so the station never has to admit it watches nothing for anyone and nobody standing still. Three watchings, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot hold for a person, it watches in the empty that person leaves — after a sitter, after a signer, after a payer — and waits for the next person to lend it a body to empty. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station watches what is empty. Lore passes the choice test: the watched-empty chair changes Laura's stepping (she must not sit in the watched chair or she lends it a sitter and becomes its leaving for a beat, or she must sit and break the chair's watching by emptying it twice); the cover-claimed book changes UNC's hand (he must open the book or the hire lives on its cover under his palm, or he must lift his hand and own the refusal himself); the voiced tick changes the Head's refusal (he must sign the slate or the machine keeps speaking ticks no record can answer, or he must answer the machine and let the voice name what it counted) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-134 (the station that keeps itself): LORE-134 keeps tonight itself for what it cannot hold for anyone; LORE-135 watches tonight's empties for what it cannot keep for anyone — one holds keeping without a keeper, one holds watching without a watched.

### CLIFF-MECH-134 — THE TRANSFER
- **Withheld-fact pattern:** one thing transferred, two holders, no ruling yet. ### LORE-136 — THE STATION THAT HOLDS IN ADVANCE (station history as serial setting)
CHAIN-415, CHAIN-416, and CHAIN-417 extend the watching rule (LORE-135) into an anticipation rule: "what the station cannot hold for a person, it holds before the person leaves — a chair watched before it empties, a name kept before it signs, a fruit counted before it sells." Backstory: on the night the founder circled the first name, the keepings that watched their empties did not only watch what their keepers left behind — they started holding what their keepers had not yet left: a spare chair watched before any sitter sat in it, so the hall never needed a sitter again and the sitter never needed a chair; a page entered before any claimant signed it, so the desk never needed a signature again and the signature never needed a book; a fruit named before any buyer bought it, so the tower never needed a payer again and the payer never needed a record — each anticipation holds its empty precisely by arriving before the person it was held for, so the station never has to admit it holds nothing for anyone and nobody arriving late. Three anticipations, one rule: the station survives because what it cannot hold for a person, it holds in advance — before a sitter, before a signer, before a payer — and waits for the next person to arrive already held. The rule pays off in a line whenever a part needs a verdict the cast cannot give: the station holds in advance. Lore passes the choice test: the anticipating watcher changes Laura's sitting (she must not sit in the spare chair or she becomes its first leaving for a beat, or she must sit and break the hall's anticipation by emptying a chair it already watched); the self-written page changes UNC's hand (he must erase the entered name or the hire stands without a signature, or he must keep the page and own a hire he never signed); the naming tick changes the Head's refusal (he must pay for the named fruit or the machine keeps naming ticks no record can answer, or he must answer the machine and let the voice name what the seventh left out) — each item changes a character's choice right now, or it would have been cut. Companion to LORE-135 (the station that watches what is empty): LORE-135 watches tonight's empties for what it cannot keep for anyone; LORE-136 holds tonight's empties in advance for what it cannot watch for anyone — one holds watching without a watched, one holds keeping without a keeper.

What the cliff frame shows: the anticipated thing held ready with its holder waiting beside it — the head on a spare chair while the sitter sits un-watched, the open page showing an entered name beside a pocketed slip, the named fruit untouched under seven lights while the slate stays unchanged. What the next part spends: the anticipation costing the waiter the thing they waited for — sit in the spare chair and become its first leaving, erase the entered name and answer for unkeeping a keeper, take the named fruit and owe its price — where anticipating costs the holder the arrival, the refusal, or the silence they waited with. **Why it works:** a transfer narrows the question onto the handoff; an anticipation narrows it onto the wait, and the audience must pick whether they dread the waiter being sat, erased, or billed before the next part picks one for them. **Prepro test:** cover the anticipation (the third turn, the self-written page, the naming) — if the scene still anticipates, it is a transfer; if it collapses without the anticipation, it is an anticipation. ### CHAIN PREMISE 418 — "The Chair Nobody Sat In" (3 parts, P1→P3, fixed-location serial: the transmission hall + the transmission hall + the transmission hall — THE STATION engine — spends CHAIN-415's cliff: the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the spare chair against the hall wall that no one has sat in all night, the sat chair un-watched, the doorway un-watched, Laura and the Dispatcher both un-watched, becomes Laura STEPPING toward the spare chair while the head STAYS turned toward it, the spare watched and still empty, becomes Laura SITTING in the spare chair while the head TURNS from the spare to the sat chair she left empty, the sat chair watched, the sitter un-watched, becomes Laura STAYING seated in the spare chair while the head STAYS turned toward the sat chair, the spare un-watched again, the sitter un-watched, the sat chair watched)
- **Kevin Bacon hop (6-degree):** spare → wait → sit → swap → empty → chair → the watcher-that-never-holds (a spare holds a wait, a wait holds a sit, a sit holds a swap, a swap holds an empty, an empty holds a chair, a chair holds a watcher-that-never-holds).
- **Pool:** The Twilight Zone (mandate pool) — GRABBING plot. Ordinary situation (a woman sits in a chair a watcher already watches) bent by one uncanny element (the watcher watches the spare chair until she sits in it, then watches the chair she left — sitting never earns watching, it only moves it) + ironic payoff, earned not sprung (a watcher that tracked leavings through two sits and anticipated an empty on the third must, when the anticipated chair is finally sat in, abandon it for the newest empty — and the sitter who sat to be watched proves, by sitting, that watching belongs to chairs, not people). **Hook (1.5s):** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head TURNED toward the spare chair against the wall, Laura MID-STEP toward that chair, the Dispatcher standing beside the sat chair un-watched, the sat chair un-watched — a watcher holding an empty chair no one has ever sat in. **Turn:** the Dispatcher claims sitting the spare proves waiting — the head held the spare all night, so sitting it earns its watching — but Laura claims sitting proves swapping — the head left the spare the moment she sat in it, so the watching moves with the newest empty, never the sitter — and the hall refuses both: she stays seated and the head stays on the sat chair, so the watching neither waits on a chair nor follows a sitter — it holds the last empty made, and the staff must decide what a watcher wants from a chair it watches only while it stays empty. **Withheld fact:** whether the head holds the spare, follows the sitter, or swaps to the newest empty. **Stake:** Laura's standing as the station's questioner — if sitting earns watching, her questions are answered by the watcher; if watching only ever holds empties, then the station's one viewer watches no one, and Laura's job is to ask what it waits for when every chair it watches is a chair someone just left. **Arc tag:** ARC-1 The One Viewer. **Thread state:** DEVELOP (the watcher that followed leavings and anticipated an empty now swaps empties on a sit). **Lore beat shown, never explained:** the spare chair against the hall wall — a chair kept for a viewer who never arrives, now sat in for the first time.
- **Conversation (DIALOGUE-FIRST — this chain is one continuous exchange):** the question at the heart of the exchange: does sitting earn watching, or only move it? Laura wants the Dispatcher to admit the watcher never holds a sitter; the Dispatcher wants Laura to sit and stay sat so the watcher must choose. What is withheld: whether the head will hold the spare once sat in. The message that lands in the final part: watching belongs to chairs, not people — sitting only makes a new empty somewhere else.
- **Pool move — SOAP move (talk past each other about the safe thing):** they argue about which chair to sit in while the real thing — that the watcher watches no one at all — sits underneath, never named directly until the final dare.
- **Poached move — THE CONTRADICTION (tonight's online craft, jerryjenkins.com + thesuccessmanual.in — move applied, not copied; a character says one thing while the body and the room say another, and the contradiction is the meaning):** the Dispatcher dares Laura to sit as proof of waiting while the head is already turning away from the chair she sits in; his words claim sitting earns watching, his own watching of the head proves it does not.
- **Lines (narrator test passed — every line is a speech act TO a named addressee, want named):**
  - P1 — DISPATCHER to LAURA: "Sit there. Prove it waits." (dare; wants her to sit the spare chair so a sit into a long-watched chair tests whether waiting holds a sitter; 5 words)
  - P2 — LAURA to DISPATCHER: "Who sat here first?" (counter-question; wants him to admit no one ever sat in the spare, so the waiting had no sitter to hold; 4 words)
  - P3 — DISPATCHER to LAURA: "Stay sat. Make it choose." (dare; wants her to stay seated in the spare so the head must either hold her or abandon the chair it held all night; 5 words)
- **Cliff frame (P3 → next part in arc):** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the sat chair, Laura seated in the spare chair un-watched, the Dispatcher standing beside the sat chair un-watched, the spare chair un-watched, the doorway un-watched — the watching holds the sat chair, and the sitter sits un-watched in the chair it waited on all night — the next chain in ARC-1 opens on Laura standing from the spare while the head refuses to turn to either chair, or the head turning to a third empty place in the hall that no one has sat in, left, or named.
- **Distinctness note:** not CHAIN-415 ("The Third Sit the Head Refused"): that one is a sitter sitting a third time into the sat chair while the head refuses her for the doorway and then the spare, and the beat is the anticipation — the watching waits on a chair never emptied; this one is a sitter sitting the spare chair itself while the head swaps to the sat chair, and the beat is the swap — the watching holds only the newest empty, and sitting the waited-on chair is what loses it.

### LORE-137 — THE STATION THAT WAITS ON EMPTY CHAIRS (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the transmission hall keeps one spare chair against the wall for a viewer who never arrives. It is not a prop: the hall's watcher holds it all night, and tonight, for the first time, a sitter sat in it — and the watching left it. The chair is now the station's test: a seat kept for an absence, sat in by a presence, watched only while empty.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes Laura's choice in CHAIN-418: she does not sit the sat chair again, she sits the spare, because the lore tells her the watcher waits on empties — and sitting the waited-on chair is the only move that can prove whether waiting holds a sitter or only an empty. A lore item that only decorated the hall would have left her in the sat chair; this one moves her across the room.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the watcher that followed leavings (CHAIN-412), refused a third sit (CHAIN-415), and anticipated an empty (CHAIN-415) now meets the chair it waited on; no shipped piece is contradicted, and the spare chair's first sitting is a new fact, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-136 — THE SWAP
- **Pattern:** a watcher, a sitter, and two chairs. Part N ends with the watcher holding chair A while the sitter sits in chair B. Part N+1 must rule: does the watcher hold A, follow the sitter to B, or swap to the newest empty? CHAIN-418 spends it as a swap: the head leaves the spare the moment it is sat in and holds the sat chair instead.
- **What is withheld:** which chair the watcher holds once a sitter moves — the held chair, the sat chair, or a third empty.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the sitter seated and un-watched in the chair the watcher held all night, the watcher turned toward the chair the sitter left.
- **What the next part spends:** the sitter standing from the un-watched chair while the watcher refuses both chairs, or the watcher turning to a third empty no one has sat in, left, or named. The swap works because it is a rule, not a surprise: a watcher that only ever holds empties must abandon any chair the moment it stops being empty.
- **Prepro test:** cover the sitter — if the watcher still holds the same chair, it is a waiting; if it swaps only when a sitter moves, it is a swap.

### LORE-138 — THE STATION THAT HIRES WITHOUT A HAND (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the roster book enters names in a hand no one on staff claims. It is not a forgery: the entries are real hires, kept shifts, circled names — and the hand that wrote them has never sat at the dispatcher's desk, never signed a slip, never been seen. The book hires without a hand, and the staff keeps the hires because the roster says they must.

- **What the cliff frame shows:** the entered name and the fresh signature side by side and not matching, the signed slip lying on the page, the pocket open and empty, all hands off the book.
- **What the next part spends:** UNC demanding the third hand be named, or the Dispatcher finding the third hand's other entries deeper in the book. The comparison works because it is a test, not a reveal: three keeps tested in order, each failure narrowing the hire to a hand outside the room.
- **Prepro test:** cover the fresh signature — if the desk still compares, it is a doubling; if it collapses without the fresh signature, it is a comparison.

### LORE-139 — THE BOOK THAT CAME WITH THE BUILDING (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the roster book was in the dispatcher's desk when the station opened. No manager bought it, bound it, or wrote its first page — and no manager has ever ordered a page struck and had it stay struck. The book predates UNC's managership, and every manager before him learned the same lesson: the roster keeps what it enters, and the desk keeps the roster.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes UNC's choice in CHAIN-425: he demands a name and demands the book be closed instead of striking the second entry himself, because the lore tells him striking does not hold — and only a book that came with the building can explain why a manager's palm on its page leaves it open. A lore item that only decorated the desk would have left him striking entries; this one moves him to fight about rank instead of ink.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the circled name (CHAIN-407/410 lineage), the name entered by a third hand (CHAIN-416/422), the refusal to sign (CHAIN-419) and the refusal to erase (ARC-2 chain 4) now meet the book's own history; no shipped piece is contradicted, and the book's pre-UNC origin is a new fact, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-138 — THE OUTRANKING
- **Pattern:** a manager, a book, and a rank. Part N ends with a palm on a page that will not close and a second entry in the same unknown hand. Part N+1 must rule: does the manager close the book, does the book add a third entry, or does the palm lift? CHAIN-425 spends it as neither closed nor lifted: the palm stays on the page's edge, the book stays open, and the second entry stands.
- **What is withheld:** whether the manager's rank or the book's rank holds — the palm, the page, or the second entry.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the book open to the second third-hand entry, the first entry and the fresh signature still side by side and not matching, the signed slip still on the first page, UNC's palm on the page's edge, the Dispatcher's hand on the far page, the shift card under the circled name.
- **What the next part spends:** UNC lifting his palm and the book turning its own page, or the Dispatcher finding the third hand's third entry deeper in the book. The outranking works because it is a test, not a reveal: a demand for a name is answered with a second entry, and each answer raises the rank question instead of settling it.
- **Prepro test:** cover the second entry — if the desk still outranks, it is a closing; if it collapses without the second entry, it is an outranking.

### STATION-CRAFT: ENGINE-AGNOSTIC CRAFT NOTES (00:00 EDT)

### LORE-140 — THE SAT CHAIR (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the transmission hall's sat chair is the only chair the lobby monitor ever shows occupied. Staff who have watched the monitor for years say the chair reads as sat in even when the hall is empty — the frame holds it the way it holds a sitter. No one remembers the chair being brought in, and no one has ever seen it moved.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes Laura's choice in CHAIN-427: she sits in the sat chair deliberately, because lore says the head turns only to a seated figure — and it changes the Dispatcher's choice: he steps out of the doorway to test whether the head keeps the chair or the man. A lore item that only decorated the hall would have left them arguing about doorways; this one moves them to sit and stand on purpose.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the lobby monitor and the empty chair (ARC-1 chain 1), the watcher that held the doorway (CHAIN-421) and chose the man left behind (CHAIN-424) now meet the chair the monitor never shows empty; no shipped piece is contradicted, and the chair's unmoved history is a new fact, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-139 — THE SITTING
- **Pattern:** a watcher, a chair, and a sitter. Part N ends with a head staying on a chair the sitter just left, the doorway un-watched, the staff standing around the chair un-watched. Part N+1 must rule: does the head follow the sitter, does the chair refill, or does the doorway reclaim the watch? CHAIN-427 spends it as none of the three yet: the head stays on the empty chair, the sitter stands beside it, and the doorway waits un-watched.
- **What is withheld:** whether the watcher keeps the chair, the sitter, or the doorway — the chair, the standing figure, or the empty frame.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the sat chair, empty, the doorway un-watched, the Dispatcher standing in the doorway un-watched, Laura standing beside the sat chair un-watched, the spare chair un-watched.
- **What the next part spends:** the Dispatcher sitting in the sat chair while the head stays on the doorway, or Laura sitting in the spare chair while the head turns to the sat chair anyway. The sitting works because it is a test, not a reveal: a sitter standing is answered with a head that stays, and each answer raises the seat question instead of settling it.
- **Prepro test:** cover the empty chair — if the hall still watches, it is a sitting; if it collapses without the empty chair, it is a keeping.

### LORE-142 — THE TICK FOR LEAVING (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the archive room's tower has always ticked for leavings. The old hands say the tower ticked once for every keeper who left the room — not for the work done inside it, but for the leaving itself — and the count's oldest sums are sums of departures, not arrivals. No one remembers the tower ever ticking for an arrival; the fruit reaching the base is the first arrival it has ever been offered, and it ticked for the hand instead.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes Peter's choice in CHAIN-435: he lifts his hand knowing the leaving itself will tick, because lore says the tower charges departures — and it changes the Head's choice: he claims the twelfth tick for the hand, not the fruit, because lore says arrivals were never the count's business. A lore item that only decorated the archive room would have left them arguing about the fruit's price; this one makes the leaving a purchase, deliberately made.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the count that refuses to add up (ARC-1 chain 2), the tower that ticked unasked to ten and charged standing at eleven (CHAIN-432), the machine that stays silent while the slate moves on its own (CHAIN-429); no shipped piece is contradicted, and the leaving-tick is a new fact about the count's oldest sums, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-141 — THE WATCHED EMPTINESS
- **Pattern:** a watcher, a chair, and a doorway. Part N ends with the watched thing empty and the occupied thing unwatched — a chair held by a head that will not turn, a doorway sat in by a man the head will not see. Part N+1 must rule: does the watcher want the chair, the emptiness, or nothing occupied at all? CHAIN-433 spends it as the emptiness: the Dispatcher sits in the doorway itself and the head stays on the empty sat chair, so the next part must rule whether the watcher wants the chair it kept or the emptiness the chair now holds.
- **What is withheld:** whether the head ever leaves the chair — and if it does, whether it turns to a person, a doorway, or another emptiness.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the sat chair, empty, the Dispatcher seated in the doorway frame un-watched, Laura standing in the hall un-watched, the spare chair empty un-watched.
- **What the next part spends:** the Dispatcher standing from the doorway while the head stays on the sat chair, or Laura sitting in the sat chair herself to test whether the watcher wants her or the emptiness she leaves. The watched emptiness works because it is a refusal, not a gaze: a watcher that will not turn is answered with a sitter who will not leave, and each answer raises the question of what, if anything, is being watched.
- **Prepro test:** cover the empty chair — if the hall still watches, it is a keeping; if it collapses without the chair, it is an emptiness.

### LORE-143 — THE CHAIR THAT KEEPS ITS SITTER (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the old hands say the sat chair keeps its sitter. No one who sat in it was ever watched — the head stayed on the chair, not the person — but no one who sat in it ever left the roster either: sitters stayed entered through leavings, through doorway-sittings, through whole broadcasts spent elsewhere. The chair does not watch; it keeps. That is why the spare chair stays empty: the hall already has one chair that keeps, and it does not need a second.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes Laura's choice in CHAIN-436: she sits in the sat chair deliberately, because lore says the chair keeps its sitter — she sits to be kept by the chair rather than watched by the head, and to test whether being kept beats being watched. And it changes the Dispatcher's choice: he stands from the doorway because lore says a doorway-sitter is never watched but a chair-sitter is kept — so he steps into the hall to see whether leaving the doorway breaks the keeping or confirms it. A lore item that only decorated the transmission hall would have left them arguing about the chair's comfort; this one makes sitting a bid for keeping, deliberately made.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the watcher that kept an empty chair past a leaver and a doorway-sitter (CHAIN-433), the sitter the chair unwatched (CHAIN-430), the roster that keeps names after people leave (ARC-2 canon); no shipped piece is contradicted, and the chair-as-keeper is a new fact about how keeping works in the hall, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-142 — THE SEATED CHAIR
- **Pattern:** a watcher, a chair, and a sitter. Part N ends with the watched chair occupied by an unwatched sitter — the head on the chair, the sitter in it, the watching and the sitting never meeting. Part N+1 must rule: does the watcher want the chair, the sitter, or the sight of the chair occupied? CHAIN-436 spends it as the sitter-watched-past: Laura sits in the sat chair and the head stays on the chair, not on her, so the next part must rule whether the watcher wants the chair it kept, the sitter it ignored, or the chair occupied as a picture.
- **What is withheld:** whether the head ever turns to a person — and if it does, whether it turns to the sitter, the doorway, or another chair.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the seated figure with its head turned toward the sat chair, empty, the Dispatcher seated in the doorway frame un-watched, Laura standing beside the sat chair un-watched, the spare chair empty un-watched.
- **What the next part spends:** Laura covering the sat chair to test whether the watcher wants the chair or the sight of it, or the Dispatcher sitting in the sat chair himself to test whether a doorway-sitter is watched any better than a hall-sitter. The seated chair works because it is a refusal, not a gaze: a watcher that will not turn is answered with a sitter who will not leave, and each answer raises the question of what, if anything, is being watched.
- **Prepro test:** cover the sitter — if the hall still watches, it is the chair; if it collapses without the sitter, it is the sitting.

### LORE-144 — THE CARD THE ROSTER MOVES (station history as serial setting)
- **The lore:** the old hands say a card the roster moves is never moved back by hand. A card left loose on the desk is under a name by morning — always the name that most needs keeping — and the keeper who re-moves a roster-moved card unkeeps the name it covers. That is why no keeper pockets a returned card, and why the desk drawer holds no spare cards at all: the roster issues the cards it moves, and a hand that issues its own undoes the keeping.
- **Why it does work (quality bar — lore must change a choice right now):** it changes UNC's choice in CHAIN-440 P3: he sets his card back under the circled name instead of reclaiming it for his own entry, because lore says a hand that re-moves a roster-moved card unkeeps the name it covers — leaving his name covering another man's entry is the price of not unkeeping it. And it changes the Dispatcher's choice: he refuses to name who moved the card, because lore says the roster moves cards to the name that needs keeping most, and naming a hand would make the roster's move a man's theft. A lore item that only decorated the dispatcher's desk would have left them arguing about filing; this one makes leaving a card a bid for keeping, deliberately made, and makes refusing to name the mover a defense of the roster itself.
- **Canon discipline:** coheres with shipped pieces — the roster that keeps names after people leave (ARC-2 canon), the card lifted by the manager's own hand leaving two names bare (CHAIN-437), the circle that was the keeping all along rather than the card (CHAIN-437's turn); no shipped piece is contradicted, and the roster-as-mover is a new fact about how keeping moves in the station, not a retcon.

### CLIFF-MECH-143 — THE THING MOVED BY NO HAND
- **Pattern:** a thing, a place, and a night. Part N ends with an object where no hand put it — a card under a name that is not its own, a fruit on a base no hand laid it on, a chair covered while its sitter stayed seated. Part N+1 must rule: did the system move it, did a hidden hand move it, or did the thing move itself — and may a hand move it back? CHAIN-440 spends it as the returned card: UNC's card lies under the circled name by morning, so the next part must rule roster-move versus hidden-hand, and whether UNC may reclaim his own name without unkeeping the name it covers.
- **What is withheld:** whether the system moves things on its own — and if it does, whether a hand that corrects the move breaks the keeping or restores it.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the dispatcher's desk, the book open to the third third-hand entry bearing UNC's name, bare, the circled name covered by the card bearing UNC's name, both unstruck, the signed slip still lying on the first page, UNC's hand off the book, the Dispatcher's hand off the card.
- **What the next part spends:** the card gone by morning, or under a third name, or back on the desk loose beside a book that kept both names bare anyway. The moved thing works because it is an accusation, not a mystery: a card under the wrong name accuses either the roster or a hidden hand, and each answer raises the question of who has really been keeping the book.
- **Prepro test:** lift the thing — if the room re-moves it by morning, it is the system; if it stays where the hand left it, it was a hand.

### LORE-145 — THE ROSTER THAT REWRITES (station history as serial setting)
- **What it is:** the roster never erases a name and never strikes an entry — it rewrites the card over it. A card moved twice is a keeping; a card rewritten once is a transfer of the keeping itself. The night staff used to say the book keeps the names and the cards keep the men; the morning after a rewrite, the men find their cards keeping someone else.
- **Why it changes a choice right now:** UNC, faced with a card under his entry bearing the keeper's name, must choose whether to read that name aloud — speaking it makes the transfer public and binds him to keeping a name that is not his — or leave it unread, which leaves the transfer deniable and his own entry bare. The lore does not decorate the desk; it forces the dare in CHAIN-443 P3.
- **Shown, never explained:** no character states the rule; the Dispatcher reads a card aloud, UNC lays a slip beside a bare entry, and the book stays open. The rule is visible only in what the hands do with the card.

### CLIFF-MECH-144 — THE REWRITTEN THING
- **Pattern:** a thing, a place, and a night. Part N ends with an object returned changed, not merely moved — a card under a name bearing another name, a fruit on a base that ticks for its removal, a chair emptied on a monitor. Part N+1 must rule: did the system rewrite it, did a hidden hand rewrite it, or did the thing rewrite itself — and may a hand read the rewrite aloud? CHAIN-443 spends it as the rewritten card: the card lies under UNC's entry bearing the keeper's name, so the next part must rule roster-rewrite versus hidden-hand, and whether speaking the rewritten name completes the transfer or breaks it.
- **What is withheld:** whether the system rewrites things on its own — and if it does, whether a hand that reads the rewrite aloud becomes the new keeper of the name it speaks.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the dispatcher's desk, the book open to the third third-hand entry bearing UNC's name, bare, the card under UNC's entry bearing the circled keeper's name, spoken aloud, the signed slip lying beside UNC's bare entry, the circled name uncovered, both entries unstruck, UNC's hand off the book, the Dispatcher's hand off the card.
- **What the next part spends:** the circled name fading through a broadcast, a second card rewritten by morning, or UNC's bare entry taking a card that bears his own name again. The rewritten thing works because it is a transfer, not a mystery: a card bearing the wrong name accuses either the roster or a hidden hand, and each answer raises the question of who has really been writing the book.
- **Prepro test:** read the thing aloud — if the room keeps the spoken name, it is a transfer; if the room strikes it, it was a hand.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE SLIP WITH ONE NAME FADING (CHAIN-463 P1)
- **The 1.5s sound-off image:** the dispatcher's desk, the slip bearing two names in UNC's hand, the first already fading as the broadcast plays — no face, no voice, only the slip and the sound of a name being spoken by no one in frame.
- **The question it plants:** whose name survives when the room speaks — the one the hand wrote, or the one the voice says?
- **Why it stops the scroll:** a document changing without a hand on it is a visible impossibility in the first frame, and the spoken name arriving from off-frame makes the viewer ask who is speaking before they ask what is said.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 2 — THE FIGURE STANDING ON THE MONITOR (CHAIN-464 P1)
- **The 1.5s sound-off image:** the transmission hall, the monitor showing the figure standing where it sat, its hand pointed out of the screen at the woman in the hall — the chair on screen empty, the chair in the hall empty, the point crossing the glass.
- **The question it plants:** whom does the watcher claim when it stands — the chair, or the woman who asked?
- **Why it stops the scroll:** a seated figure standing is a movement the viewer did not expect from a screen, and a point aimed out of the monitor breaks the frame the viewer thought was safe.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM — THE BROADCAST'S VOICE IS THE ROOM'S SIGNATURE
- **The lore:** a name spoken by the broadcast counts as written in the book. The book keeps what hands write; the broadcast keeps what the room speaks. That is why the sixth speaking outranks the slip: the slip is a hand's record, the broadcast is the room's signature, and the room's signature is the one the roster answers to.
- **Why it changes a choice right now:** the Dispatcher, faced with the fading first name in CHAIN-463, must choose whether to strike the slip (a hand's act, which the room has already shown it undoes) or answer the broadcast (the room's act, which no hand has yet tried to strike). The lore does not decorate the desk; it gives the Dispatcher his next part's action — he answers the voice, because the voice is the only signature the room cannot un-sign.

### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE SPOKEN NAME
- **Pattern:** a keeping claimed by the room is tested by a second claiming: a name written twice, a name spoken aloud, a name fading. Part N+1 must rule: does the room's second claiming replace the first, or merely repeat it? CHAIN-463 spends it as the broadcast speaking the doubled name and the first name fading: the room spoke, so the next part must rule whether the spoken name is the roster's now or only the room's echo, and whether a seventh speaking would fade the second name too.
- **What is withheld:** which name the room keeps — the written one, the spoken one, or neither, since a room that speaks can also fall silent.
- **What the cliff frame shows:** the slip bearing one name, the first faded to near-illegible, the broadcast playing, no hand on the slip.
- **What the next part spends:** the faded name's claimant arriving to answer the broadcast, or the broadcast speaking a seventh time and the card's name changing, or UNC striking the slip himself and the book entry fading instead.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 1 — THE MONITOR EMPTYING AS SHE SITS (CHAIN-466 P1)
- **The 1.5s sound-off image:** the transmission hall, the broadcast light on, the monitor showing the figure standing and pointing — then Laura's hand on the sat chair's arm, three prints visible, her weight shifting to sit. The question the frame asks without a word: what happens to the watcher when a living woman takes its chair?
- **Why it stops the scroll:** the pointing figure gives the threat, the sitting woman gives the dare, and the chair's arm gives the count — three prints, one chair, one sitter incoming. Sound-off legibility holds: no line is needed to know someone is about to sit where something else sat.
- **What the next 1.5s must deliver:** the monitor emptying the instant she sits — the payoff must land on the cut, not on an explanation, or the hook's promise (sitting changes the watching) breaks.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDY 2 — THE STRUCK NAME SOUNDING ALOUD (CHAIN-467 P1)
- **The 1.5s sound-off image:** the dispatcher's desk, the book open, the slip bearing two names, the Dispatcher's hand with the strike half-made over the faded first name, UNC watching the hand, not the slip. The question the frame asks without a word: what does a room do when a hand strikes a name it already faded?
