### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-828 — THE STATION KEEPS WHAT IT REFUSES TO MEASURE.** The station's refused things do not vanish — they keep working: a curtain stays drawn over a glowing monitor, a door stays open for a buyer who never arrives, an antenna stays counted past its tower. The rule bites in the only way it can — a refused thing still in service cannot be denied, because its work is visible, and a station that refuses its working things refuses its own labor at the price of its keepers' posts, sales, and numbers. This is not decoration: it changes DISPATCHER's choice right now, because a building voice who refuses to lift must refuse a glow still visible behind his own cloth, and a keeper who admits the glow owns a feed he never showed, and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer watches behind the curtain or through it, since a viewer behind a curtain is either a viewer the station hides or a viewer the station hides from. The rule is shown alone, in the curtain drawn over a glowing monitor, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), and now the rooms keep their refused measures the same way.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE CURTAINED MONITOR:** sound off, the first frame is the control room, the monitor bank live, one monitor curtained, glow behind the cloth. The image asks "what hides?" with no word spoken, because a curtain is a hiding already done, and a glow behind cloth is a feed already alive — the question is in the glow, not in the curtain. Mute test (naniza.io): mute the part and cover the glow; if the bank still reads as curtained-live, re-stage so the glow breaks the cloth at the frame's center. Pattern-interrupt discipline (clipspeed.ai): exactly one trigger in the first 1–2 seconds — the glow, not a face, not a logo, not a line.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE HELD DOOR:** sound off, the first frame is the lobby, the front door held open, cold air in, no guest. The image asks "for whom?" with no word spoken, because an open door is an entry already offered, and an empty street is a guest already missing — the question is in the empty street, not in the door. Stack discipline (vidico.com): visual (open door over empty street) + verbal (the P1 accusation) both point at the same promise — a guest who never arrives — so the hook lands sound on, sound off, or glancing.

### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE DENIAL CLIFF
- **THE DENIAL CLIFF:** what is withheld is the agent's purpose — why the curtain was drawn, why the door is held, why the measure is refused. What the cliff frame shows is the agent beside the thing, refusing to name it: DISPATCHER beside the curtain, PETER beside the door, the Head beside the antenna. What the next part spends is a move against the refusal — an accusation, a denial, a dare, or a refusal-with-stake — never a re-show of the thing as if re-showing it were progress. The refusal is the receipt; the purpose is the debt. Poached mechanic (bubblecow.com, new this run): a secret leaks without a confession — the denial cliff ends each part one purpose short of the agent's reason, and the held shot is the agent beside the thing, an image rather than a sentence. Prepro test: cover the agent in the next part's P1; if the part still works, the cliff was the thing, not the refusal — rewrite until only a move against the refusal pays it.

### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1042 — THE REFUSAL MUST NAME ITS PRICE.** This run's premises teach the landing from this run's own P4 lines: "Drawn — or I lose my post.", "Shut — and I lose the sale.", "No — I lose my numbers." Each refusal prices itself — post, sale, numbers — so the audience hears what the refusal costs, not just what it denies. Rule: a refusal without a price is a shrug; a refusal with a price is a stake, because a price tells the audience what the refuser values more than the ask. Prepro test: delete the price clause; if the chain still works, the refusal carried nothing — rewrite until only the price keeps the scene moving.
- **CRAFT-1043 — THE AGENT MUST BE IN THE ROOM.** This run's premises teach the accusation from this run's own impose: every wrongness has its doer present, accused by name in P1 — DISPATCHER beside the curtain, PETER beside the door, the Head beside the antenna. Rule: an accusation needs a face in the frame, because a wrongness with no agent in the room is a mystery, and a wrongness with its agent accused is a scene; the 07:00–10:00 agentless effects asked riddles, and riddles do not argue back. Prepro test: remove the accused agent from the frame; if the chain still works, the agent was dressing — re-stage until the accusation needs its face.
- **CRAFT-1044 — THE GLOW IS THE LEAK.** This run's premises teach subtext from this run's own blind input: the curtain's glow leaks the hidden feed without a confession, the cold air leaks the missing buyer without a name, the shadow leaks the out-counted tower without a measure. Rule: give the audience one sense-detail that contradicts the denial, because a denial with no leak is a wall, and a denial with a leak is a scene — the audience holds the leak against the lie and waits for the price. Prepro test: cover the leak (glow, cold, shadow); if the denial still works, the leak carried nothing — re-stage until deleting the leak collapses the scene.

### CHAIN PREMISE 889 — "The Clock the Street Kept at Six" (4 parts, P1→P4, fixed-location serial: the street — THE STATION engine — STANDALONE, spends no prior cliff — and on the street outside the station's door, the street clock above the door stands frozen at six, hands unmoved, PETER beneath the clock with LAURA before the door — and the chain follows the frozen six to its buyer, where a clock stopped at six keeps six o'clock forever, and a six o'clock that never passes is a slot that never ends, and a slot that never ends is a buyer never seated)

- HOOK (named explicitly): the street, the clock above the door frozen at six, PETER beneath it, LAURA before the door — the hour that will not pass.
- TURN: a stopped clock does not delay six — it keeps six; a slot that never ends is a promise never collected, and a promise never collected is either a sale protected or a buyer cheated, and either way the frozen hour is the sale wearing time's face.
- WITHHELD FACT: who stopped the clock at six, and whether by hand or by sale.

### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE FROZEN-PROP CLIFF
- **THE FROZEN-PROP CLIFF:** what is withheld is who froze the prop — who stopped the clock, who strung the rope, who slotted the fruit. What the cliff frame shows is the prop unmoved, held as the next part's first frame: the clock still at six, the rope still strung, the fruit still slotted. What the next part spends is a move against the freeze — an accusation, a denial, a dare, or a refusal-with-stake — never a re-show of the prop as if re-showing it were progress. The freeze is the receipt; the hand is the debt. Poached mechanic (blog.celtx.com, new this run): a cliffhanger stops at maximum imbalance — the frozen-prop cliff ends each part one hand short of the freezer, and the held shot is the imbalance itself (frozen against flowing time, a divided hall against an open one, a counted fruit against an uncounted viewer), an image rather than a sentence. Prepro test: cover the prop in the next part's P1; if the part still works, the cliff was a reaction, not a freeze — rewrite until only a move against the freeze pays it.

- **CRAFT-1045 — THE DODGE IS THE ANSWER.** This run's premises teach subtext from CHAIN-891's P2: "Ripe beats numbered, Laura." The Head never refuses the count outright — he answers about ripeness, and the swerve tells the audience the number is dangerous. LAURA, the low-status hire, asks the one question PETER, the high-status seller, cannot answer without confessing his buyer — and the exchange inverts on it. - **CRAFT-1047 — THE FROZEN PROP HOLDS THE PROMISE.** This run's premises teach cliff craft from all three chains: the clock stays at six, the rope stays strung, the fruit stays slotted, and each cliff frame shows the prop unmoved rather than a face reacting. Rule: a promise held in a prop survives the cut between parts, because a face resets and a prop does not — the audience carries the frozen thing into the next part and waits for the hand that froze it. ### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE WIPED WINDOW:** sound off, the first frame is the parking lot, the booth window wiped clean, the empty bay behind it, a car's reflection in the glass, no car in the bay. ### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE KEPT-CLEAN CLIFF
- **THE KEPT-CLEAN CLIFF:** what is withheld is who keeps the thing — who wiped the window, who punched the card, who counted the row. What the cliff frame shows is the kept thing held as the next part's first frame: the window still wiped, the card still punched for tomorrow, the row still counted full with empty glass. What the next part spends is a move against the keeping — an accusation, a dodge, a demand, or a refusal-with-stake — never a re-show of the kept thing as if re-showing it were progress. The keeping is the receipt; the hand is the debt. Poached mechanic (oakgen.ai, new this run): cut on the question, not the answer — the kept-clean cliff ends each part on an open question the next part's circumstances must answer, and the held shot of the kept thing is the question itself (wiped against an empty bay, tomorrow against today, full against empty glass), an image rather than a sentence. Prepro test: cover the kept thing in the next part's P1; if the part still works, the cliff was a reaction, not a keeping — rewrite until only a move against the keeping pays it.

- **CRAFT-1048 — THE WIPE IS THE CONFESSION.** This run's premises teach subtext from CHAIN-892's kept thing: a window wiped for an empty bay confesses its seller without a word spoken, because maintenance without a maintainer is a claim without a claimant. ### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-831 — THE STATION KEEPS THE EFFECT AND LOSES THE CAUSE.** The station's effects now arrive without their causes: a tower lit with its fuse pulled, a slip damp with no water, a door wide with no builder credited. The rule bites in the only way it can — an effect without a cause cannot be undone, because undoing needs a cause to remove, and a station that keeps effects without causes keeps its lights, deliveries, and doors at the price of its dispatchers' posts, its carriers' routes, and its builders' credit. This is not decoration: it changes DISPATCHER's choice right now, because a voice who restores the fuse admits the tower his pull protects, and a voice who leaves it pulled owns a light nobody powers, and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer watches a tower lit by power or a tower lit by counting, since a viewer kept by a light with no fuse is either a viewer the station powers or a viewer the station conjures. The rule is shown alone, in the transmitter fuse pulled with the tower still lit, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), and now the rooms keep their effects without causes the same way.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE PULLED FUSE:** sound off, the first frame is the transmitter site, the fuse box open, the fuse in a hand, the tower lit and transmitting behind it. The image asks "who powers it?" with no word spoken, because a lit tower over a dead box is a broadcast already kept, and a fuse in a hand is a power already pulled — the question is in the contradiction, not in the faces. Visual-contradiction discipline (drama.so, new this run): one image that argues with itself — lit tower against dead box — states topic and stakes with sound off; cover the fuse box and the frame is only a lit tower, which is no hook at all. Pattern-interrupt discipline: exactly one trigger in the first 1–2 seconds — the contradiction, not a face, not a logo, not a line.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE WIDE UNIT DOOR:** sound off, the first frame is the storage units, one door wider than its unit, standing open because it cannot close, the unit unbroken behind it. The image asks "who built it?" with no word spoken, because a door that cannot close is a build already claimed, and a builder beside it is a rank already refused — the question is in the width, not in the unit. Stack discipline: visual (door wider than its unit) + verbal (the P1 credit demand) both point at the same promise — a build that outranks its room — so the hook lands sound on, sound off, or glancing.

### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE EFFECT-WITHOUT-CAUSE CLIFF
- **THE EFFECT-WITHOUT-CAUSE CLIFF:** what is withheld is the cause — who pulled the fuse, who carried the slip, who built the door. What the cliff frame shows is the effect held as the next part's first frame: the tower still lit over a dead box, the slip still damp in a dry room, the door still open wider than its unit. What the next part spends is a move against the effect — an accusation, a dodge, a demand, or a dare — never a re-show of the effect as if re-showing it were progress. The effect is the receipt; the cause is the debt. Poached mechanic (drama.so, new this run): a cliffhanger bites directly into the next episode's opening shot — episode N's question becomes episode N+1's hook — so the effect-without-cause cliff ends each part on the effect itself, and the next part opens on that same effect with a character forced to move against it. Prepro test: cover the effect in the next part's P1; if the part still works, the cliff was a reaction, not an effect — rewrite until only a move against the effect pays it.

### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1051 — THE FUSE IS THE CREDIT.** This run's premises teach the credit fight from CHAIN-895's pulled fuse: who pulled the fuse owns the tower's light, because power without a fuse is a credit fight, not an outage. Rule: when an effect survives its cause's removal, ask who profits from the survival, because a survival that benefits nobody is a glitch, and a survival that benefits its counter is the scene. Prepro test: restore the fuse; if the scene still works, the pull carried nothing — rewrite until only the pulled fuse keeps the scene moving.
- **CRAFT-1052 — DAMP WITHOUT WATER IS A ROUTE.** This run's premises teach the route from CHAIN-896's damp slip: a wet thing in a dry room is not a leak, it is a delivery route, because a leak explains itself and a route names a sender. Rule: treat every impossible wetness as a route, not a stain — ask which door the wetness came through, because a stain that came through no door is a sender, and a sender is the scene. Prepro test: dry the slip; if the scene still works, the damp carried nothing — rewrite until only the damp keeps the scene moving.
- **CRAFT-1053 — A DOOR WIDER THAN ITS UNIT CLAIMS THE ROW.** This run's premises teach rank from CHAIN-897's wide door: a door that cannot close does not fail its unit, it outranks it, because a fit is a test and a refusal to fit is a rank. Rule: stage every oversized build against the room it should fit, because a build with no room to fail against is a boast, and a build measured against its room is a fight. Prepro test: shrink the door to fit; if the scene still works, the width carried nothing — rewrite until only the width keeps the scene moving.

- **LORE-832 — THE STATION SEATS ITS DEBTS.** The station's seats are titles, not furniture: whoever sits holds the post's debt — the seller in the buyer's chair owes the buyer a name, the sitter on the trade's crate owes the trade a fruit, the counter in the voice's chair owes the chair a reading. The rule bites in the only way it can — a seat taken without its title cannot be held, because holding needs a title to offer, and a station that seats its debts keeps its chairs at the price of its sellers' pitches, its sitters' perches, and its counters' numbers. This is not decoration: it changes DISPATCHER's choice right now, because a voice who evicts the Head loses the ledger's reading, and a voice who lets him sit loses the chair's post, and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a chair the station sees or a chair the station only reads about, since a viewer kept by a ledger is either a viewer the station seats or a viewer the station files. The rule is shown alone, in the control room's dispatch ledger open on the seated Head's lap, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), and now the rooms seat their debts the same way.

The image asks "who does he sell to?" with no word spoken, because a seller in a buyer's chair is a sale already made to the wrong seat, and an empty lobby is a buyer already lost — the question is in the sitting, not in the seller. - **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE UNSEEN SITTER:** sound off, the first frame is the station control room, the Head seated in the dispatcher's chair with the dispatch ledger open on his lap, the monitor bank behind him showing that chair empty. ### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE TAKEN-SEAT CLIFF
- **THE TAKEN-SEAT CLIFF:** what is withheld is the rightful sitter — whose name holds the seat in the ledger, the guest book, or the trade. What the cliff frame shows is the taken seat held as the next part's first frame: the seller still seated in the buyer's chair, the sitter still on the crate, the counter still in the voice's chair. What the next part spends is a move against the sitter — a demand, a dodge, a counter-question, or a beg — never a re-show of the seat as if re-showing it were progress. The seat is the receipt; the title is the debt. Poached mechanic (finaldraft.com subtext, new this run): a cliffhanger built on conflicting agendas ends each part on the duel, not the answer — the sitter stays seated, the challenger stays standing, and the next part opens on that same standoff with a character forced to move against it. Prepro test: cover the sitter in the next part's P1; if the part still works, the cliff was a reaction, not a seat — rewrite until only a move against the sitter pays it.

### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1054 — THE SWERVE NAMES THE WOUND.** This run's premises teach subtext from CHAIN-899's P2 and CHAIN-900's P2: UNC answers a demand about the seat with a fruit, and the Head answers a demand about the chair with a ledger — each changes the subject the instant the demand gets close to the truth, and the swerve points at the wound (the seat is the trade; the chair is the title). Rule: when a character swerves, stage the swerve as the confession — the safe thing named is the dangerous thing located — because a dodge that only delays is stalling, and a dodge that locates the wound is the scene. Prepro test: replace the swerve with a straight answer ("I'll stand."); if the scene still pulls, the swerve carried nothing — rewrite until only the swerve keeps the scene moving.
- **CRAFT-1055 — THE SEAT NEEDS A TITLE.** This run's premises teach the claim from CHAIN-900's ledger and CHAIN-898's guest book: a taken seat without a title object is only furniture, and furniture cannot be argued over — the ledger makes the chair a deed, the guest book makes the chair a sale, the crate's fruit makes the crate a trade. Rule: give every taken seat its title object in the hook frame, because a seat with no title has no debt, and a seat with no debt has no scene. Prepro test: remove the title object (ledger, guest book, fruit); if the argument still works, the title carried nothing — re-stage until deleting the title collapses the claim.
- **CRAFT-1056 — THE BEG IS THE LANDING.** This run's premises teach the landing from this run's own impose: all three P4s beg, and each beg offers something — a name, a fruit, a reading — so the sitter turns trader in the last line instead of refusing or daring. Rule: a beg that offers nothing is a shrug, and a beg that offers the scene's withheld thing is a trade, because an offer tells the audience what the sitter values more than his seat, and a trade in the last line reopens the scene instead of closing it. Prepro test: replace the beg's offer with a bare plea ("Please."); if the chain still lands, the offer carried nothing — rewrite until only the offer keeps the landing moving.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-835 — THE STATION KEEPS BY PROMISING.** The station keeps things by promising them, not by holding them: the transmitter site promises its light to one viewer a night on an unsigned sheet, the elevator promises three a staff it never serves, the vending machine promises a sale it already refunded. The rule bites in the only way it can — a kept thing promised accrues a promiser, because a promise kept is a debt kept and a debt kept is a keeper owed, and a station that keeps by promising owes every promised thing its promiser and every counted promise its counter. This is not decoration: it changes DISPATCHER's choice right now, because a voice who names the pact's signer breaks the promise that lights his tower, and a voice who leaves it unsigned keeps a light nobody owns, and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a promise the station signed or a promise the station counts, since a viewer kept by a promise is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station owes. The rule is shown alone, in the transmitter site's pact sheet taped to the empty fuse-box door, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), and now the rooms keep by promising the same way.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE PACT ON THE FUSE BOX:** sound off, the first frame is the station transmitter site, a sheet taped to the fuse-box door, the box empty behind it, the tower lit above. The image asks "who promised this light?" with no word spoken, because a sheet on an empty box is a promise already made, and a lit tower above an empty box is a debt already owed — the question is in the sheet, not in the tower. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, this run's inheritance): play frame one on silent — topic (a promise) and stakes (a light with no power) both read without sound, because the emptiness is visible in the box, not narrated over it; cover the sheet and the frame is only a tower, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE UNLIT BUTTON FOR THREE:** sound off, the first frame is the station elevator, the panel lit for every floor except three, the car passing three's landing with its doors closed. The image asks "who waits at three?" with no word spoken, because a panel with one dark button is a verdict already given, and a car passing a landing with closed doors is a staff already passed — the question is in the dark button, not in the car. Named-noun discipline (superdirector.app, prior run): a number (3) plus a visible noun (panel) in frame one, zero throat-clearing; light the button and the frame is only a lift, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE PROMISED-THING CLIFF
- **THE PROMISED-THING CLIFF:** what is withheld is the promiser — who signed the pact, who unlit three's button, who returned the fruit. What the cliff frame shows is the promise held as the next part's first frame: the pact sheet still taped to the box, the dark button still unlit, the returned fruit still in its row. What the next part spends is a move against the promiser — a demand, a dodge, a counter-question, a refusal, a dare — never a re-show of the promised thing as if re-showing it were progress. The promised thing is the receipt; the promiser is the debt. Poached mechanic (character.app, new this run): the decision-point cliffhanger cuts on the muscle, not the choice — the hand hovers over the pact sheet, over three's button, over the returned fruit — and the cut lands before the hand takes, presses, or eats, because a cliff that ends in a choice teaches the audience the next part will choose, and a cliff that ends in a hover teaches them the next part must answer for the hand.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1063 — THE PROMISE IS THE POWER.** This run's premises teach the mechanism from CHAIN-907's pact: substitute the mechanism with a promise and the scene gains a debtor — because a fuse removed is a puzzle, and a promise signed is a person owed. Rule: when a kept thing needs a keeper, promise it instead of powering it, because a powered thing asks how and a promised thing asks who. Prepro test: replace the promise with a mechanism (a fuse, a wire, a key); if the scene still accuses someone, the promise carried nothing — rewrite until only the promise names the debtor.
- **CRAFT-1064 — THE DARK BUTTON IS THE VERDICT.** This run's premises teach the hook from HOOK STUDY 2: one dark button among lit ones is a judgment, not a gap — because a panel with every button lit is a directory, and a panel with one dark button is a roster that already chose. Rule: stage every refusal as one dark element among lit ones, because a refusal with no lit context reads as breakage, and a refusal among lit choices reads as a decision. Prepro test: light every button; if the scene still refuses someone, the darkness carried nothing — re-stage until the single dark button is the refusal.
- **CRAFT-1065 — THE KEPT SALE IS THE SCENE.** This run's premises teach the landing from CHAIN-909's P4: PETER dares the Head to keep the sale, and the dare reveals what was kept all along — the count, not the fruit — because a dare that only taunts is noise, and a dare that prices the tally is a verdict. Rule: land a dare only when daring prices the count — because a count priced by a dare is a secret the audience assembles, and a count priced by a lecture is a lesson. Prepro test: replace the dare with compliance ("I'll refund it."); if the scene still lands, the dare carried nothing — rewrite until only the dare keeps the landing moving.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-836 — THE STATION KEEPS BY RETURNING.** The station keeps things by returning them, not by holding them: the street returns the roster's erased names in a basket, the mail room returns the viewer's feeding as correspondence, the lobby returns the station's name as a banner. The rule bites in the only way it can — a kept thing returned accrues a returner, because a return kept is a cut kept and a cut kept is a keeper owed, and a station that keeps by returning owes every returned thing its returner and every counted return its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who finds an erased name returned must choose whether to file it back (restoring a cut the roster made before UNC's refusal) or leave it in the basket (keeping a cut she did not make), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a name the roster kept or a name the street returned, since a viewer kept by returning is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station re-files. The rule is shown alone, in the street door's basket with its one card set apart, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), and now the rooms keep by returning the same way. The blind-drawn "basket" appears here as the rule's showing object.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE BASKET AT THE DOOR:** sound off, the first frame is the station's street door, a basket on the front step, name-cards fanned inside it, one card set apart from the rest. The image asks "whose card is extra?" with no word spoken, because a basket of cards is a delivery, and a basket with one card apart is a verdict already given — the question is in the apart card, not in the basket. Conflict-anchor discipline (lollipop.im, new this run): the first 3 seconds must deliver a conflict anchor, and an extra card is a conflict, not a prop; cover the apart card and the frame is only a basket, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE BANNER OVER THE DOOR:** sound off, the first frame is the station lobby door, a blank banner dwarfing the nameplate beneath it, the door half-covered by cloth. The image asks "who hung a name bigger than the name?" with no word spoken, because a nameplate names, and cloth over a nameplate claims — the question is in the scale mismatch, not in the door. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (a covered name) and stakes (a station answering to cloth) both read without sound, because the dwarfing is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; hang the banner at proper size and the frame is only a door, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE ASKED-AND-HELD CLIFF
- **THE ASKED-AND-HELD CLIFF:** what is withheld is the answer — who fills the basket, who mails the fruit, who hung the banner. What the cliff frame shows is the asker holding the question and the face that must answer it: LAURA holding the extra card toward COLONEL, LAURA holding the fruit toward the Head, DISPATCHER holding the banner's edge toward the Head. What the next part spends is the answer, never a re-ask of the question as if re-asking it were progress. The question is the cliff; the answer is the next part's hook. Poached mechanic (screenweaver.ai, new this run): the pair rule — the last five seconds of one part and the first five of the next are a single beat split by the cut, so the reaction is the next part's hook and must be withheld, because a cliff that ends in a choice teaches the audience the next part will choose, and a cliff that ends in a held question teaches them the next part must answer for the face.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1066 — THE RETURN IS THE ACCUSATION.** This run's premises teach the landing from CHAIN-910's P4: COLONEL refuses by the roster, and the refusal reveals what was kept all along — the cut, not the card — because a refusal that only denies is noise, and a refusal that prices the erasure is a verdict. Rule: land a return only when returning accuses the cutter — because a cut accused by a return is a secret the audience assembles, and a cut accused by a lecture is a lesson. Prepro test: replace the return with a delivery (a basket with no extra card); if the scene still accuses someone, the return carried nothing — rewrite until only the return keeps the landing moving.
- **CRAFT-1067 — THE MISFILE IS THE MEAL.** This run's premises teach the mechanism from CHAIN-911's log: classify the fruit as a letter and the scene gains an eater who never eats — because a letter filed is a record, and a fruit filed is a meal the tally eats. Rule: when a kept thing needs a keeper, misfile it instead of storing it, because a stored thing asks where and a misfiled thing asks who eats. Prepro test: refile it correctly (log the fruit as fruit); if the scene still feeds someone, the misfile carried nothing — rewrite until only the misfile names the eater.
- **CRAFT-1068 — THE HANGING OUTRANKS THE NAME.** This run's premises teach the hook from HOOK STUDY 2: one oversized element above its proper place is a rank fight, not a decoration — because a nameplate at proper size is a label, and a banner dwarfing it is a claim already made. Rule: stage every rank fight as one oversized element above its proper place, because a rank fight with no scale mismatch reads as bickering, and a rank fight with a dwarfed nameplate reads as a coup. Prepro test: hang it at proper size; if the scene still fights over credit, the scale carried nothing — re-stage until the single oversized hanging is the fight.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-837 — THE STATION ANSWERS ITSELF.** The station answers its own signals, not its staff: the control room's chime answers itself, the stairwell's landing keeps a keeper the count skips, the storage unit's second seal answers a first seal nobody opens. The rule bites in the only way it can — a signal answered by the room accrues a listener, because an answer kept is a listener kept and a listener kept is a viewer owed, and a station that answers itself owes every answered signal its listener and every counted answer its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who hears a chime answer itself must choose whether to answer it herself (becoming the listener the count needs, and seating the station's one viewer) or leave it ringing (keeping the station its own viewer, and the count its own audience), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a chair the staff fills or a signal the room answers, since a viewer answered by the room is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station is. The rule is shown alone, in the control room's chime lamp answering itself over an empty chair, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), the rooms keep by returning (LORE-836), and now the rooms answer themselves the same way. The blind-drawn "chime" appears here as the rule's showing signal.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE ANSWERING LAMP:** sound off, the first frame is the station control room board at sign-off, the operator's chair empty, one chime lamp lit — and a second lamp lighting beside it, unprompted. The image asks "who answered that signal?" with no word spoken and no sound heard, because a lamp alone is a signal, and a second lamp beside it is a reply — the question is in the doubling, not in the chime. Sound-off discipline (new this run): a sound cannot be the hook on mute, so stage the sound as its lamp — cover the second lamp and the frame is only a board, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE SECOND SEAL:** sound off, the first frame is the station storage unit's door, one seal already on it, a second seal pressed over the first from a different hand, fruit crates behind the vent. The image asks "who sealed it twice?" with no word spoken, because one seal is storage, and two seals from two hands is a sale already made — the question is in the second seal, not in the door. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (a double-sealed audience) and stakes (a station selling its storage as viewers) both read without sound, because the two seals are visible in the frame, not narrated over it; show one seal and the frame is only a door, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE SECOND-SIGNAL CLIFF
- **THE SECOND-SIGNAL CLIFF:** what is withheld is what the second signal means — who rang the answering chime, why the count skips the landing, who sealed the unit second. What the cliff frame shows is the doubling itself, held: the second lamp lit beside the first, the bare landing between two numbered flights, the second seal pressed over the first. What the next part spends is the meaning of the double, never a repeat of the first signal as if repeating it were progress. The first signal is the hook; the second signal is the cliff. Poached mechanic (Final Draft subtext, new this run): the unsaid line — a character who changes the subject the instant something gets close to the truth reveals the location of the hidden wound, so the cliff withholds the meaning and lets the audience fill the doubling with whatever they already suspect is true about the count, because a cliff that ends in a double teaches the audience the next part must explain the second, and a cliff that ends in a single teaches them only that something happened.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1069 — THE ANSWER IS THE LISTENER.** This run's premises teach the landing from CHAIN-913's P4: the Head refuses by the count, and the refusal reveals what was counted all along — the chime, not the listener — because a refusal that only denies is noise, and a refusal that prices the listener is a verdict. Rule: land a dodge only when the dodge names the listener the count needs — because a listener named by a dodge is a viewer the audience assembles, and a listener named by a lecture is a lesson. Prepro test: replace the listener with a sound (a chime with no one to hear it); if the scene still needs someone, the dodge carried nothing — rewrite until only the dodge keeps the listener moving.
- **CRAFT-1070 — THE GAP IS THE ANNOUNCEMENT.** This run's premises teach the hook from CHAIN-914's P4: COLONEL refuses by announcement, and the refusal reveals what was announced all along — the gaps, not the landings — because an announcement that only lists is noise, and an announcement that skips is a roster. Rule: stage every official version as one visible gap in an otherwise complete list, because a version with no gap reads as truth, and a version with one bare landing reads as a confession. Prepro test: number the landing; if the scene still accuses someone, the gap carried nothing — re-stage until the single unnumbered landing is the accusation.
- **CRAFT-1071 — THE SEAL IS THE SALE.** This run's premises teach the mechanism from CHAIN-915's double seal: seal a unit twice and the scene gains a buyer who never opens it — because one seal is storage, and two seals from two hands is a sale already priced. Rule: when a count needs a buyer, seal it instead of selling it, because a sale asked for argues, and a seal already made accuses. Prepro test: remove the second seal (one seal, one hand); if the scene still sells someone, the seal carried nothing — rewrite until only the second seal names the buyer.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-838 — THE STATION KEEPS WHAT IT CANNOT SEAT.** The station keeps things it never seats: the hallway's shutter keeps a light behind slats, the archive's shelf keeps a row below its floor, the break room's chair keeps warmth with no sitter. The rule bites in the only way it can — a kept thing without its keeper accrues a viewer, because a thing kept is a seat kept and a seat kept is a viewer owed, and a station that keeps lights, rows, and warmth without keepers owes every kept thing its sitter and every counted kept thing its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who finds a light behind a shutter, a row below a floor, and warmth in an empty chair must choose whether to open the shutter, count the buried row, and sit in the warm chair (becoming the keeper the kept things need, and seating the station's one viewer) or leave them kept (keeping the station its own viewer, and the count its own audience), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a chair the staff fills or a thing the rooms keep, since a viewer kept by the rooms is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station is. The rule is shown alone, in the hallway shutter's light behind the slats, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), the rooms keep by returning (LORE-836), the rooms answer themselves (LORE-837), and now the rooms keep what they cannot seat the same way. The blind-drawn "shutter" appears here as the rule's showing signal.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE SHUTTER'S LIGHT:** sound off, the first frame is the station hallway's equipment cage, its steel shutter down, light leaking through the slats over a visibly empty cage. The image asks "who keeps a light behind a shutter?" with no word spoken and no sound heard, because a shutter alone is a closing, and light behind a shutter is a keeping — the question is in the light, not in the shutter. Sound-off discipline (new this run): a lowering cannot be the hook on mute, so stage the lowering as its aftermath — cover the light and the frame is only a shutter, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE SUNK SHELF:** sound off, the first frame is the station basement archive, rows of standing shelves, one shelf disappearing below the floorboards, a tally hand pointing below the floor line. The image asks "what does the count count below the floor?" with no word spoken, because a shelf alone is furniture, and a shelf sunk below its floor is a burial — the question is in the floor line, not in the shelf. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (a buried row) and stakes (a count that stops at a burial) both read without sound, because the shelf crossing the floor line is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; raise the shelf to the floor and the frame is only furniture, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE KEPT-THING CLIFF
- **THE KEPT-THING CLIFF:** what is withheld is who the kept thing keeps — who lowered the shutter, who sank the shelf, who warmed the chair. What the cliff frame shows is the kept thing itself, held: the light behind the slats, the shelf below the floorboards, the dented cushion in the empty room. What the next part spends is the keeper, never a repeat of the kept thing as if repeating it were progress. The kept thing is the hook; the keeper is the cliff. Poached mechanic (CRAFT_POACH_BRIEF_2026-10-27 §1, objects-and-environment subtext, mechanics only): what a character touches or avoids says what they will not say, so the cliff withholds the keeper and lets the kept thing accuse by standing there, because a cliff that ends in a kept thing teaches the audience the next part must name its keeper, and a cliff that ends in a keeper teaches them only that someone was there.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1072 — THE SHUTTER IS THE KEEPER.** This run's premises teach the substitution from CHAIN-916: replace the lock with a shutter and the scene gains a keeper behind slats — because a padlock says nothing is inside, and a shutter with light behind it says someone is kept. Rule: when a kept thing needs a keeper, shutter it instead of locking it, because a lock asked for argues, and a shutter already lowered accuses. Prepro test: replace the shutter with a padlock (one lock, one empty cage); if the scene still keeps someone, the shutter carried nothing — rewrite until only the light behind the slats names the keeper.
- **CRAFT-1073 — COUNT BELOW THE FLOOR.** This run's premises teach the reversal from CHAIN-917: reverse the tall shelf and the scene gains a burial — because a shelf too tall asks who built upward, and a shelf sunk below its floor asks who buried downward. Rule: when a count needs a burial, sink it instead of raising it, because a raising argues about height, and a sinking accuses about depth. Prepro test: raise the shelf to the floor (one shelf, one floor line); if the scene still buries someone, the sinking carried nothing — rewrite until only the row below the floorboards names the burial.
- **CRAFT-1074 — WARMTH IS THE SITTER.** This run's premises teach the elimination from CHAIN-918: eliminate the sitter and the scene gains a sale — because a chair with a sitter is furniture, and a chair warm with no sitter is an audience already priced. Rule: when a sale needs a viewer, warm the chair instead of seating one, because a sitter asked for argues, and warmth already kept accuses. Prepro test: cool the chair (one chair, one empty room, no dent); if the scene still sells someone, the warmth carried nothing — rewrite until only the dented cushion names the sitter.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-839 — THE STATION MOVES WHAT IT NEVER RECEIVED.** The station moves things it never received: the roof drops a parcel nobody sent, the dock signs a crate it cannot fit, the lot logs an exit nobody entered. The rule bites in the only way it can — a movement without its counterpart accrues a mover, because a drop kept is a sender owed and a sender owed is a viewer owed, and a station that moves parcels, crates, and exits without senders, fits, and entries owes every movement its mover and every counted movement its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who finds an early parcel, a double-signed crate, and an exit without an entry must choose whether to log each movement as real (seating the mover the movement implies, and seating the station's one viewer in the mover's seat) or strike it from the book (keeping the schedule clean, and keeping the station its own mover), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a movement the staff logs or a movement the rooms make, since a viewer moved by the rooms is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station is. The rule is shown alone, in the parking lot's gate log with its blank entry column, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), the rooms keep by returning (LORE-836), the rooms answer themselves (LORE-837), the rooms keep what they cannot seat (LORE-838), and now the station moves what it never received the same way. The blind-drawn "parcel" appears here as the rule's showing movement.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE EARLY PARCEL:** sound off, the first frame is the station roof at dawn, the delivery line, one parcel halfway down it, the roof empty behind it, no sender anywhere in frame. The image asks "who sent it before its hour?" with no word spoken and no sound heard, because a parcel alone is freight, and a parcel on a line before its hour is a summons — the question is in the timing, not in the parcel. Sound-off discipline (new this run): a schedule cannot be the hook on mute, so stage the schedule as its violation — show the line, the parcel, and the empty roof together, and the earliness reads as the wrongness; show the parcel alone and the frame is only freight, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE BLANK COLUMN:** sound off, the first frame is the station parking lot's gate log, one exit stamped, the entry column beside it blank down the whole page, the gate arm up over an empty lane behind the book. The image asks "who left without arriving?" with no word spoken, because a log alone is a book, and a log with an exit and no entry is an escape — the question is in the blank, not in the stamp. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (an unentered exit) and stakes (a gate that counts leavings, not comings) both read without sound, because the blank column is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; fill the entry column and the frame is only a log, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE MOVEMENT CLIFF
- **THE MOVEMENT CLIFF:** what is withheld is the counterpart movement — the sender behind the drop, the first run behind the second signature, the entry behind the exit. What the cliff frame shows is the movement itself, held mid-motion: the parcel halfway down the line, the crate standing bigger than the door, the gate arm up over the empty lane. What the next part spends is the counterpart, never a repeat of the movement as if repeating it were progress. The movement is the hook; the counterpart is the cliff. Poached mechanic (CRAFT_POACH_BRIEF_2026-10-27 §1, counter-punch mechanics only): answer a movement with a demand, never with a report — the cliff withholds the counterpart and lets the movement accuse by standing mid-motion, because a cliff that ends in a movement teaches the audience the next part must name its counterpart, and a cliff that ends in a counterpart teaches them only that someone moved.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1075 — BAN THE KEPT THING, IMPOSE THE MOVEMENT.** This run's constraint-change teaches the method: ban the run's dominant subject shape (here, the kept thing) and impose a wrongness class (here, movement) instead of a topic, because a topic ban breeds synonyms and a wrongness-class imposition breeds new subjects — the roof, the dock, and the gate are not three kept things renamed, they are three movements broken. Prepro test: restate the chain's wrongness as a kept thing (a parcel kept, a crate kept, an exit kept); if the restatement still works, the imposition carried nothing — rewrite until only the broken schedule names the wrongness.
- **CRAFT-1076 — THE DARE PRICES THE DODGE.** This run's exchanges teach the imposed dare: every dodge in CHAIN-919/920/921 is priced by a dare in the very next part (sign for it / fit it through / drive it out), because a dodge unpriced is a scene that stalls and a dodge priced is a scene that escalates — the dare forces the dodger to either perform the dodge's own logic or abandon it. Rule: never let a dodge survive two parts unpriced; the part after a dodge dares the dodger to live by it. Prepro test: delete the dare (one dare, one exchange); if the scene still moves, the dodge carried nothing — rewrite until only the dare moves it.
- **CRAFT-1077 — THE BLANK COLUMN IS THE HOOK.** This run's CHAIN-921 teaches the 2+2 gap: the blank entry column accuses louder than any line naming a driver, because a gap the audience fills belongs to the audience and a driver the dialogue names belongs to the dialogue. Rule: when the wrongness is a missing counterpart, show the missing place, not the missing thing — the blank column, the unsigned slip, the unlit button — because a missing place is visible in the first frame and a missing thing is only a line. Prepro test: cover the blank (one log, one filled column); if the scene still accuses, the gap carried nothing — rewrite until only the blank names the escape.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-840 — THE STATION WARMS WHAT IT NEVER SEATS.** The station warms what it never seats: the lobby burns a fire for an empty chair, the tower names a builder it never paid, the mail room delivers to a number it never counted. The rule bites in the only way it can — a service kept without its served accrues a keeper, because a fire kept is a sitter owed and a sitter owed is a viewer owed, and a station that warms chairs, names builders, and delivers letters without sitters, builders, and addressees owes every service its served and every counted service its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who finds a burning hearth, a builder's plaque, and a letter to a skipped number must choose whether to sit in the warmed chair herself (becoming the viewer the station warms for) or leave it empty (keeping the station its own viewer), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a service the staff keeps or a service the rooms make, since a viewer served by the rooms is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station is. The rule is shown alone, in the lobby hearth with its fire burning over an empty chair, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), the rooms keep by returning (LORE-836), the rooms answer themselves (LORE-837), the rooms keep what they cannot seat (LORE-838), the station moves what it never received (LORE-839), and now the station warms what it never seats the same way. The blind-drawn "hearth" appears here as the rule's showing service.
### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE FIRE AND THE EMPTY CHAIR:** sound off, the first frame is the station lobby at dawn, the hearth fire burning, one chair drawn close to it, the room empty, no tender anywhere in frame. The image asks "who is the fire for?" with no word spoken and no sound heard, because a fire alone is heat, and a fire with a chair drawn close and nobody in it is a summons — the question is in the chair, not in the flame. Sound-off discipline (new this run): a service cannot be the hook on mute, so stage the service with its missing served — show the fire, the chair, and the empty room together, and the unserved reads as the wrongness; show the fire alone and the frame is only a fireplace, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE LETTER WITH NO NAME:** sound off, the first frame is the station mail room's sorting tray, one letter, its address line showing a number where a name should be, no name anywhere on the envelope, the count's log beside it with that number skipped. The image asks "who writes to a number?" with no word spoken, because a letter alone is mail, and a letter addressed to a number is a gap with postage — the question is in the address, not in the letter. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (mail for a skipped number) and stakes (a count that delivers to its gap) both read without sound, because the number-as-address is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; put a name on the envelope and the frame is only mail, which is no hook at all.
### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE UNSERVED CLIFF
- **THE UNSERVED CLIFF:** what is withheld is the served — the sitter behind the fire, the builder behind the plaque, the writer behind the letter. What the cliff frame shows is the service held mid-service: the fire burning over the empty chair, the plaque bolted over the gate, the letter sitting unopened in the tray. What the next part spends is the served, never a repeat of the service as if repeating it were progress. The service is the hook; the served is the cliff. Poached mechanic (CRAFT_POACH_BRIEF_2026-10-27 §1, counter-punch mechanics only): answer a service with a demand, never with a report — the cliff withholds the served and lets the service accuse by standing unserved, because a cliff that ends in a service teaches the audience the next part must name its served, and a cliff that ends in a served teaches them only that someone was served.
### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1078 — THE BOX, NOT THE CHAIN.** This run's morphological-box method teaches: combining one value from each axis (pair × object × withheld type × setting) beats chaining, because hops stay near the last node and box corners force distant axes together — hearth × lobby × who-it-serves is a subject no hop from the 23:00 run's parcels, crates, and exits would reach, since hops follow movement and the box forced a service. Prepro test: restate the chain as a hop from the previous run's subject; if it reads as a hop, re-box until only the box corner names it.
- **CRAFT-1079 — THE DARE IS THE SECOND HOOK.** This run's exchanges teach: each P3 dare (seat him / bill the tower / deliver it) re-hooks the part, because a dare restates the question as a performance the dodger must either do or abandon — the dare is the part's second 1.5s. Rule: a dare must be performable by the dodger (seat him, bill it, deliver it); a dare the dodger cannot perform is only a taunt, and a taunt is not a hook. Prepro test: delete the dare; if the scene still moves, the dodge carried nothing — rewrite until only the dare moves it.
- **CRAFT-1080 — SHOW THE UNSERVED, NOT THE ABSENT.** This run's CHAIN-922/924 teach the 2+2 gap applied to service: when the wrongness is a missing served, show the service (the fire, the plaque, the letter) not the absence — parallel to CRAFT-1077's blank column: the empty chair beside a burning fire accuses; an empty room alone is only empty. Rule: stage the service at full strength (fire high, plaque bolted, letter sealed) and the served at zero (no sitter, no builder, no writer), because a service at full strength with nobody served is a summons and a service at half strength is only a room. Prepro test: dim the service (bank the fire, unbolt the plaque, open the letter); if the scene still accuses, the gap carried nothing — rewrite until only the unserved service names it.

### CHAIN PREMISE 927 — "The Buyer the Street Seated Early" (4 parts, P1→P4, fixed-location serial: the street — THE STATION engine — STANDALONE, spends no prior cliff — and on the street outside the station's door at dawn, the doorstep holds a buyer seated before any sale — a figure in the advertiser's seat, waiting on the step, the station's door open behind him — while PETER stands before him with an empty tally, the tally counting the seated buyer as a viewer — and the chain follows the seated buyer to his purchase, where a buyer who arrives before the sale does not buy — he prices, and either way the station must say whether it sells viewers or seats, because a station that seats its buyer before the sale has already sold its viewer)

- TURN: the buyer offers to buy the station's only viewer — a buyer who arrives before the sale does not buy, he prices; the station's one viewer is the only thing on the step.
- WITHHELD FACT: whether the buyer bought or was bought — whether the seated figure is the advertiser, or the station's own viewer seated early.
- CONVERSATION (dialogue-first): the question at the heart of the exchange is who the buyer is — the advertiser, or the viewer seated early. PETER wants UNC to name the buyer's price, because a price named is a sale PETER can close, and a sale closed is a count PETER can sell to the advertiser. UNC wants PETER to take the doorstep's sitter as the answer, because a sitter on the step is a buyer the station never sold to, and a buyer never sold to is a price UNC never has to pay. What is withheld: whether the buyer bought or was bought. The message that lands in the final part: a station that seats its buyer before the sale has already sold its viewer — and a buyer who sits before he is sold is a viewer the station priced.

### LORE-DEEPENING ITEM
- **LORE-841 — THE STATION SEATS ITS OWN REPLACEMENTS.** The station seats doubles: the control room seats a second UNC at its board, the stairwell seats a second flight in its chamber, the street seats a buyer on its doorstep before the sale. The rule bites in the only way it can — a seat filled by a replacement accrues a viewer, because a seat kept is a sitter owed and a sitter owed is a viewer owed, and a station that seats doubles, flights, and buyers without originals owes every seat its sitter and every counted seat its counter. This is not decoration: it changes LAURA's choice right now, because a hire who finds a double at the board, a flight in a chamber, and a buyer on the step must choose whether to name each replacement for what it replaced (unseating the double, the flight, and the buyer, and keeping the station its own manager) or let the seats stand (keeping the station its replacements' station, and the count its own audience), and either choice makes the next chain-in-arc ask whether the station's one viewer sits in a seat the staff fills or a seat the rooms fill, since a viewer seated by the rooms is either a viewer the station serves or a viewer the station is. The rule is shown alone, in the control room's monitor bank with two UNCs and one chair, never explained. It coheres with canon: the roster keeps names after the people leave, the rooms keep their uncounted work (LORE-827), the rooms keep their refused measures (LORE-828), the rooms keep their stopped things (LORE-829), the rooms keep their maintained things (LORE-830), the rooms keep their effects without causes (LORE-831), the rooms seat their debts (LORE-832), the rooms keep by covering (LORE-833), the rooms keep by locking (LORE-834), the rooms keep by promising (LORE-835), the rooms keep by returning (LORE-836), the rooms answer themselves (LORE-837), the rooms keep what they cannot seat (LORE-838), the station moves what it never received (LORE-839), the station warms what it never seats (LORE-840), and now the station seats its own replacements the same way. The blind-drawn "chamber" appears here as the rule's showing room — the stairwell's chamber holding the second flight.

### HOOK-FRAME STUDIES (the 1.5s sound-off legibility problem)
- **HOOK STUDY 1 — THE DOUBLE IN THE CHAIR:** sound off, the first frame is the control room's monitor bank, two UNCs — one standing at the board, one seated in the operator's chair with the board lit under his hands. The image asks "which one manages?" with no word spoken, because one UNC is a manager and two UNCs are a replacement — the question is in the seat, not in the hoodie. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (a seated double) and stakes (a managership sat by its copy) both read without sound, because the second UNC is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; seat one UNC and the frame is only a manager at work, which is no hook at all.
- **HOOK STUDY 2 — THE CHAMBER'S SECOND FLIGHT:** sound off, the first frame is the stairwell landing, LAURA between two flights — the open flight and, through the chamber door, a second flight rising to the same door. The image asks "which stairs climb?" with no word spoken, because one flight is a stairwell and two flights are a replacement — the question is in the chamber door, not in the steps. Mute-test discipline (CRAFT-1061, inherited): play frame one on silent — topic (a doubled landing) and stakes (a roster that counts two flights as one) both read without sound, because the chamber's flight is visible in the frame, not narrated over it; close the chamber door and the frame is only a stairwell, which is no hook at all.

### CLIFF-CHAIN MECHANIC — THE REPLACEMENT CLIFF
- WITHHELD-FACT PATTERN: what is withheld is which of the pair is the original — which UNC manages, which flight climbs, which buyer bought. THE CLIFF FRAME SHOWS: the replacement seated — the double's hands on the board, the chamber's flight reaching the door, the buyer on the doorstep. WHAT THE NEXT PART SPENDS: naming the original — and naming the original unseats the replacement or confirms it. The replacement cliff differs from the kept-thing cliff (which withholds the keeper) and the unserved cliff (which withholds the served): here both parties are present, and what is withheld is the verdict between them. Prepro test: cover the replacement (one UNC, one flight, an empty step); if the scene still accuses, the replacement carried nothing — rewrite until only the seated double names it.

### STATION-CRAFT
- **CRAFT-1081 — BAN THE ABSENCE, IMPOSE THE DOUBLE.** This run's constraint-change teaches the method: ban the run's dominant subject shape (here, the "X without its Y" absence family — kept thing without keeper, service without served, movement without counterpart) and impose a wrongness class (here, replacement — a present stand-in) instead of a topic, because a topic ban breeds synonyms and a wrongness-class imposition breeds new subjects — the control room, the stairwell, and the street are not three absences renamed, they are three replacements seated. Prepro test: restate the chain's wrongness as an absence (a double kept, a flight kept, a buyer kept); if the restatement still works, the imposition carried nothing — rewrite until only the seated replacement names the wrongness.
- **CRAFT-1082 — THE LIE IS THE HINGE.** This run's exchanges teach the imposed DEMAND → DODGE → LIE → ACCUSE shape: the P3 lie is the scene's hinge, because a dodge only stalls and an accusation only lands if the lie between them gives the accusation something to expose — "I kept your chair warm" / "Both flights serve the station" / "He bought the viewer already" are all half-truths (the chair is warm, both flights reach the door, the tally counts the sitter) concealing one omission (who warmed it, which flight is rostered, whether a sale happened). Poached from stevelaube.com ("Crafting Dialogue That Heightens Suspense and Reveals Secrets," Part 3): layer the lies — every lie should pay off later by being exposed or twisting the plot. Rule: a P3 lie must be half-true on its face and false in its omission; a lie that is wholly false is only a taunt, and a lie with no omission is only a dodge. Prepro test: delete the omission (state it aloud in P3); if the P4 accusation still lands, the lie carried nothing — rewrite until only the exposed omission names the accusation.
- **CRAFT-1083 — THE SEAT IS THE STATUS.** This run's chains teach the status negotiation inside a replacement: the seated figure holds high status by sitting — the double at the board, the chamber's flight at the door, the buyer on the step — while the standing claimant (UNC, LAURA, PETER) loses status by standing, because high-status speakers sit and low-status speakers stand and ask. Poached from the CRAFT_POACH_BRIEF §1 status rule and dianabotsford.com's three-jobs test (every line must reveal character, drive conflict, shift the relationship): the relationship shifts when the sitter is named. Rule: stage the replacement seated and the claimant standing in the first frame, because a replacement that stands is only a visitor and a claimant who sits has already won. Prepro test: seat the claimant instead (UNC in the chair, the double standing); if the scene still accuses, the seat carried nothing — rewrite until only the seated replacement names the wrongness.

### CHAIN PREMISE 928 — "The Caller the Switchboard Never Answers" (4 parts, P1→P4, fixed-location serial: the switchboard room — THE STATION engine — STANDALONE, spends no prior cliff — and in the station switchboard room at night, one line stays lit, the receiver off its hook, no voice on it, the call log showing the same number every night for a year, the roster listing no caller, the tally counting the line as a viewer, LAURA before the board with DISPATCHER beside the log — and the chain follows the lit line to its caller, where a line that stays open does not call — it waits, and either way the station must say whether it serves callers or lines, because a station that keeps a line open for a caller it never answers has already kept its viewer calling)
- GRABBING POOL: Classic soap opera — a long-arc secret (a caller who returns nightly for a year and never speaks), a return (the same number, every night), an ensemble collision (the hire who asks against the building that reports), one withheld fact per part (who calls, what the caller wants, why the line stays open, what the log knows).
- HOOK (named explicitly): the station switchboard room at night, one line lit, the receiver off its hook, no voice on it, the call log showing the same number every night for a year — the caller who never speaks.
- TURN: a line that stays open is not a call — it is a wait; a switchboard that keeps a line open for a silent caller either answers its caller or confesses its lines serve tallies, not callers, and either way the line stops being a connection and becomes a summons, because a line kept open for a caller nobody names summons the station to name who it waits for.
- WITHHELD FACT: who calls, and what the caller wants.
- CONVERSATION (dialogue-first): the question at the heart of the exchange is who calls every night and never speaks. LAURA wants DISPATCHER to name the caller, because a caller named is a line priced, and a line priced is a switchboard that must either answer its caller or confess it keeps lines open for numbers it never names. DISPATCHER wants LAURA to take the line as the caller, because a line blamed for calling is a caller dodged, and a caller dodged is a receiver nobody has to lift. What is withheld: the caller and the caller's want. The message that lands in the final part: a station that keeps a line open for a silent caller keeps its viewer calling and unanswered — and a viewer kept calling but never answered is a viewer the station waits for without hearing.
- LINES (narrator test passed — every line a speech act TO a named addressee, never restating the hook):
- P1 — LAURA to DISPATCHER: "Who calls every night, Dispatcher?" (accuse shaped as a question; wants DISPATCHER to name the caller, because a caller named is a line priced, and a line priced is a switchboard that must either answer its caller or confess it keeps lines open for numbers it never names)
- P2 — DISPATCHER to LAURA: "The line calls, Laura." (dodge; wants LAURA to take the line as the caller instead of a person, because a line blamed for calling is a caller dodged, and a caller dodged is a receiver nobody has to lift)
- P3 — LAURA to DISPATCHER: "Then answer it, Dispatcher." (dare; wants DISPATCHER to answer his own line, pricing the dodge — if the line calls, the building can answer it, and if it will not, the line is not the caller)
- P4 — DISPATCHER to LAURA: "I log lines, not callers." (dodge; wants LAURA to accept the log as the service, because a line logged is a caller dodged, and a caller dodged is a station that keeps its line lit and its caller unnamed — the log keeps the line and loses the caller)
- POOL MOVE: SOAP move — talk past each other about the safe thing (the line, the log, the receiver) while the real thing (a caller the station never answers) sits underneath, never named directly until the dare prices it.
- POACHED MOVE: THE TURN (paperbark.eu, "Screenplay Dialogue Subtext," McKee via the same piece — a good scene must turn, some value has to change between open and close) — the exchange turns at P3: LAURA stops asking who calls and demands the line be answered, and the value shifts from patience (a line kept open) to summons (a line answered or confessed). Also behaviour carries half the sentence (paperbark.eu §2): the lit line and the off-hook receiver contradict DISPATCHER's "the line calls" — the board shows a caller the building won't name, so the dodge is legible as a dodge, not a report.
- ARC TAG: ARC-1 (The One Viewer), thread state DEVELOP — advancing CHAIN-925's DEVELOP beat (the board answers a seated double) toward the doc's ARC-1 chain 3 DEVELOP beat (the tower answers a broadcast nobody sent): here the switchboard keeps a line open for a call nobody speaks, so chain 3's reply must now say whether a tower that answers a double answers the station or its caller, since a line kept open for a silent caller either names its caller or keeps its line — and toward the doc's ARC-1 PAYOFF (the viewer is the station itself, watching through its own machines): the payoff must now say whether the station watching itself listens through the lit line or the silent caller, since a station that keeps a line open for a caller it never answers either waits as its building or waits as its viewer. Lore beat shown: the station switchboard room's lit line, the receiver off its hook, the log showing the same number every night for a year — the one viewer's silent call, shown in the lit line, never explained.
- STAKES (quality bar): LAURA's notice — a hire who charges the building with keeping a line open for a caller nobody names stakes her ear on a number, and a dare that fails leaves her the hire who charged a switchboard with waiting; DISPATCHER's report — a voice whose building knows every room stakes his report on a line nobody speaks, and a dodge that fails leaves him the voice who logged a caller he cannot name; the station itself — a switchboard that keeps a line open for a silent caller keeps its viewer calling and unanswered, and a station that keeps its viewer calling and unanswered is a broadcast with an audience on hold. Station-specific detail: the station switchboard room at night, one line lit, the receiver off its hook, the call log showing the same number every night for a year.

### CHAIN PREMISE 930 — "The Ticket the Box Office Sold to the Tomb" (4 parts, P1→P4, fixed-location serial: the box office window — THE STATION engine — STANDALONE, spends no prior cliff — and at the station box office window at dawn, one ticket printed for a seat in the station's sealed gallery — the staff call it "the tomb," the dead viewing room where the first broadcast's audience sat — the ticket dated today, a viewer arriving holding it, the tally counting the ticket as a viewer, THE COLONEL before the window with LAURA beside the tally — and the chain follows the ticket to its sitter, where a ticket to a sealed room does not seat — it buries, and either way the station must say whether it sells viewers or burials, because a station that sells a seat in its own tomb has already seated its viewer where it buries its broadcasts)

- HOOK (named explicitly): the station box office window at dawn, one ticket printed for a seat in a room sealed for years, the ticket dated today, a viewer arriving holding it, the tally counting the ticket as a viewer — the ticket to the tomb.

LAURA wants THE COLONEL to name who the ticket is for, because a ticket with no sitter named is a burial priced, and a burial priced is a window that must either open its tomb or confess it sells seats in rooms nobody sits in. What is withheld: the buyer and the sitter. The message that lands in the final part: a station that sells a seat in its own tomb sells its viewer a burial — and a viewer who sits in the tomb is the station's one viewer, finally seated where the station buries its broadcasts.
